subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define physical examination. Explain its purposes, the methods (techniques) of physical examination and the role of the nurse. (2 + 3 + 6 + 4)

diagram.caption: Techniques of physical examination
labels: auscultation with diaphragm and bell of stethoscope

answer_html:
Introduction Health assessment has two parts – the health history (subjective data) and the physical examination (objective data). A careful physical examination gives the nurse reliable information for nursing diagnoses, care planning and early detection of complications.

A. Definition (2 marks)

  • Physical examination is a systematic, head-to-toe or system-wise examination of the body using the techniques of inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation (with olfaction), to collect objective data about the person's health status
  • It may be complete (comprehensive, on admission), focused (on one problem or body system) or ongoing (repeated to monitor change)

B. Purposes (3 marks)

  1. To collect baseline data about the patient's health status
  2. To confirm or add to the information obtained in the health history
  3. To detect early signs of disease – screening (e.g. breast lump, high BP)
  4. To help in medical diagnosis and to identify nursing diagnoses
  5. To plan and evaluate nursing care and the patient's response to treatment
  6. To detect changes in condition (deterioration or improvement) quickly
  7. For fitness certificates – admission to school or college, employment, insurance, sports
  8. For medico-legal purposes (injury, assault cases)
  9. To give health education – the examination is a good time to teach (breast self-examination, foot care)
  10. For research and record keeping

C. Methods of physical examination (6 marks)

1. Inspection

  • Visual examination of the body – the first and most frequently used technique; also uses hearing and smell
  • Starts with the general survey and continues part by part
  • Requirements: good light (natural daylight is best), adequate exposure of the part, a warm room, patient in a comfortable position
  • What is observed: colour, size, shape, symmetry, position, movement, contour, skin lesions, swelling, scars, deformities, discharges; compare both sides
  • Instruments: penlight/torch, otoscope, ophthalmoscope, nasal speculum

2. Palpation

  • Examination by touch using the hands
  • Parts of the hand used:
    • fingertips – fine discrimination: texture, pulses, lymph nodes, size of lumps
    • palmar (ulnar) surface – vibrations (vocal fremitus, thrills)
    • dorsum (back) of the hand – temperature
  • Types:
    • light palpation – about 1 cm deep; superficial tenderness, muscle guarding, skin texture
    • deep palpation – about 4 cm deep; organs (liver, spleen, kidneys) and masses
    • bimanual palpation – using both hands (kidneys, uterus)
  • What is assessed: temperature, moisture, texture, tenderness, swelling, masses (size, shape, consistency, mobility), pulsations, organ size, crepitus, vibration
  • Precautions: warm hands, short nails, explain first, palpate tender areas last, watch the face for pain

3. Percussion

  • Tapping the body surface to produce sounds and vibrations that show the density of underlying structures (air, fluid or solid), and the size and borders of organs
  • Methods:
    • direct (immediate) – tapping the surface directly with fingertips (e.g. over sinuses)
    • indirect (mediate) – the middle finger of the non-dominant hand (pleximeter) is placed firmly on the skin and struck on its distal joint by the tip of the middle finger of the dominant hand (plexor), using a quick, loose wrist movement
    • blunt (fist) percussion – a fist strikes the other hand placed over the area – e.g. renal angle (costovertebral) tenderness
  • Percussion sounds:
    • resonance – normal lung
    • hyper-resonance – emphysema, pneumothorax
    • tympany – air-filled stomach and bowel
    • dullness – liver, fluid, solid mass, full bladder
    • flatness – muscle, bone

4. Auscultation

  • Listening to sounds produced inside the body – heart, lungs, bowel and blood vessels – usually with a stethoscope
  • Diaphragm – for high-pitched sounds: breath sounds, bowel sounds, normal heart sounds (S1, S2)
  • Bell – for low-pitched sounds: murmurs, extra heart sounds (S3, S4), bruits
  • Requirements: quiet room, stethoscope placed on bare skin (not over clothes), warm chest piece, patient breathing normally or as instructed
  • Sounds are described by pitch, loudness (intensity), quality, duration and timing

5. Olfaction (smell)

  • Detecting abnormal body odours:
    • fruity (acetone) breath – diabetic ketoacidosis
    • ammonia/urine-like breath – kidney failure (uraemia)
    • alcohol – intoxication
    • foul-smelling wound or discharge – infection (anaerobic organisms)
    • musty breath – liver failure
    • faecal odour of vomit – intestinal obstruction

Sequence

  • Usually inspection → palpation → percussion → auscultation
  • For the abdomen: inspection → auscultation → percussion → palpation (so that palpation does not change bowel sounds)
  • Approach – head-to-toe (cephalocaudal), or body-system approach in focused assessment

Equipment

  • Thermometer, stethoscope, sphygmomanometer, pulse oximeter, penlight, tongue depressor, otoscope, ophthalmoscope, tuning fork, percussion (reflex) hammer, measuring tape, weighing machine and height scale, Snellen chart, cotton wisps and safety pin, gloves, lubricant, vaginal speculum, swabs, specimen containers, kidney tray, drapes, watch with a second hand

D. Role of the nurse (4 marks)

1. Before the examination

  • Explain the purpose and procedure; obtain consent; answer questions and reduce anxiety
  • Ensure privacy (screens, closed door) and a warm, well-lit, quiet room
  • Ask the patient to empty the bladder; collect a urine sample if required
  • Help the patient to change into a gown; drape so that only the part examined is exposed
  • Arrange the equipment tray; check that instruments work
  • Record vital signs, height, weight and SpO₂
  • Arrange a female attendant (chaperone) when a male doctor examines a female patient

2. During the examination

  • Position the patient as needed (sitting, supine, dorsal recumbent, lithotomy, Sims', prone, knee-chest) and give support
  • Hand instruments to the examiner in order; maintain hand hygiene and wear gloves where needed
  • Observe the patient's reactions; give reassurance; cover parts not being examined
  • In everyday ward work the nurse performs general and focused assessments herself

3. After the examination

  • Help the patient to dress and make them comfortable
  • Clean, disinfect and replace equipment; dispose of waste correctly
  • Label and send specimens to the laboratory
  • Document findings accurately, using correct terms; report abnormal findings promptly
  • Use the findings to frame nursing diagnoses and plan care

E. Principles to follow during physical examination

  • Follow a systematic order (head to toe) so that nothing is missed
  • Compare both sides of the body for symmetry
  • Begin with the least uncomfortable parts; examine painful areas last
  • Keep the patient warm, covered and comfortable; allow rest for weak or elderly patients
  • Maintain hand hygiene; clean the stethoscope and other equipment between patients
  • Respect cultural and religious beliefs; offer a same-sex examiner or chaperone
  • Record findings in clear, descriptive terms (e.g. "liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin") – not just "normal" or "good"

F. Positions used for physical examination

Position Parts examined
Sitting head, neck, back, posterior and anterior chest, lungs, breasts, axillae, heart, upper limbs, reflexes
Supine head, neck, anterior chest, breasts, heart, abdomen, limbs, peripheral pulses
Dorsal recumbent head, neck, chest, female genitalia (for patients who cannot tolerate lithotomy)
Lithotomy female genitalia, vagina and cervix (speculum examination)
Sims' (left lateral) rectum and vagina
Prone back, spine, hip joint
Knee-chest rectum (rarely used – tiring)
Standing gait, posture, spine, hernia, varicose veins

Conclusion Physical examination is the systematic collection of objective data by inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation and olfaction; it serves diagnosis, planning and evaluation of care, and the nurse prepares the patient and environment, assists or performs the examination and records and reports the findings.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Describe the assessment of the abdomen – preparation, sequence of examination, and normal and abnormal findings.

diagram.caption: Quadrants and nine regions of the abdomen

answer_html:
Introduction Abdominal assessment helps detect problems of the gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, urinary and reproductive organs. It follows a special order – inspection, auscultation, percussion and palpation (IAPP) – because palpation and percussion can change bowel sounds.

A. Landmarks and divisions

1. Four quadrants (by two imaginary lines crossing at the umbilicus)

  • Right upper (RUQ) – liver, gallbladder, duodenum, head of pancreas, right kidney
  • Left upper (LUQ) – stomach, spleen, body and tail of pancreas, left kidney
  • Right lower (RLQ) – caecum, appendix, right ovary and tube
  • Left lower (LLQ) – sigmoid colon, left ovary and tube

2. Nine regions – right and left hypochondriac, epigastric, right and left lumbar, umbilical, right and left iliac, and hypogastric (suprapubic)

3. Landmarks – xiphoid process, costal margins, umbilicus, anterior superior iliac spines, symphysis pubis

B. Preparation

  1. Explain the procedure; ask about pain and ask the patient to point to it
  2. Empty the bladder before the examination
  3. Position – supine, a small pillow under the head and under the knees (relaxes abdominal muscles), arms by the sides
  4. Expose the abdomen from the xiphoid to the symphysis pubis; drape the chest and groin
  5. Warm room, warm hands and stethoscope; short nails
  6. Privacy; chaperone when needed
  7. Examine painful areas last; watch the patient's face for discomfort
  8. Equipment – stethoscope, measuring tape, marker pen, penlight, gloves

C. Sequence of examination

1. Inspection

  • Contour – flat, rounded, scaphoid (sunken – malnutrition) or protuberant/distended (the "5 Fs" – fat, fluid, flatus, faeces, fetus)
  • Symmetry – bulges, masses, visible organs
  • Skin – colour (jaundice), scars, striae (silvery – old; purple – Cushing's syndrome), dilated veins (caput medusae in portal hypertension), rashes, bruising
    • Cullen's sign (bluish periumbilical discoloration) and Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising) – bleeding into the abdomen, haemorrhagic pancreatitis
  • Umbilicus – normally midline and inverted; everted in ascites or hernia
  • Movements – visible peristalsis (intestinal obstruction), pulsations (aortic aneurysm), movement with respiration
  • Hernias – ask the patient to cough or raise the head

2. Auscultation (before percussion and palpation)

  • Bowel sounds – use the diaphragm; start in the RLQ (ileocaecal valve) and listen in all four quadrants
    • normal: irregular gurgles, about 5–35 per minute
    • hyperactive: diarrhoea, gastroenteritis, early intestinal obstruction (loud rumbling – borborygmi)
    • hypoactive: after surgery, constipation
    • absent: listen for up to 5 minutes before saying absent – paralytic ileus, peritonitis
  • Vascular sounds – use the bell over the aorta, renal, iliac and femoral arteries: a bruit suggests narrowing or aneurysm
  • Friction rubs over the liver or spleen (rare)

3. Percussion

  • Tympany is the predominant sound (gas in the bowel); dullness over organs, masses, fluid, faeces and a full bladder
  • Liver span – percuss downwards in the right midclavicular line from lung resonance to liver dullness (upper border, about the 5th intercostal space) and upwards from tympany to dullness (lower border, near the costal margin); normal span 6–12 cm
  • Spleen – dullness in the lower left intercostal spaces (Traube's space) suggests enlargement
  • Ascites – shifting dullness and fluid thrill
  • Kidneys – fist (blunt) percussion over the costovertebral angle; tenderness suggests pyelonephritis

4. Palpation

  • Light palpation (1–2 cm) in all quadrants – tenderness, muscle guarding, superficial masses
  • Deep palpation (4–5 cm) – organs and deeper masses (size, shape, consistency, mobility, tenderness)
  • Liver – right hand below the right costal margin; ask the patient to breathe deeply; normally not palpable or only a smooth, firm, non-tender edge
  • Spleen – normally not palpable; palpable only when enlarged
  • Kidneys – bimanual palpation; usually not palpable
  • Bladder – palpable above the symphysis when distended (retention of urine)
  • Aorta – pulsation felt in the upper abdomen, slightly left of midline
  • Hernial orifices – inguinal and femoral regions

Special signs

  • Rebound tenderness (Blumberg's sign) – pain on quick release of pressure – peritoneal irritation
  • McBurney's point tenderness – one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus – appendicitis
  • Rovsing's sign – pressure in the LLQ causes pain in the RLQ – appendicitis
  • Murphy's sign – patient stops breathing in when the RUQ is pressed – acute cholecystitis
  • Psoas and obturator signs – appendicitis (pelvic or retrocaecal)
  • Board-like rigidity and guarding – peritonitis

D. Normal findings (summary)

  • Abdomen flat or rounded, symmetrical, umbilicus midline and inverted, no visible peristalsis
  • Bowel sounds 5–35/min, no bruits
  • Tympany over most of the abdomen; liver span 6–12 cm
  • Soft, non-tender, no masses; liver, spleen and kidneys not palpable

E. Documentation (example) "Abdomen flat, symmetrical, no scars. Bowel sounds present in all quadrants, 12/min. Tympanic on percussion; liver span 9 cm. Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly or masses."

F. Nurse's role

  • Prepare the patient correctly (empty bladder, position, exposure)
  • Report abnormal findings – absent bowel sounds after surgery, distension, rigidity, rebound tenderness
  • Measure abdominal girth daily in ascites at the same level (mark the site)
  • Re-assess regularly after abdominal surgery and in patients with acute abdomen

G. Common abnormal findings and their significance

Finding Possible cause
Generalised distension ascites, intestinal obstruction, gas, obesity
Visible peristalsis intestinal obstruction
Absent bowel sounds paralytic ileus, peritonitis
Bruit over the aorta aortic aneurysm, narrowing
Enlarged liver (hepatomegaly) hepatitis, heart failure, liver cancer
Enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) malaria, leukaemia, portal hypertension
Shifting dullness, fluid thrill ascites
Rigidity, rebound tenderness peritonitis
Pulsatile mass abdominal aortic aneurysm
Suprapubic dullness retention of urine

H. Measuring abdominal girth (ascites)

  1. Patient supine, bladder empty
  2. Pass a measuring tape around the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus (widest part)
  3. Mark the site on the skin with a marker so the same level is used every time
  4. Measure at the same time each day, with the same tape, and record

I. Special groups

  • Children – the abdomen is normally protuberant; breathing is mainly abdominal; distract the child during palpation
  • Pregnant women – fundal height and fetal parts are assessed instead of deep palpation
  • Elderly – weaker abdominal muscles; pain and guarding may be less marked even in serious disease

J. Precautions

  • Do not palpate deeply over a pulsatile mass (risk of rupture of an aneurysm)
  • In a child with a suspected Wilms' tumour, avoid palpating the abdomen, as the tumour may rupture or spread
  • Avoid repeated deep palpation in suspected appendicitis; one gentle examination by the doctor is enough
  • Stop if pain is severe; watch the facial expression and guarding throughout
  • Hernias and varicose veins are best seen with the patient standing
  • Remember referred pain – gallbladder pain may be felt in the right shoulder, and pain of a heart attack may be felt in the epigastrium
  • In ascites, record weight and intake–output daily along with abdominal girth

Conclusion Abdominal assessment is done in the order inspection, auscultation, percussion and palpation, with the patient supine and relaxed and the bladder empty; normal findings are a soft, non-tender abdomen with active bowel sounds and tympany, while signs such as distension, absent bowel sounds, rigidity and rebound tenderness need urgent reporting.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the components of a nursing health history. Add a note on the techniques of interviewing. (10 + 5)
answer_html:
Introduction The health history is the subjective data collected from the patient (and family) through an interview. It tells the nurse about the patient's current problems, past health, lifestyle, family and social background and how the illness affects daily life. Together with the physical examination, it forms the basis of nursing diagnoses and the care plan.

Purposes of the health history

  1. To collect subjective data about the patient's health and the problem for which care is sought
  2. To identify the patient's health needs, risk factors and strengths
  3. To guide the physical examination to areas that need closer attention
  4. To form nursing diagnoses and plan individualised care
  5. To build a trusting nurse–patient relationship
  6. To serve as a baseline for comparison and as a legal record

PART A – COMPONENTS OF THE HEALTH HISTORY (10 marks)

1. Biographic (demographic) data

  • Name, age, sex, address and contact number
  • Marital status, religion, education, occupation
  • Date of admission, source of information (patient, relative, records) and its reliability

2. Chief complaint (reason for seeking care)

  • The main problem in the patient's own words, with its duration – e.g. "fever and cough for 5 days"

3. History of present illness

  • A detailed account of each complaint – remembered as OLDCARTS or PQRST:
    • Onset – sudden or gradual; what the patient was doing
    • Location and radiation
    • Duration and frequency
    • Character / quality – sharp, dull, burning, colicky
    • Aggravating and relieving factors
    • Timing – constant or intermittent; day or night
    • Severity – on a 0–10 scale
  • Associated symptoms (e.g. vomiting with abdominal pain)
  • Treatment already taken and its effect; the patient's own idea of the cause

4. Past health history

  • Childhood illnesses (measles, rheumatic fever) and immunisations
  • Previous illnesses – diabetes, hypertension, asthma, tuberculosis, epilepsy, jaundice
  • Hospitalisations and surgeries (with dates), injuries, accidents
  • Blood transfusions
  • Allergies – drugs (e.g. penicillin), food, latex – and the type of reaction
  • Current medications – prescribed, over-the-counter, herbal and Ayurvedic

5. Obstetric and menstrual history (women)

  • Age at menarche, cycle, flow, pain; last menstrual period (LMP)
  • Gravida, para, abortions, living children; contraception; menopause

6. Family history

  • Age and health, or cause of death, of parents, siblings and children
  • Family diseases – diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer, tuberculosis, mental illness, hereditary disorders (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease)
  • A genogram (family tree) may be drawn

7. Personal and social history

  • Habits – diet pattern, sleep, exercise, bowel and bladder habits
  • Tobacco, alcohol and other substance use (type, amount, duration)
  • Occupation and occupational hazards
  • Living conditions – housing, ventilation, safe water, sanitation, pets
  • Economic status, family support, social relationships
  • Culture, religion and health beliefs; spiritual needs
  • Travel history (malaria, dengue areas)
  • Stress and coping methods

8. Functional health patterns (Gordon's 11 patterns) – a useful nursing framework

  • health perception–management, nutritional–metabolic, elimination, activity–exercise, sleep–rest, cognitive–perceptual, self-perception, role–relationship, sexuality–reproduction, coping–stress tolerance, values–beliefs

9. Review of systems

  • Systematic questions about symptoms in each system – general (fever, weight change, fatigue), skin, head, eyes, ears, nose, throat, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, musculoskeletal, nervous, endocrine, blood, mental health
  • Helps to find problems the patient forgot to mention

10. Developmental and psychosocial assessment

  • Developmental tasks for age; self-concept, mood, anxiety
  • The patient's perception of the illness, expectations and goals

PART B – TECHNIQUES OF INTERVIEWING (5 marks)

1. Phases of the interview

  • Preparation – read records, plan questions, arrange a private, quiet, comfortable place
  • Introduction (orientation) – greet, introduce yourself, explain the purpose and time needed, assure confidentiality, take consent
  • Working phase – collect the data
  • Termination – summarise, ask "Is there anything else you want to tell me?", explain what happens next

2. Communication techniques

  • Open-ended questions – "Tell me about your pain" – give detailed answers
  • Closed questions – "Do you smoke?" – for specific facts
  • Active listening – attention, nodding, not interrupting
  • Facilitation – "Go on…", "Mm-hmm"
  • Clarification – "What do you mean by weakness?"
  • Reflection and restatement – repeating the patient's words or feelings
  • Focusing – keeping to the main problem
  • Silence – allows the patient to think
  • Summarising – checks accuracy
  • Empathy – "This must be very painful for you"
  • Non-verbal communication – eye contact, open posture (SOLER), appropriate touch

3. Things to avoid

  • Leading or biased questions ("You don't drink, do you?"), several questions at once, medical jargon
  • Judgemental remarks, false reassurance, giving advice too early, rushing, interruptions

4. Observation during the interview

  • Appearance, behaviour, mood, speech, breathing, signs of pain or distress, family interaction

5. Special situations

  • Children – history from parents; involve the child where possible
  • Elderly – speak clearly, check hearing, allow more time
  • Language barrier – use a trained interpreter
  • Anxious or angry patients – stay calm, acknowledge feelings
  • Sensitive topics – ask privately and respectfully

Documentation

  • Record in the patient's own words where important (chief complaint), objectively and in a logical order; date, time and signature

PART C – Sources and validation of data

Sources of data

  • Primary source – the patient (most reliable when conscious and oriented)
  • Secondary sources – family members and caregivers, previous medical records, doctors' notes, laboratory reports, other members of the health team (doctor, dietitian, physiotherapist), referral letters
  • Secondary sources are used when the patient is a child, unconscious, confused, very ill or does not speak the language; record who gave the information

Validation

  • Double-check data that seem inconsistent (e.g. the patient says "no breathing problem" but is breathless while talking) by asking again, examining or checking records
  • Separate facts from interpretations; record the patient's own words in quotation marks

Sample recording (part) "Mrs S, 52 years, housewife, admitted 12/11/2026. Source: patient (reliable). Chief complaint: 'pain in the upper abdomen for 3 days'. HPI: sudden onset after a fatty meal; right upper abdomen, radiating to the right shoulder; colicky; 7/10; worse after food, relieved by lying still; nausea and two episodes of vomiting; antacid gave no relief. Past history: hypertension for 5 years on amlodipine 5 mg daily; no surgery; allergic to sulpha drugs (rash). Family history: mother diabetic. Personal: mixed diet, no tobacco or alcohol, sleeps 6 hours, bowels regular."

Role of the nurse

  • Take the history soon after admission, once the patient is comfortable; in emergencies take a brief history first and complete it later
  • Keep the information confidential; share it only with the care team
  • Use the data to prioritise problems and start the care plan; update the history as new information comes

Errors to avoid while recording

  • Vague words such as "normal", "good" or "fine" without description
  • Recording opinions as facts (write "patient says…" where needed)
  • Leaving blanks – write "nil" or "not known" instead

Conclusion The nursing health history covers biographic data, chief complaint, history of present illness, past, family, personal–social and functional history, and review of systems; a well-planned interview using open questions, active listening and empathy gives complete and accurate subjective data for nursing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the preparation of the patient and the unit for a general physical examination. Add a note on focused assessment.
answer_html:
Introduction Good preparation makes the physical examination comfortable, safe, accurate and quick, and protects the patient's privacy and dignity.

A. Preparation of the environment (unit)

  1. Privacy – screens or curtains, closed door; limit people in the room
  2. Lighting – good light, preferably natural daylight, plus a torch
  3. Temperature – warm room, no draughts (the patient will be partly undressed)
  4. Quiet – essential for auscultation
  5. Examination couch or bed at a convenient height, clean linen
  6. Hand-washing facilities and waste containers nearby

B. Preparation of equipment

  • Tray with thermometer, stethoscope, sphygmomanometer, pulse oximeter, penlight, tongue depressor, otoscope, ophthalmoscope, tuning fork, reflex hammer, measuring tape, weighing scale, height scale, Snellen chart, cotton wisps, safety pin, gloves, lubricant, speculum (if needed), swabs, specimen containers, kidney tray, drapes

C. Preparation of the patient

1. Psychological

  • Explain the purpose and steps in simple words; answer questions
  • Obtain consent; reduce anxiety; respect cultural and religious concerns
  • Arrange a female attendant (chaperone) when needed

2. Physical

  • Ask the patient to empty the bladder (and bowel if needed); collect urine specimen if ordered
  • Remove clothing and give a gown; remove jewellery if it interferes
  • Drape with a sheet – expose only the part being examined
  • Measure vital signs, height, weight, BMI and SpO₂ before the examination
  • Position for each part – sitting (head, neck, chest, back), supine (abdomen, heart, limbs), dorsal recumbent or lithotomy (genital and rectal examination); help and support the patient
  • Make sure the patient is comfortable; offer a blanket

D. Focused assessment

  • Definition: an assessment limited to a specific problem, body system or area related to the patient's current complaint or condition
  • Examples:
    • chest pain → cardiovascular and respiratory assessment
    • post-operative patient → wound, vital signs, pain, bowel sounds, urine output
    • head injury → neurological observations (GCS, pupils)
  • Uses – emergencies, ongoing monitoring, shift assessment
  • Preparation is the same but quicker and targeted: explain, privacy, position, only the needed equipment; in emergencies assess airway, breathing and circulation first

E. After the examination

  • Help the patient dress and settle; clean and replace equipment; send specimens; document and report findings

Conclusion Preparation for physical examination includes a private, warm, well-lit and quiet environment, a complete equipment tray and a well-informed, comfortable, correctly positioned and draped patient; focused assessment uses the same preparation but concentrates quickly on the problem area.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the assessment of the thorax and lungs.
answer_html:
Introduction Assessment of the thorax and lungs detects problems of breathing and gas exchange. The patient sits upright; the posterior chest is usually examined first, then the anterior, comparing one side with the other.

A. Landmarks

  • Suprasternal notch, sternal angle (angle of Louis) – level of the 2nd rib; C7 (vertebra prominens)
  • Vertical lines – midsternal, midclavicular, anterior, mid- and posterior axillary, scapular and vertebral lines

B. Inspection

  • Shape – normal antero-posterior : lateral diameter about 1 : 2; barrel chest (1 : 1) in COPD; pigeon chest, funnel chest, kyphoscoliosis
  • Respiratory rate, rhythm, depth and effort; use of accessory muscles, intercostal retractions, nasal flaring
  • Symmetry of chest movement
  • Colour – cyanosis of lips and nails; clubbing of fingers
  • Skin lesions, scars, chest tubes, wounds

C. Palpation

  • Tenderness, masses, crepitus (crackling under the skin – subcutaneous emphysema)
  • Trachea – central or shifted (pushed away by effusion/pneumothorax, pulled by collapse)
  • Chest expansion – thumbs at the 10th rib posteriorly; symmetrical movement of about 3–5 cm
  • Tactile (vocal) fremitus – palms on the chest while the patient says "ninety-nine"
    • increased in consolidation (pneumonia)
    • decreased in pleural effusion, pneumothorax, emphysema

D. Percussion

  • Resonant over normal lungs
  • Dull – consolidation; stony dull – pleural effusion
  • Hyper-resonant – pneumothorax, emphysema
  • Diaphragmatic excursion – about 3–5 cm

E. Auscultation

  • Use the diaphragm; ask the patient to breathe slowly and deeply through the mouth; compare side to side
  • Normal breath sounds:
    • vesicular – soft, low-pitched; most of the lung fields; inspiration longer than expiration
    • bronchovesicular – near the main bronchi (1st–2nd intercostal spaces in front, between the scapulae)
    • bronchial – loud, high-pitched; over the trachea; abnormal if heard over the lung fields (consolidation)
  • Adventitious (abnormal) sounds:
    • crackles (crepitations) – fine or coarse; fluid in alveoli – pneumonia, pulmonary oedema
    • wheeze – narrowed airways – asthma, COPD
    • rhonchi – secretions in large airways; may clear on coughing
    • pleural friction rub – grating sound – pleurisy
    • stridor – harsh inspiratory sound – upper airway obstruction (emergency)
  • Voice sounds (bronchophony, egophony, whispered pectoriloquy) – louder over consolidation

F. Nurse's role

  • Ensure privacy and warmth; position the patient sitting or leaning forward
  • Record and report abnormal findings – rising respiratory rate, reduced air entry, new crackles, stridor
  • Repeat chest assessment regularly in respiratory and post-operative patients

Conclusion Assessment of the thorax and lungs uses inspection of shape and breathing, palpation of expansion and fremitus, percussion for resonance and auscultation of breath and added sounds, always comparing both sides; it helps detect consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax and airway obstruction early.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the assessment of the cardiovascular system.

diagram.caption: Auscultation areas of the heart
labels: tricuspid area 4th-5th left ICS lower sternal border
mitral area 5th left ICS midclavicular line (apex)

answer_html:
Introduction Cardiovascular assessment includes the heart (precordium) and the peripheral vessels. It helps detect heart failure, valve disease, arrhythmias and poor circulation.

A. History (brief)

  • Chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness (on exertion, lying flat, at night), swelling of feet, fainting, fatigue, cyanosis; history of hypertension, diabetes, rheumatic fever, smoking

B. Inspection

  • General appearance, distress, skin colour (cyanosis, pallor)
  • Jugular venous pressure (JVP) – with the patient at 45°; normally the pulsation is not more than about 3–4 cm above the sternal angle; raised in right heart failure
  • Precordium – visible pulsations, apex beat, heaves
  • Oedema of feet and legs; clubbing; varicose veins

C. Palpation

  • Apex beat (point of maximal impulse) – normally at the left 5th intercostal space, in the midclavicular line, about 1–2 cm in size; displaced in heart enlargement
  • Heaves (lifts) and thrills (palpable murmurs)
  • Peripheral pulses – radial, brachial, carotid (one side at a time), femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial – rate, rhythm, volume, equality
  • Capillary refill – normally less than 2–3 seconds
  • Pitting oedema – graded 1+ to 4+
  • Skin temperature of the limbs

D. Auscultation of the heart

  • Areas (mnemonic "All Patients Eat Too Much"):
    • Aortic – 2nd right intercostal space beside the sternum
    • Pulmonary – 2nd left intercostal space
    • Erb's point – 3rd left intercostal space
    • Tricuspid – 4th–5th left intercostal space at the lower sternal border
    • Mitral – 5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line (apex)
  • Normal heart sounds:
    • S1 ("lub") – closure of mitral and tricuspid valves; start of systole; loudest at the apex
    • S2 ("dub") – closure of aortic and pulmonary valves; loudest at the base
  • Abnormal sounds:
    • S3 – ventricular gallop; heart failure (normal in children and young adults)
    • S4 – atrial gallop; stiff ventricle (hypertension)
    • Murmurs – turbulent flow through valves; graded I–VI; systolic or diastolic
    • Pericardial friction rub – pericarditis
  • Use diaphragm then bell; positions – supine, left lateral (mitral), sitting forward (aortic)
  • Carotid bruit with the bell – narrowing of the artery

E. Other measurements

  • BP in both arms; postural (orthostatic) BP in dizzy patients
  • Pulse deficit (apical minus radial rate) in atrial fibrillation
  • ECG, SpO₂

F. Nurse's role

  • Record findings; report irregular pulse, new murmur, raised JVP, absent peripheral pulses, cold pale limbs or sudden oedema
  • Monitor heart patients regularly – vital signs, intake–output, weight

Conclusion Cardiovascular assessment includes inspection for JVP, cyanosis and oedema, palpation of the apex beat and peripheral pulses, and auscultation of S1, S2 and abnormal sounds at the five standard areas, helping to detect heart failure, valve disease and circulatory problems.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the neurological assessment.
answer_html:
Introduction Neurological assessment examines the brain, spinal cord and nerves. A full examination is done on admission; a focused neuro-observation (consciousness, pupils, limb power, vital signs) is repeated in head injury, stroke and after neurosurgery.

1. Mental status and cerebral function

  • Level of consciousness – alert, lethargic, obtunded, stuporous, comatose; Glasgow Coma Scale (3–15)
  • Orientation – time, place, person
  • Memory – immediate, recent and remote
  • Attention, calculation, judgement, abstract thinking
  • Speech and language – clarity; aphasia (expressive or receptive), dysarthria
  • Mood and behaviour

2. Cranial nerves (brief tests)

  • I Olfactory – identify a familiar smell (coffee, soap) with eyes closed
  • II Optic – visual acuity (Snellen chart), visual fields
  • III, IV, VI – pupils (size, equality, reaction to light) and eye movements in six directions
  • V Trigeminal – facial sensation, clenching the jaw, corneal reflex
  • VII Facial – smile, frown, raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly (facial symmetry)
  • VIII Vestibulocochlear – hearing (whisper test, Rinne and Weber tests), balance
  • IX, X Glossopharyngeal, Vagus – swallowing, gag reflex, uvula in midline, voice
  • XI Accessory – shrug shoulders and turn the head against resistance
  • XII Hypoglossal – protrude the tongue (midline), move it side to side

3. Motor function

  • Muscle size (wasting), tone (flaccid, spastic, rigid), involuntary movements (tremor)
  • Muscle power – graded 0 (no contraction) to 5 (normal strength)
  • Coordination – finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, rapid alternating movements
  • Balance and gait – Romberg test (standing with feet together, eyes closed)

4. Sensory function (eyes closed, compare both sides)

  • Light touch (cotton wisp), pain (sharp/dull with a pin), temperature
  • Vibration (tuning fork on bony points), position sense (big toe up or down)
  • Stereognosis (identifying an object in the hand), two-point discrimination

5. Reflexes

  • Deep tendon reflexes with the reflex hammer – biceps (C5–6), triceps (C7), knee (L3–4), ankle (S1); graded 0 (absent) to 4+ (very brisk with clonus); 2+ is normal
  • Superficial reflexes – abdominal, plantar
    • Babinski sign – upward movement of the big toe and fanning of toes on stroking the sole – abnormal in adults (upper motor neuron lesion), normal in infants

6. Meningeal signs – neck stiffness, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs (meningitis)

Equipment: penlight, reflex hammer, tuning fork, cotton wisp, safety pin, Snellen chart, tongue depressor, smell items.

Nurse's role

  • Use the neuro-observation chart; compare with previous findings
  • Report immediately a fall in GCS, unequal or non-reacting pupils, new weakness, or fits

Conclusion Neurological assessment covers mental status, cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, coordination, reflexes and meningeal signs; regular focused neuro-observations help detect deterioration early.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the assessment of the skin, hair and nails.
answer_html:
Introduction The skin, hair and nails reflect general health, hydration, nutrition and circulation. They are assessed by inspection and palpation in good light, throughout the head-to-toe examination.

A. Skin

1. Colour

  • Pallor – anaemia, shock
  • Cyanosis – lips, tongue, nail beds – lack of oxygen
  • Jaundice – sclera, skin – raised bilirubin
  • Erythema (redness) – inflammation, fever
  • Hyper- or hypopigmentation – vitiligo, Addison's disease
  • In dark skin, check the conjunctiva, lips, palms, soles and oral mucosa

2. Temperature – felt with the dorsum of the hand; warm in fever, cold in shock or poor circulation

3. Moisture – dry (dehydration, hypothyroidism) or sweaty (fever, anxiety, hypoglycaemia)

4. Texture and thickness – smooth or rough; thin, fragile skin in the elderly and on steroids

5. Turgor (elasticity) – pinch a fold of skin over the sternum or forearm; normally it returns at once; tenting (slow return) in dehydration (less reliable in the elderly)

6. Oedema – pitting or non-pitting; site and grade

7. Vascular changes – petechiae (pinpoint bleeding), purpura, ecchymosis (bruises), spider naevi

8. Lesions – describe type, size, shape, colour, distribution, discharge

  • Primary – macule, papule, vesicle, pustule, nodule, wheal, bulla, plaque
  • Secondary – scale, crust, ulcer, fissure, scar, keloid
  • Moles – look for warning signs (ABCDE: asymmetry, irregular border, colour variation, diameter over 6 mm, evolving)

9. Pressure areas – sacrum, heels, hips, elbows, back of head – redness or breaks (pressure ulcers)

10. Wounds, scars, rashes, infestation, injection sites, tattoos

B. Hair

  • Distribution (normal for age and sex; hirsutism), quantity (alopecia), texture (dry, brittle in hypothyroidism and malnutrition; easily pluckable in protein deficiency)
  • Scalp – dandruff, lesions, lice and nits (pediculosis)

C. Nails

  • Colour – pale (anaemia), cyanosed, yellow (fungal infection)
  • Shape:
    • clubbing – nail-bed angle 180° or more (chronic lung and heart disease)
    • koilonychia – spoon-shaped nails (iron deficiency)
  • Capillary refill – normally less than 2–3 seconds
  • Texture, thickness, splitting; splinter haemorrhages (endocarditis), Beau's lines (past illness)
  • Hygiene – length, cleanliness, ingrown nails (especially in diabetics)

D. Nurse's role

  • Inspect skin daily, especially pressure areas of bedridden patients
  • Record and report rashes, jaundice, cyanosis, bruising, pressure injuries, wounds and infestation
  • Use the findings to plan hygiene, skin care, nutrition and fluid needs

Conclusion Assessment of the skin, hair and nails – colour, temperature, moisture, turgor, lesions, pressure areas, hair distribution and nail shape and colour – gives valuable clues to hydration, nutrition, circulation, infection and systemic diseases.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is a general survey? Explain its components.
answer_html:
Definition The general survey is the overall first impression of the patient's health, gathered by observation from the moment the nurse meets the patient. It guides the rest of the examination.

Components

1. Physical appearance

  • Apparent age compared with stated age
  • Sex, level of consciousness (alert, drowsy, confused)
  • Skin colour – pallor, cyanosis, jaundice, flushing
  • Facial features and expression – symmetry, pain, anxiety, flat expression
  • Signs of acute distress – breathlessness, pain, sweating, restlessness

2. Body structure

  • Build and nutrition – thin, well-nourished, obese, cachexia (severe wasting)
  • Stature – height; dwarfism, gigantism
  • Symmetry and obvious deformities (amputation, kyphosis)
  • Posture and position – e.g. sitting upright and leaning forward (tripod position) in breathlessness; lying still with knees flexed in peritonitis

3. Mobility

  • Gait – steady, limping, shuffling (Parkinson's disease), ataxic (unsteady), use of aids
  • Range of movement; involuntary movements – tremors, tics, fits

4. Behaviour

  • Mood and affect – appropriate, anxious, depressed, angry
  • Speech – clear, slurred, rapid, hesitant; language used
  • Dress, grooming and personal hygiene – appropriate to season and situation; body or breath odour
  • Eye contact and interaction with others

5. Measurements

  • Vital signs – temperature, pulse, respiration, BP, SpO₂, pain score
  • Height, weight, BMI, waist circumference

Example of documentation "A 45-year-old man, alert and oriented, appears his stated age, well nourished, sitting comfortably, not in distress; walks with a steady gait; dressed appropriately, good hygiene; speech clear; T 98.6 °F, P 82/min, R 18/min, BP 126/80 mmHg, SpO₂ 98%, weight 68 kg, height 168 cm, BMI 24.1."

Importance

  • Gives a quick picture of how ill the patient is and what needs urgent attention
  • Helps detect nutritional problems, neglect, pain, mental changes
  • Sets the baseline for later comparison

Nurse's role

  • Observe from the first contact; record objectively without labelling
  • Report distress, confusion, cyanosis or sudden change

Common abnormal findings in the general survey

  • Cachexia (severe wasting) – cancer, tuberculosis, malnutrition
  • Moon face and central obesity – Cushing's syndrome, long-term steroids
  • Tripod position – severe breathlessness (asthma, COPD)
  • Confusion or drowsiness – hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, head injury, sepsis
  • Poor hygiene and grooming – self-neglect, depression, dementia, inability to care for self

Conclusion The general survey is the overall impression of the patient's appearance, body structure, mobility, behaviour and basic measurements; it tells the nurse at a glance how ill the patient is and guides the detailed examination.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the assessment of the head and neck, including the eyes, ears, nose, mouth and throat.
answer_html:
Introduction Assessment of the head and neck includes the skull, face, eyes, ears, nose, sinuses, mouth, throat, lymph nodes and thyroid. The patient usually sits facing the examiner, in good light.

1. Head and face

  • Skull – size, shape, symmetry, lumps, tenderness; scalp for lesions and lice
  • Face – symmetry, expression, swelling (moon face), involuntary movements
  • Temporomandibular joint – movement, clicking, tenderness

2. Eyes

  • External structures – eyebrows; eyelids (ptosis, oedema, styes); lashes
  • Conjunctiva – pallor (anaemia), redness (conjunctivitis); sclera – yellow in jaundice
  • Cornea – clarity, ulcer, arcus
  • Pupils – size (normally 3–5 mm), shape, equality, reaction to light and accommodation (PERRLA)
  • Eye movements in six directions; nystagmus
  • Visual acuity – Snellen chart at 6 metres (normal 6/6)
  • Visual fields – confrontation test
  • Ophthalmoscopy – red reflex, optic disc

3. Ears

  • External ear – shape, lesions, discharge, tenderness (pulling the pinna is painful in otitis externa)
  • Otoscope – ear canal (wax, foreign body); tympanic membrane normally pearly grey with a cone of light
  • Hearing – whisper test, Rinne and Weber tests with a tuning fork

4. Nose and sinuses

  • External shape; patency of each nostril; septum (deviation); mucosa (pale, swollen, bleeding); discharge, polyps
  • Sinus tenderness – frontal and maxillary areas

5. Mouth and throat

  • Lips – colour, cracks (angular stomatitis), lesions
  • Buccal mucosa, gums – bleeding, swelling, ulcers, white patches (thrush)
  • Teeth – caries, missing teeth, dentures
  • Tongue – colour, coating, moisture, position (midline)
  • Palate, uvula (midline), tonsils (size graded 1+ to 4+, exudate), pharynx
  • Breath odour; gag reflex

6. Neck

  • Symmetry, swelling, range of movement
  • Trachea – central
  • Thyroid – inspect while the patient swallows; palpate from behind for size, nodules, consistency; auscultate for a bruit (hyperthyroidism)
  • Lymph nodes – preauricular, posterior auricular, occipital, submental, submandibular, tonsillar, superficial and posterior cervical, supraclavicular – note size, consistency, tenderness, mobility
  • Jugular veins – distension

Nurse's role

  • Prepare equipment (penlight, otoscope, ophthalmoscope, tongue depressor, tuning fork, Snellen chart, gloves)
  • Record findings; report unequal pupils, sudden vision or hearing loss, enlarged or hard lymph nodes, goitre, oral lesions

Conclusion Head and neck assessment examines the skull, face, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, lymph nodes and thyroid by inspection and palpation with simple instruments, and helps detect anaemia, jaundice, infection, thyroid disease and sensory problems.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the assessment of the musculoskeletal system.
answer_html:
Introduction Musculoskeletal assessment examines bones, joints and muscles for structure, movement and strength. It is important in fractures, arthritis, immobility, neurological disease and the elderly (risk of falls).

1. Posture and gait

  • Standing posture, alignment of head, shoulders and hips
  • Gait – smooth, limping, shuffling, waddling; use of walking aids
  • Spinal curvature – kyphosis (hunchback), lordosis (exaggerated lumbar curve), scoliosis (lateral curve – check by asking the patient to bend forward)

2. Inspection of joints and muscles

  • Swelling, redness, deformity, contractures, nodules
  • Muscle size and symmetry – wasting (atrophy) or hypertrophy
  • Compare both sides

3. Palpation

  • Tenderness, warmth (inflammation), swelling, crepitus (grating), effusion
  • Bulge sign for fluid in the knee joint

4. Range of motion (ROM)

  • Active (patient moves) and passive (nurse moves the joint gently)
  • Movements – flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation (internal, external), pronation, supination, inversion, eversion
  • Note pain, limitation or abnormal movement; never force a painful joint

5. Muscle strength (against resistance) – graded:

  • 0 – no contraction
  • 1 – flicker of contraction
  • 2 – movement with gravity eliminated
  • 3 – movement against gravity only
  • 4 – movement against some resistance
  • 5 – normal strength

6. Special tests (examples)

  • Phalen's and Tinel's signs – carpal tunnel syndrome
  • Straight leg raising – sciatica (nerve root irritation)

7. Measurements

  • Limb length and circumference (swelling, wasting)

Nurse's role

  • Assess mobility, self-care ability and risk of falls
  • Check neurovascular status (colour, warmth, pulses, sensation, movement) in fractures and casts
  • Encourage exercises; record and report findings

Common abnormal findings

  • Swelling, warmth and redness of a joint – arthritis, gout, infection
  • Crepitus – osteoarthritis, fracture
  • Contractures – prolonged immobility, burns
  • Muscle wasting – disuse, nerve injury, malnutrition
  • Deformities – knock knees (genu valgum), bow legs (genu varum), hallux valgus, ulnar deviation of fingers in rheumatoid arthritis, Heberden's nodes in osteoarthritis
  • Painful, limited range of motion – arthritis, injury, frozen shoulder

Equipment – goniometer (measures the angle of joint movement), measuring tape, reflex hammer.

Documentation example "Gait steady without aids; spinal curvature normal; all joints have full range of motion without pain or swelling; muscle strength 5/5 in all limbs except the left lower limb (3/5)."

Conclusion Musculoskeletal assessment covers posture, gait, spine, joints, muscles, range of motion and muscle strength; it identifies deformities, inflammation, weakness and mobility problems and guides nursing care and fall prevention.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Name the percussion sounds with examples.
answer_html:
Sound Quality Where heard / cause
Resonance hollow, low-pitched normal lung
Hyper-resonance booming, louder emphysema, pneumothorax
Tympany drum-like, high-pitched stomach and gas-filled bowel
Dullness thud-like, medium liver, heart, consolidation, fluid, full bladder
Stony dullness very dull pleural effusion
Flatness very soft, high-pitched muscle, bone (thigh)

Use: percussion shows whether the tissue below contains air, fluid or solid, and the size of organs (e.g. liver span).

Method (indirect percussion): the middle finger of the non-dominant hand (pleximeter) is placed firmly on the skin and struck on its distal joint with the tip of the middle finger of the other hand (plexor), using a quick wrist movement.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Differentiate between light and deep palpation.
answer_html:
Point Light palpation Deep palpation
Depth about 1 cm about 4–5 cm
Technique fingertips of one hand, gentle circular pressure one hand or two hands (one over the other) with firm pressure
Done first after light palpation
Assesses skin, superficial tenderness, muscle guarding, superficial masses, temperature, moisture organs (liver, spleen, kidneys), deep masses – size, shape, consistency, mobility
Discomfort minimal may cause discomfort; avoided over tender areas

Bimanual palpation – using both hands, one on each side of the part (kidneys, uterus).

Rule: always do light palpation before deep palpation, and palpate tender areas last.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is the capillary refill test?
answer_html:
Definition The capillary refill test checks peripheral circulation (perfusion) by measuring how quickly colour returns to the nail bed after pressure.

Procedure

  1. Hold the patient's hand at heart level
  2. Press the nail bed (or fingertip) firmly for about 5 seconds until it blanches (turns white)
  3. Release and count the seconds until the pink colour returns

Normal: less than 2 seconds (up to 3 seconds in the elderly).

Prolonged refill (more than 2–3 seconds) suggests:

  • Dehydration, shock, poor peripheral circulation
  • Peripheral arterial disease; tight cast or bandage
  • Hypothermia (cold limbs)

Note: also used in children to assess dehydration and shock (IMNCI).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: How is pitting oedema graded?
answer_html:
Definition Pitting oedema – a depression (pit) remains after pressing a swollen area firmly for a few seconds, due to excess fluid in the tissues.

Method: press firmly with the thumb over a bony area (front of the shin, ankle, dorsum of foot or sacrum in bedridden patients) for about 5 seconds and release.

Grading

Grade Depth of pit Rebound time
1+ about 2 mm disappears rapidly
2+ about 4 mm 10–15 seconds
3+ about 6 mm up to 1 minute
4+ about 8 mm 2–5 minutes

Causes: heart failure, kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome), liver cirrhosis, malnutrition, pre-eclampsia, venous insufficiency.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is PERRLA?
answer_html:
PERRLA is an abbreviation used to record normal pupil findings:

  • Pupils Equal (in size – normally 3–5 mm)
  • Round (regular shape)
  • Reactive to Light (constrict promptly when light is shone – direct and consensual reflex)
  • Accommodation (constrict when looking at a near object)

Method: dim the room; shine a penlight from the side into each eye in turn; watch both pupils; then ask the patient to look at a far object and then at a finger brought close to the nose.

Abnormal findings

  • Unequal pupils (anisocoria) or a fixed, dilated pupil – raised intracranial pressure, head injury – report immediately
  • Pinpoint pupils – opioid or organophosphate poisoning, pontine haemorrhage
  • Bilateral fixed dilated – severe brain damage, atropine

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the Rinne and Weber tests.
answer_html:
Both use a 512 Hz tuning fork to tell conductive from sensorineural hearing loss.

1. Rinne test

  • Place the vibrating fork on the mastoid bone (bone conduction); when no longer heard, hold it near the ear canal (air conduction)
  • Normal (Rinne positive) – air conduction longer than bone conduction
  • Conductive loss (wax, otitis media) – bone conduction longer (Rinne negative)

2. Weber test

  • Place the vibrating fork on the middle of the forehead or top of the head
  • Normal – sound heard equally in both ears
  • Conductive loss – sound heard louder in the affected ear
  • Sensorineural loss – sound heard louder in the normal ear

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is breast self-examination? How is it done?
answer_html:
Definition Breast self-examination (BSE) is a simple method by which a woman examines her own breasts every month to detect lumps or changes early.

When: once a month, a week after the menstrual period begins (breasts are least tender); after menopause on a fixed date each month.

Steps

  1. Look in a mirror – arms by sides, then raised, then hands on hips: check size, shape, dimpling, puckering, nipple changes or discharge
  2. Feel while lying down (pillow under the shoulder) and in the bath – use the pads of three middle fingers in small circles, with light, medium and firm pressure, covering the whole breast and the armpit in a set pattern (circular or up-and-down)
  3. Squeeze the nipple gently for discharge

Report any lump, thickening, skin changes, nipple retraction or bloody discharge to a doctor at once.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is clubbing of fingers? Name its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Clubbing is bulbous enlargement of the ends of the fingers (and toes) with loss of the normal angle between the nail and the nail bed (the angle becomes 180° or more) and sponginess of the nail bed.

Test – Schamroth's window test: the backs of the same fingers of both hands are placed together; normally a small diamond-shaped window is seen; it is lost in clubbing.

Causes

  1. Lungs – bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema, lung cancer, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis
  2. Heart – cyanotic congenital heart disease (e.g. Fallot's tetralogy), infective endocarditis
  3. Gastrointestinal – liver cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease
  4. Others – thyrotoxicosis, familial

Note: simple COPD alone does not usually cause clubbing – its presence calls for search for another cause (e.g. cancer).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define nursing process. Explain the characteristics and phases of the nursing process, with emphasis on evaluation. (2 + 3 + 6 + 4)

diagram.caption: The nursing process – a cyclic, continuous process
labels: feedback arrow from evaluation back to assessment

answer_html:
Introduction The nursing process is the scientific, problem-solving method that nurses use to give individualised and holistic care. The term was first used by Lydia Hall (1955); early models had three or four steps, and nursing diagnosis was added in the 1970s. Today the process has five phases – Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation and Evaluation (ADPIE) – and it is the framework for nursing practice, documentation and nursing education.

A. Definition (2 marks)

  • The nursing process is a systematic, rational method of planning and providing individualised nursing care to a person, family or community
  • It is a deliberate, problem-solving approach used to identify, prevent and treat actual or potential health problems and to promote wellness, based on the patient's responses to illness rather than on the disease alone

B. Characteristics (3 marks)

  1. Systematic – follows an orderly sequence of steps, each depending on the previous one
  2. Cyclic and dynamic – the phases overlap and are repeated continuously as the patient's condition changes
  3. Client-centred (individualised) – care is planned around the needs, values and preferences of the particular patient
  4. Goal-directed – every activity aims at a measurable outcome for the patient
  5. Problem-solving and decision-making – based on critical thinking and clinical judgement
  6. Interpersonal and collaborative – the patient, family and health team members take part
  7. Universally applicable – used in hospital, home and community, for all ages and conditions
  8. Holistic – covers physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs
  9. Scientific and evidence-based – uses knowledge from nursing and other sciences
  10. Flexible – adapts to the patient's changing needs and to different settings
  11. Documented – each phase is recorded, which gives continuity and legal protection

C. Phases of the nursing process (6 marks)

1. Assessment

  • The systematic and continuous collection, organisation, validation and documentation of data about the patient's health status
  • Types of data – subjective (what the patient says: pain, nausea, worry) and objective (what is observed or measured: BP 150/96 mmHg, wound discharge)
  • Sources – primary (the patient) and secondary (family, records, health team, laboratory reports)
  • Methods – observation, interview, physical examination, review of records and investigations
  • Types of assessment – initial (on admission), problem-focused, emergency, and time-lapsed reassessment
  • Data are organised using a framework (Gordon's functional health patterns, Maslow's hierarchy or body systems), validated and recorded

2. Nursing diagnosis

  • Analysis of the assessment data to identify the patient's actual and potential health problems, risks and strengths
  • A clinical judgement about the person's response to health problems, written using NANDA-I labels
  • Steps – analyse and cluster data, identify problems, formulate diagnostic statements (problem, etiology, signs and symptoms – PES), validate and prioritise
  • Example: Ineffective airway clearance related to thick secretions as evidenced by ineffective cough and crackles in both lung bases

3. Planning

  • Setting priorities – life-threatening problems first (airway, breathing, circulation; Maslow's hierarchy)
  • Writing goals and expected outcomes – patient-centred, specific, measurable, realistic and time-bound
  • Selecting nursing interventions that will remove or reduce the cause of the problem
  • Writing the nursing care plan so that all staff give the same care

4. Implementation

  • Putting the plan into action – carrying out nursing interventions
  • Steps – reassess the patient, decide whether help is needed, perform the interventions, supervise delegated care and document the care given and the patient's response
  • Types of interventions:
    • independent – started by the nurse (positioning, health teaching, mouth care)
    • dependent – carried out on a doctor's order (giving medicines, IV fluids)
    • collaborative (interdependent) – done with other team members (physiotherapy, diet planning)
  • Requires cognitive, interpersonal and technical (psychomotor) skills

5. Evaluation (explained in detail below)

D. Evaluation (4 marks)

Definition

  • Evaluation is a planned, ongoing, purposeful activity in which the nurse and the patient judge the patient's progress towards the goals and the effectiveness of the nursing care plan

Types

  • Ongoing evaluation – during or immediately after an intervention (e.g. checking SpO₂ after suctioning)
  • Intermittent evaluation – at fixed times (e.g. end of a shift, every 24 hours)
  • Terminal evaluation – at discharge, showing the patient's condition when care ends
  • In quality assurance: structure (facilities, staff), process (how care was given) and outcome (change in the patient's health) evaluation

Steps of evaluation

  1. Collect data related to the desired outcomes (reassess the patient)
  2. Compare the data with the expected outcomes
  3. Judge goal achievement – goal met, partially met or not met
  4. Relate the nursing activities to the outcomes – did the interventions cause the result?
  5. Draw conclusions about the status of the problem
  6. Continue, modify or terminate the care plan

Evaluative statement – the conclusion plus the supporting data: "Goal met. Patient walked 50 metres with a walker without breathlessness on the third post-operative day."

Reasons why goals are not met (reviewing the plan)

  • Incomplete or inaccurate assessment
  • Wrong or unclear nursing diagnosis
  • Unrealistic goals or wrong time frame
  • Unsuitable or inadequately carried-out interventions
  • Change in the patient's condition, or lack of patient cooperation

Importance of evaluation

  • Shows whether care is effective; avoids continuing useless interventions
  • Provides accountability and quality assurance
  • Gives the basis for revising the plan – the process starts again (cyclic)

E. Example – nursing process applied

Phase Patient with pneumonia
Assessment RR 30/min, SpO₂ 89%, crackles, says "I can't breathe"
Diagnosis Impaired gas exchange related to alveolar consolidation as evidenced by SpO₂ 89% and dyspnoea
Planning SpO₂ will be 95% or above within 24 hours
Implementation semi-Fowler's position, oxygen as prescribed, deep breathing and coughing, monitor SpO₂ every 2 hours
Evaluation after 24 hours SpO₂ 96%, RR 20/min – goal met

F. Historical development

  • 1955 – Lydia Hall first used the term "nursing process"
  • 1959–1963 – Johnson, Orlando and Wiedenbach described three-step processes
  • 1967 – Yura and Walsh described four phases: assessing, planning, implementing and evaluating
  • 1973 – first conference on nursing diagnosis; the American Nurses Association published standards of practice based on the nursing process, and diagnosis became a separate phase
  • Today the five-phase process (ADPIE) is used worldwide and is part of the INC curriculum

G. Requirements for using the nursing process effectively

  • Knowledge of nursing, biological and behavioural sciences
  • Cognitive skills (critical thinking, decision making), interpersonal skills (communication, rapport) and technical skills (procedures)
  • Patient and family participation at every step
  • Adequate time, staff and standard documentation formats
  • Continuous updating of the plan as the patient's condition changes

H. Documentation in each phase

  • Assessment – admission assessment form, flow sheets
  • Diagnosis and planning – nursing care plan
  • Implementation – nurses' notes, medication and treatment records
  • Evaluation – progress notes, revised care plan and discharge summary

Conclusion The nursing process is a systematic, cyclic, client-centred and goal-directed method of care made up of assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation; evaluation measures the patient's progress towards the goals and decides whether the plan is continued, modified or ended.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define critical thinking. Explain the competencies and attitudes of critical thinking. Describe the planning phase of the nursing process. (2 + 5 + 8)
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses make many decisions every day – which patient to see first, whether a change in vital signs is serious, which intervention will work best. Critical thinking is the thinking skill behind these decisions and is used in every phase of the nursing process, especially in planning care.

PART A – CRITICAL THINKING

1. Definition (2 marks)

  • Critical thinking is purposeful, disciplined and self-directed thinking in which a person analyses, interprets and evaluates information and reasons carefully in order to reach sound clinical judgements and decisions
  • In nursing it means applying knowledge and experience to identify patient problems and choose the best action

Characteristics – purposeful, reasoned, reflective, open-minded, questioning, creative, based on evidence and directed at a goal

2. Levels of critical thinking (Kataoka-Yahiro and Saylor model)

  • Basic level – concrete thinking; follows rules and procedures exactly; believes there is one right answer (beginning student)
  • Complex level – analyses and examines choices more independently; recognises that problems may have more than one solution
  • Commitment level – chooses an action, takes responsibility for it and anticipates when to act (experienced nurse)

3. Competencies (5 marks, with attitudes)

a. General critical thinking competencies

  • Scientific method – identify the problem, collect data, form a hypothesis, test it, evaluate
  • Problem solving – obtain information and use it to find a solution
  • Decision making – choose the best option from several alternatives

b. Specific competencies in clinical situations

  • Diagnostic reasoning – analysing cues to identify the patient's problem
  • Clinical inference – drawing conclusions from the data
  • Clinical decision making – choosing nursing actions for each patient

c. Competency specific to nursing – the nursing process itself

d. Cognitive skills used – interpretation, analysis, inference, evaluation, explanation and self-regulation (checking one's own thinking)

4. Critical thinking attitudes

  1. Confidence – belief in one's own ability, gained through knowledge and practice
  2. Thinking independently – does not accept ideas without examining them
  3. Fairness – considers all viewpoints without bias
  4. Responsibility and accountability – follows standards and accepts the results of one's actions
  5. Risk taking (courage) – willing to question practices that are not helpful
  6. Discipline – thorough and orderly
  7. Perseverance – keeps trying until a solution is found
  8. Creativity – thinks of new or unusual solutions
  9. Curiosity – asks "why?"; seeks more information
  10. Integrity – honest; admits mistakes and inconsistencies in one's own thinking
  11. Humility – recognises limits of one's knowledge and asks for help
  12. Open-mindedness – willing to consider new ideas

5. Use in nursing

  • In every phase of the nursing process – assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation
  • Prioritising care, preventing errors, recognising early deterioration
  • Evidence-based practice and ethical decision making
  • Developed by – reflective journals, concept mapping, case studies, simulation, clinical discussions and asking questions

PART B – PLANNING PHASE OF THE NURSING PROCESS (8 marks)

1. Definition

  • Planning is the deliberate, systematic phase of the nursing process in which the nurse, with the patient, sets priorities, establishes goals and expected outcomes, and selects nursing interventions to prevent, reduce or resolve the patient's problems, and records them in a nursing care plan

2. Types of planning

  • Initial planning – after the admission assessment, by the nurse who admits the patient
  • Ongoing planning – throughout the stay, as the patient's condition changes (e.g. at the start of each shift)
  • Discharge planning – begins on admission; prepares the patient for care after discharge

3. Steps of planning

Step 1: Setting priorities

  • Ranking the nursing diagnoses as high, medium or low priority
  • High – life-threatening problems (e.g. ineffective airway clearance)
  • Medium – not life-threatening but can cause unhealthy physical or emotional changes
  • Low – related to developmental needs or needing only minimal support
  • Guides – Maslow's hierarchy of needs (physiological needs first), the ABC rule (airway, breathing, circulation), actual problems before risk problems (in general), the patient's own preferences, available resources and time

Step 2: Establishing goals and expected outcomes

  • Goal – a broad statement of the desired change in the patient's health; short-term (hours to a week) or long-term (weeks or months)
  • Expected outcome – a specific, measurable change that shows the goal is achieved
  • Components of a goal/outcome statement:
    • Subject – the patient or part of the patient (understood)
    • Action verb – measurable (walks, states, demonstrates, drinks) – avoid "knows" or "understands"
    • Conditions – under what circumstances ("with a walker")
    • Criterion – standard of performance ("50 metres")
    • Target time – "by the third post-operative day"
  • Example – Patient will walk 50 metres with a walker without breathlessness by the third post-operative day
  • Guidelines – derived from the nursing diagnosis, patient-centred, SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, time-bound), set together with the patient, and consistent with the medical plan

Step 3: Selecting nursing interventions

  • Interventions are chosen to remove or reduce the cause (etiology) of the problem and to achieve the outcomes
  • Types – independent, dependent and collaborative; also direct care (done with the patient) and indirect care (done away from the patient, e.g. care coordination)
  • Criteria – safe, appropriate to the patient's age, health and culture, based on scientific knowledge and evidence, acceptable to the patient, and practical with available resources
  • Writing nursing orders – date, action verb, content (what and where), time element (when, how often, how long) and signature
    • Example: "14/11 – Turn the patient from side to side every 2 hours and inspect the sacrum and heels. – Sign"

Step 4: Writing the nursing care plan

  • Format (columns) – assessment data, nursing diagnosis, goal/expected outcome, nursing interventions, rationale, evaluation
  • Types of care plans:
    • individualised – written for one patient
    • standardised – pre-printed for a group of patients with the same condition, then individualised
    • computerised care plans
    • critical pathways – multidisciplinary, day-by-day plans
    • concept maps – diagrams linking problems and interventions
  • Purposes of the care plan – direction for individualised care, continuity of care across shifts, communication within the team, basis for evaluation, legal record, staff assignment and teaching tool for students
  • Guidelines – date and sign the plan, use standard terms and abbreviations, be specific, include psychological, social and spiritual needs, include health teaching and discharge needs, and keep the plan current

6. Barriers to critical thinking

  • Doing things only by routine or habit ("we always do it this way")
  • Time pressure, heavy workload and fatigue
  • Lack of knowledge or experience
  • Anxiety, fear of authority or of making mistakes
  • Bias and assumptions, stereotyping patients
  • Rigid rules that discourage questioning

PART C – Sample entry in a nursing care plan

Nursing diagnosis Goal / outcome Interventions Rationale Evaluation
Risk for impaired skin integrity r/t immobility after hip surgery Skin over sacrum and heels will remain intact throughout the hospital stay Turn 2-hourly; inspect pressure points each shift; keep skin clean and dry; use a pressure-relieving mattress; encourage protein-rich diet Relieves pressure and improves blood supply; early detection of redness Skin intact on day 5 – goal met; continue plan

Conclusion Critical thinking is purposeful, reflective thinking that uses specific competencies and attitudes to reach sound clinical judgements; it guides the planning phase, in which the nurse sets priorities, writes measurable goals, selects interventions and records them in a nursing care plan.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define nursing diagnosis. Explain the types, components and steps of formulating a nursing diagnosis, with examples. Add a note on common errors in writing nursing diagnoses.
tags: actual risk health promotion syndrome diagnosis
answer_html:
Introduction The nursing diagnosis is the second phase of the nursing process. It changes assessment data into clear statements of the patient's problems that nurses can treat independently. A common language of diagnoses, developed by NANDA International (NANDA-I), helps nurses communicate, plan care and record it in a standard way.

A. Definition

  • NANDA-I defines a nursing diagnosis as a clinical judgement concerning a human response to health conditions or life processes, or a vulnerability for that response, by an individual, family, group or community
  • It provides the basis for selecting nursing interventions to achieve outcomes for which the nurse is accountable

Historical note

  • First national conference on nursing diagnosis – 1973 (USA)
  • NANDA (North American Nursing Diagnosis Association) formed in 1982; renamed NANDA International in 2002
  • Taxonomy II groups the diagnoses into 13 domains (e.g. nutrition, elimination and exchange, activity/rest, safety/protection, coping/stress tolerance)

B. Purposes

  • Identifies the patient's problems that nursing can treat
  • Gives direction for planning goals and interventions
  • Promotes individualised care and communication among nurses
  • Defines the independent scope of nursing practice
  • Helps in documentation, research, education and quality assurance

C. Types of nursing diagnoses

1. Actual (problem-focused) diagnosis

  • A problem present at the time of assessment, with defining characteristics
  • Example: Acute pain related to the surgical incision as evidenced by pain score 8/10, grimacing and guarding of the abdomen

2. Risk diagnosis

  • A vulnerability to develop a problem; no signs and symptoms yet – only risk factors
  • Example: Risk for impaired skin integrity related to immobility and incontinence

3. Health promotion diagnosis

  • The patient's motivation and desire to increase well-being
  • Example: Readiness for enhanced nutrition as evidenced by the patient's wish to learn about a balanced diet

4. Syndrome diagnosis

  • A cluster of nursing diagnoses that occur together and are treated together
  • Examples: Disuse syndrome, Chronic pain syndrome, Relocation stress syndrome

Note – collaborative problems (potential complications such as haemorrhage) are not nursing diagnoses; they are monitored by the nurse and treated with both medical and nursing interventions.

D. Components of a nursing diagnosis statement (PES format)

1. Problem (P) – the diagnostic label

  • The NANDA-I name for the patient's response, e.g. Impaired physical mobility
  • Qualifiers add meaning – impaired, deficient, ineffective, excess, decreased, acute, chronic, risk for, readiness for enhanced

2. Etiology (E) – related factors

  • The probable cause or contributing factors, joined by "related to" (r/t)
  • Should be something nursing can influence; it guides the choice of interventions

3. Signs and symptoms (S) – defining characteristics

  • The cues (subjective and objective data) that show the problem exists, joined by "as evidenced by" (AEB)

Formats

  • Three-part (PES) – actual diagnoses
  • Two-part – risk diagnoses (problem + risk factors)
  • One-part – some health promotion and syndrome diagnoses

E. Steps of formulating a nursing diagnosis (diagnostic process)

Step 1: Analysing the data

  • Compare the data with standards and normal values (normal vital signs, lab values, growth charts)
  • Cluster the cues – group related data together (e.g. dry mouth + low urine output + tachycardia)
  • Identify gaps and inconsistencies and collect more data if needed

Step 2: Identifying health problems, risks and strengths

  • Decide whether each problem is a nursing diagnosis, a collaborative problem or a medical problem needing referral
  • Identify the patient's strengths (supportive family, motivation) – they help in planning

Step 3: Formulating the diagnostic statements

  • Select the NANDA-I label that fits the cluster
  • Add the etiology ("related to") and the defining characteristics ("as evidenced by")

Step 4: Validating, prioritising and documenting

  • Validate with the patient, family or colleagues
  • Arrange in order of priority
  • Record in the care plan

F. Examples

Situation Nursing diagnosis
COPD with sputum Ineffective airway clearance r/t thick secretions AEB ineffective cough and crackles
Gastroenteritis Deficient fluid volume r/t vomiting and diarrhoea AEB dry mucosa, BP 90/60 mmHg, urine 20 mL/hour
Fractured femur Impaired physical mobility r/t pain and traction AEB inability to move the left leg
Before surgery Anxiety r/t impending surgery AEB restlessness and saying "I am afraid"
Stroke with dysphagia Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements r/t difficulty swallowing AEB weight loss of 4 kg in 2 weeks
Elderly on sedatives Risk for falls r/t dizziness and weakness
New mother Readiness for enhanced breastfeeding AEB mother's wish to learn correct positioning

G. Common errors in writing nursing diagnoses

  1. Writing a medical diagnosis as the nursing diagnosis – e.g. "Pneumonia" (correct: Ineffective airway clearance…)
  2. Writing a nursing need, goal or intervention – e.g. "Needs suctioning" or "Encourage fluids"
  3. Writing a sign or symptom as the problem – e.g. "Dyspnoea related to…" (correct: Ineffective breathing pattern)
  4. Writing a diagnostic test or equipment – e.g. "Catheter care", "ECG monitoring"
  5. Problem and etiology meaning the same – e.g. "Pain related to pain"
  6. Using a medical diagnosis alone as the etiology, which nursing cannot change – write the response nurses can influence
  7. Legally inadvisable statements that blame staff – e.g. "Risk for injury related to side rails left down by the night nurse"
  8. Value judgements – e.g. "related to laziness" or "poor attitude"
  9. Two problems in one statement – write them separately
  10. Not supporting the diagnosis with data (missing defining characteristics)

H. NANDA-I Taxonomy II – the 13 domains
