  1. Health promotion 2. Nutrition 3. Elimination and exchange 4. Activity/rest 5. Perception/cognition 6. Self-perception 7. Role relationships 8. Sexuality 9. Coping/stress tolerance 10. Life principles 11. Safety/protection 12. Comfort 13. Growth/development

I. Older terms still seen in textbooks

  • Possible nursing diagnosis – the nurse suspects a problem but has insufficient data (e.g. Possible low self-esteem); more data are collected to confirm or rule it out
  • Wellness diagnosis – a healthy response the person wishes to improve; now called health promotion diagnosis

J. Advantages of using a standard language (NANDA-I)

  • All nurses understand the diagnosis in the same way
  • Makes documentation, computerised records and research easier
  • Links with standard interventions (NIC) and outcomes (NOC)
  • Shows clearly the independent contribution of nursing to patient care

K. Guidelines for writing a correct diagnosis

  • Write the patient's response, not the medical condition or the nurse's action
  • Use "related to" rather than "due to" or "caused by" (the nurse identifies a relationship, not proof of cause)
  • Make sure the etiology can be changed by nursing care
  • Keep it brief, specific and legally advisable, and support it with assessment data

Conclusion A nursing diagnosis is a clinical judgement about the patient's response to health problems, written with NANDA-I labels as actual, risk, health promotion or syndrome diagnoses in PES format; correctly formed and error-free diagnoses give clear direction for planning individualised nursing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the assessment phase of the nursing process.
answer_html:
Introduction Assessment is the first phase of the nursing process. It is the systematic and continuous collection, organisation, validation and documentation of data about the patient. All later phases depend on accurate assessment.

1. Types of assessment

  • Initial (admission) assessment – complete baseline assessment within a fixed time after admission
  • Problem-focused assessment – ongoing assessment of a specific problem (e.g. pain every 4 hours)
  • Emergency assessment – rapid assessment of life-threatening problems (airway, breathing, circulation)
  • Time-lapsed reassessment – done after some time (e.g. at a follow-up clinic) to compare with the baseline

2. Collecting data

  • Types of data:
    • subjective – the patient's own feelings and statements (symptoms) – "I feel dizzy"
    • objective – observed or measured by the nurse (signs) – pulse 120/min, pallor
  • Sources:
    • primary – the patient
    • secondary – family, health team members, medical records, laboratory and X-ray reports, literature
  • Methods:
    • observation – using the senses (look, listen, feel, smell)
    • interview – directive (structured) or non-directive (patient-led)
    • physical examination – inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation

3. Organising data

  • Using a framework so that nothing is missed:
    • Gordon's functional health patterns (11 patterns)
    • Maslow's hierarchy of needs
    • Body systems (head-to-toe)
    • Nursing theory models (e.g. Orem's self-care)

4. Validating data

  • Double-checking that the data are accurate and complete
  • Separating facts from interpretations (inferences)
  • Re-checking data that are extremely abnormal or inconsistent (e.g. temperature 104 °F in a patient whose skin feels cool)
  • Methods – repeating the measurement, asking someone else to check, comparing subjective and objective data

5. Documenting data

  • Record promptly, accurately and completely in the assessment form
  • Write subjective data in the patient's own words in quotation marks
  • Avoid judgements such as "good", "normal" without description

Role of the nurse

  • Builds rapport, ensures privacy and comfort
  • Uses observation, interview and examination skills
  • Reports urgent findings immediately

Characteristics of a good assessment

  • Systematic – follows a set framework so nothing is missed
  • Continuous – repeated throughout the stay, not done once
  • Accurate and complete – verified data, both subjective and objective
  • Holistic and patient-centred – includes physical, emotional, social and spiritual aspects
  • Documented – recorded promptly on standard assessment forms

Conclusion The assessment phase involves collecting subjective and objective data from primary and secondary sources by observation, interview and examination, organising them in a framework, validating and documenting them; it forms the base for accurate nursing diagnoses.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Differentiate between medical diagnosis and nursing diagnosis.
answer_html:
Introduction Both medical and nursing diagnoses are clinical judgements based on assessment data, but they differ in focus, scope and treatment. Understanding the difference helps the nurse write correct nursing diagnoses.

Point Medical diagnosis Nursing diagnosis
Definition Identification of a disease or pathological condition Clinical judgement about the person's response to a health problem or life process
Focus Disease – its cause, pathology and cure Human response – physical, emotional, social and spiritual
Made by Doctor Nurse
Treatment Medical – drugs, surgery, radiotherapy Nursing interventions, many of them independent
Duration Remains the same as long as the disease is present Changes as the patient's responses change (may change from day to day)
Number Usually one or a few Several for one patient
Classification ICD (International Classification of Diseases) NANDA-I taxonomy
Applies to Usually the individual Individual, family, group or community
Includes risk/wellness? Mainly existing disease Includes risk and health promotion diagnoses
Scope Within the legal scope of medical practice Within the legal scope of nursing practice
Example Myocardial infarction Acute pain r/t myocardial ischaemia; Activity intolerance; Anxiety r/t fear of death
Example Fracture of the femur Impaired physical mobility; Risk for impaired skin integrity

Similarities

  • Both are based on systematic assessment and critical thinking
  • Both guide the plan of care and are documented
  • Both need validation and are revised when new data appear

Relationship

  • The medical diagnosis tells what disease the patient has; the nursing diagnosis tells how the patient is responding to it and what the nurse can do
  • Problems that need both medical and nursing actions are written as collaborative problems (e.g. Potential complication: haemorrhage)

Example – one patient, both diagnoses

  • Medical diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus – treated with diet, oral drugs or insulin prescribed by the doctor
  • Nursing diagnoses for the same patient:
    • Risk for unstable blood glucose level r/t irregular meals
    • Deficient knowledge regarding insulin self-injection AEB incorrect technique on demonstration
    • Risk for infection r/t high blood glucose and foot wound
  • The medical diagnosis stays the same, but the nursing diagnoses change as the patient learns and the wound heals

Conclusion A medical diagnosis names the disease and is treated by the doctor, while a nursing diagnosis describes the patient's changing responses to illness and is treated mainly by independent nursing actions; both together give complete care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the implementation phase of the nursing process.
answer_html:
Introduction Implementation is the fourth phase of the nursing process, in which the nursing care plan is put into action. The nurse carries out or delegates the planned interventions and records the patient's response.

1. Definition

  • Implementation is the action phase in which the nurse performs the nursing interventions needed to achieve the goals and expected outcomes

2. Types of nursing interventions

  • Independent – activities the nurse is licensed to start on her own judgement: positioning, mouth care, deep-breathing exercises, health teaching, emotional support
  • Dependent – carried out under a doctor's order: medications, IV therapy, diet orders, investigations
  • Collaborative (interdependent) – carried out with other health team members: physiotherapy, nutrition planning, social work
  • Direct care – performed with the patient (bathing, feeding, dressing a wound)
  • Indirect care – performed away from the patient for the patient's benefit (arranging referrals, consulting, documenting)

3. Skills needed

  • Cognitive (intellectual) – knowledge, problem solving, decision making, critical thinking
  • Interpersonal – communication, therapeutic relationship, teaching, counselling, team work
  • Technical (psychomotor) – performing procedures safely (injections, catheterisation, suctioning)

4. Process (steps) of implementation

  1. Reassessing the patient – just before acting, to make sure the intervention is still appropriate (e.g. check BP before giving an antihypertensive)
  2. Determining the need for assistance – some tasks need two persons (moving a heavy patient)
  3. Implementing the nursing interventions – explain to the patient, ensure privacy and safety, follow standards and principles, and involve the patient
  4. Supervising delegated care – the nurse remains accountable for tasks delegated to auxiliary staff (right task, right person, right direction, right supervision)
  5. Documenting – record the activities and the patient's response promptly

5. Guidelines for implementing care

  • Base interventions on scientific knowledge and evidence
  • Understand the purpose of each intervention; clarify unclear orders
  • Adapt to the individual patient (age, culture, preferences)
  • Provide a safe environment; prevent injury and infection
  • Teach, support and comfort the patient
  • Respect dignity and promote self-care
  • Be holistic; carry out care at the right time

6. Common activities in implementation

  • Assisting with activities of daily living, counselling and teaching, giving care to achieve goals, giving care to compensate for adverse reactions, preventive measures, monitoring, communicating with the health team

Conclusion Implementation is the action phase of the nursing process in which the nurse uses cognitive, interpersonal and technical skills to carry out independent, dependent and collaborative interventions, supervises delegated care and documents the patient's response.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the advantages (significance) of the nursing process.
tags: benefits for patient nurse and profession
answer_html:
Introduction The nursing process is not just a paperwork exercise. Used well, it improves the quality of care for patients and the professional standing of nurses and nursing.

A. Advantages for the patient

  1. Individualised care – planned for the patient's own needs, not routine care
  2. Holistic care – physical, emotional, social and spiritual needs are considered
  3. Patient participation – the patient takes part in setting goals and decisions, which increases cooperation
  4. Continuity of care – the written plan guides all nurses on all shifts, so care is consistent
  5. Quality and safety – early identification of problems and risks prevents complications
  6. Faster recovery and possibly a shorter hospital stay
  7. Includes health teaching and discharge planning

B. Advantages for the nurse

  1. Gives an organised, systematic way of working and saves time
  2. Develops critical thinking, problem-solving and decision-making skills
  3. Increases job satisfaction and confidence as the nurse sees the results of her care
  4. Defines accountability and responsibility
  5. Documentation of each phase gives legal protection
  6. Promotes professional growth and teamwork

C. Advantages for the profession and the institution

  1. Defines the independent scope of nursing practice – nurses diagnose and treat human responses
  2. Provides a common language (NANDA-I, NIC, NOC) for communication and research
  3. Basis for quality assurance, nursing audit and standards of care
  4. Supplies data for nursing research and evidence-based practice
  5. A framework for nursing education – students learn to plan care systematically
  6. Supports cost-effective use of resources and staff assignment

D. Limitations (to be overcome)

  • Takes time and needs skill; may become routine paperwork if not individualised
  • Needs adequate staff and training

E. Example

  • Without the nursing process, every post-operative patient may receive the same routine care
  • With the nursing process, the nurse finds that one patient has severe pain, another is anxious about his job and a third cannot cough effectively – each gets care planned for his own problem, and the results are evaluated and recorded

Conclusion The nursing process benefits the patient through individualised, continuous and safe care, the nurse through organised work, critical thinking and accountability, and the profession through a defined scope of practice, common language, research and quality assurance.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the problem-solving approach and compare it with the nursing process.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses solve problems every day. Problem solving is a general thinking method; the nursing process is a specialised problem-solving method adapted for nursing care.

A. Methods of problem solving

  1. Trial and error – trying several solutions until one works; unsafe and time-consuming in patient care, used only when nothing else is possible
  2. Intuition – understanding a situation immediately without conscious reasoning, based on experience ("gut feeling"); useful for experienced nurses but must be supported by data
  3. Scientific method (research process) – a logical, step-by-step method: define the problem, collect data, form a hypothesis, plan, test the hypothesis, interpret results and evaluate
  4. Modified scientific method – used in clinical settings, e.g. the nursing process, decision-making models

B. Steps of the problem-solving approach

  1. Identify (recognise) the problem
  2. Collect data about the problem
  3. Analyse the data and find the cause
  4. Develop possible solutions (alternatives)
  5. Choose the best solution and plan its use
  6. Implement the chosen solution
  7. Evaluate the result; if not solved, start again

C. Comparison

Point Problem-solving approach Nursing process
Nature General method used in any field Specialised method for nursing care
Starting point Begins when a problem appears Begins with assessment, even before a problem appears
Focus Solving a single problem The whole patient – actual, risk and wellness needs
Prevention Mainly reactive Proactive – includes risk and health promotion diagnoses
Continuity Ends when the problem is solved Cyclic and continuous
Participation Done by the problem solver Done with the patient and family
Documentation Not necessarily written Each phase documented
Steps Identify, collect data, plan, implement, evaluate Assess, diagnose, plan, implement, evaluate

D. Similarities

  • Both are logical, systematic and goal-directed
  • Both need data collection, analysis, planning, action and evaluation
  • Both use critical thinking and decision making

E. Example

  • Problem: a patient's IV infusion has stopped
  • Problem solving: check the clamp and tubing, look for kinks, check the cannula site for swelling, lower the bottle to see back-flow, re-site the cannula if needed
  • Nursing process: also asks why (patient bends the arm), plans prevention (splint, teaching), and evaluates the patient's hydration status as a whole

Conclusion Problem solving is a general method of finding solutions by identifying a problem, collecting data, choosing and applying a solution and evaluating it; the nursing process uses the same logic but is continuous, patient-centred, proactive and documented.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Differentiate between a cue and an inference.
answer_html:
Cue Inference
A piece of data – a sign or symptom – collected by the nurse The nurse's interpretation or conclusion drawn from the cues
Fact – what is seen, heard, felt or measured Judgement – what the nurse thinks it means
Example: "skin hot to touch", temperature 102 °F, patient says "I feel cold" Example: "the patient has fever"
Example: patient refuses meals, weight loss of 3 kg Example: "nutrition is inadequate"

Note: an inference may be wrong, so it must be validated by more data before a nursing diagnosis is made.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is a collaborative problem? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition A collaborative problem is a potential physiological complication that the nurse monitors to detect its onset or change, and which is managed with both doctor-prescribed and nurse-prescribed interventions (Carpenito).

Written as – "Potential complication (PC): …"

Examples

  • PC: haemorrhage – after surgery
  • PC: hypoglycaemia – patient on insulin
  • PC: increased intracranial pressure – head injury
  • PC: arrhythmias – myocardial infarction

Nurse's role – monitor, detect early, report and start emergency measures as per protocol.

Difference from a nursing diagnosis – for a nursing diagnosis, the nurse prescribes the main treatment; for a collaborative problem, the nurse monitors and the doctor prescribes the main treatment.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is a concept map in nursing?
answer_html:
Definition A concept map is a diagram of the patient's care that shows the relationships between assessment data, nursing diagnoses, interventions and outcomes.

Steps to prepare

  1. Write the main reason for admission in the centre
  2. Draw branches to each nursing diagnosis with its supporting data
  3. Draw lines linking related problems (e.g. pain → impaired mobility)
  4. Add interventions and evaluation under each diagnosis

Uses – develops critical thinking, gives a holistic picture of the patient, helps students organise data and see links between problems.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is a clinical (critical) pathway?
answer_html:
Definition A clinical pathway (critical pathway or care map) is a multidisciplinary, standardised plan of care for patients with a specific diagnosis or procedure (e.g. caesarean section, knee replacement, CABG), showing the interventions and expected outcomes day by day on a timeline.

Features – covers assessment, tests, treatment, nutrition, activity, teaching and discharge planning for each day.

Variance – any deviation from the expected pathway (e.g. fever on day 2) is recorded and acted upon.

Advantages – reduces length of stay and cost, coordinates the team, standardises quality of care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define evidence-based practice (EBP). State its steps.
answer_html:
Definition Evidence-based practice is the integration of the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's values and preferences to make decisions about patient care.

Steps (5 A's)

  1. Ask – frame a clinical question (PICO: patient, intervention, comparison, outcome)
  2. Acquire – search for the best evidence
  3. Appraise – critically evaluate the evidence
  4. Apply – use it in practice with the patient's preferences
  5. Assess – evaluate the outcome

Example – using chlorhexidine for skin preparation before IV cannulation because research shows fewer infections.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is reflective practice?
answer_html:
Definition Reflective practice is the process of thinking carefully about one's own experiences and actions in practice in order to learn from them and improve future care.

Types (Schön)

  • Reflection-in-action – thinking while doing the task
  • Reflection-on-action – thinking back after the event

Gibbs' reflective cycle – description → feelings → evaluation → analysis → conclusion → action plan.

Uses – develops critical thinking and self-awareness, learning from mistakes, professional growth; maintained through a reflective journal.

Example – after a near-miss medication error, the nurse thinks about what happened, why it happened and how she felt, and decides to always double-check high-alert drugs in future.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define nasogastric intubation. Explain the purposes, contraindications, equipment and procedure of insertion of a nasogastric tube, the methods of confirming its placement, the procedure of tube feeding and the nursing care of a patient on nasogastric feeding.

diagram.caption: Measuring and inserting a nasogastric tube
labels: tape fixing the tube on the nose

answer_html:
Introduction Many patients cannot take food by mouth because they are unconscious, cannot swallow or have had surgery of the mouth or throat. If the stomach and intestines work, enteral feeding through a nasogastric (NG) tube is the simplest, safest and cheapest way to meet their nutritional needs. Nurses insert the tube, check its position, give feeds and prevent complications.

A. Definition

  • Nasogastric intubation is the insertion of a flexible tube through the nose, nasopharynx and oesophagus into the stomach
  • Nasogastric (tube) feeding is the administration of liquid feeds, water and medicines into the stomach through this tube

Types of tubes

  • Ryle's tube – PVC, single lumen, weighted tip; commonly used in India (adult sizes 14–18 Fr)
  • Levin's tube – single-lumen tube for decompression or feeding
  • Salem sump tube – double lumen with an air vent; used for continuous gastric suction
  • Fine-bore feeding tubes (polyurethane or silicone, 8–12 Fr) – more comfortable for long-term feeding; inserted with a guide wire (stylet)

B. Purposes

  1. Feeding (enteral nutrition) when the patient cannot or should not eat by mouth
  2. Gastric decompression – removing gas and fluid in intestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, after abdominal surgery
  3. Gastric lavage – washing out the stomach in poisoning or drug overdose
  4. Giving medicines to patients who cannot swallow
  5. Diagnosis – collecting gastric contents for analysis (e.g. gastric aspirate for tuberculosis in children), checking for bleeding
  6. Preventing vomiting and aspiration in some surgical patients

Indications for NG feeding

  • Unconscious patients, stroke with dysphagia, head injury
  • Surgery or cancer of the mouth, jaw, throat
  • Severe weakness, burns, critical illness, mechanical ventilation
  • Anorexia with severe malnutrition, preterm and sick newborns (orogastric in neonates)

C. Contraindications

  • Fracture of the base of the skull and severe facial fractures – the tube may enter the brain; the oral (orogastric) route is used instead
  • Recent nasal surgery, nasal obstruction or severe nosebleed
  • Oesophageal obstruction, stricture or recent oesophageal surgery
  • Oesophageal varices (relative – risk of bleeding)
  • Severe bleeding disorders (relative)

D. Equipment

  • Tray with NG tube of correct size (and a spare), water-soluble lubricant or lignocaine jelly
  • 50 mL catheter-tip syringe, pH indicator strips, kidney tray, gauze, tissues
  • Glass of water with a straw (if the patient can swallow), towel or mackintosh
  • Adhesive tape, scissors, marker pen, safety pin, spigot or clamp
  • Clean gloves, torch, tongue depressor, stethoscope
  • Prescribed feed at room temperature, measuring jug, water for flushing

E. Procedure of insertion

Preparation

  1. Check the doctor's order; identify the patient
  2. Explain the procedure and agree on a signal (raising a hand) to stop if distressed; obtain consent
  3. Ensure privacy; perform hand hygiene and wear gloves
  4. Position – high Fowler's (sitting upright at 45–90°) with the head slightly flexed; an unconscious patient is placed in semi-Fowler's or lateral position
  5. Inspect the nostrils; clean them; choose the nostril with better airflow; remove dentures

Measurement (NEX method)

  1. Measure from the tip of the Nose to the Earlobe and then to the Xiphisternum (about 45–55 cm in adults); mark the length with tape or a marker

Insertion

  1. Lubricate the first 10–15 cm of the tube
  2. Insert gently into the nostril, directing it backwards and downwards along the floor of the nose (not upwards)
  3. When the tube reaches the nasopharynx (the patient may gag), ask the patient to flex the head forward (chin to chest) and swallow sips of water through a straw; advance the tube with each swallow until the mark is reached
  4. Stop and withdraw the tube at once if the patient coughs, chokes, becomes cyanosed or cannot speak – the tube may be in the trachea
  5. Do not force the tube against resistance; try the other nostril if needed

Securing

  1. Confirm placement (see below)
  2. Fix the tube to the nose and cheek with tape without pressing on the nostril; pin it to the gown
  3. Note the mark at the nostril; close with a spigot
  4. Make the patient comfortable; dispose of waste; wash hands
  5. Record – date, time, tube type and size, nostril used, length inserted, method of confirming position, and the patient's tolerance

F. Methods of confirming tube placement

  1. Chest X-ray – the most reliable method (gold standard); essential for fine-bore tubes and in unconscious or ventilated patients before the first feed
  2. pH of the aspirate – aspirate gastric contents with a 50 mL syringe and test with pH paper; pH 5.5 or below indicates gastric placement (antacids, H₂ blockers or proton pump inhibitors may raise the pH)
  3. Appearance of the aspirate – gastric contents are usually cloudy, green or colourless with mucus
  4. External length mark – check the mark at the nostril before every feed; a change suggests displacement
  5. Patient's ability to speak without coughing or distress - Not reliable – the "whoosh" test (auscultating air pushed into the stomach) and placing the end of the tube in water to look for bubbles; these should not be used alone - Placement is checked before every feed or medicine, after vomiting, coughing bouts or suctioning, and whenever displacement is suspected

G. Procedure of tube feeding (intermittent / bolus by gravity)

  1. Check the order – type, amount and frequency of feed; check the expiry date; bring the feed to room temperature
  2. Explain; wash hands; wear gloves; place a towel under the tube
  3. Position – sit the patient up at 30–45° (or higher) during feeding and for 30–60 minutes after
  4. Check placement (pH and external mark)
  5. Check gastric residual volume (GRV) – aspirate the stomach contents; if the residue is large (as per hospital policy, e.g. more than 200–250 mL), withhold the feed and inform the doctor; usually return the aspirate to avoid loss of electrolytes
  6. Flush with 30 mL of water
  7. Pinch the tube, attach the barrel of the syringe (without the plunger), pour in the feed and let it flow slowly by gravity, holding it about 30–45 cm above the stomach; adjust the height to control the speed (usually 200–300 mL over 15–20 minutes)
  8. Never force the feed with the plunger; add feed before the barrel empties so that air does not enter
  9. Stop if the patient coughs, vomits, becomes breathless or complains of fullness
  10. Flush with 30–50 mL of water after the feed (and between medicines) to keep the tube clear
  11. Clamp or close the tube; keep the patient upright
  12. Clean the equipment; record the time, type and amount of feed and water, residual volume and tolerance; add to the intake–output chart

Continuous feeding – given with an enteral feeding pump at a set rate; the head end is kept raised all the time; giving sets and feed containers are changed as per policy

Medicines through the tube – use liquid preparations where possible; crush tablets only if allowed (never enteric-coated or sustained-release tablets); give each medicine separately and flush before, between and after

H. Nursing care of a patient on NG feeding

  1. Mouth care every 2–4 hours – the mouth becomes dry because nothing is taken orally; keep lips moist
  2. Nasal care – clean the nostril, change the tape daily and re-position the tube slightly to prevent pressure sores on the nose
  3. Check tube position before each feed; keep the mark visible
  4. Head end elevated 30–45° to prevent aspiration
  5. Monitor – intake–output, daily weight, blood sugar, electrolytes, bowel habits, signs of dehydration
  6. Observe for complications (below) and report early
  7. Hygiene of feeds and equipment – prepare feeds hygienically; discard unused feed as per policy; wash and dry equipment
  8. Change the tube as per manufacturer and policy (PVC Ryle's tube about every 7–10 days; fine-bore tubes last longer)
  9. Psychological support – the patient may feel deprived of the pleasure of eating; offer explanation and encouragement
  10. Teach the family about home NG feeding when the patient is discharged with the tube

I. Complications

  • Aspiration pneumonia – the most serious complication
  • Tube misplacement into the trachea or lungs; displacement into the oesophagus
  • Diarrhoea (rapid feeding, contaminated or concentrated feed) or constipation (low fibre, low fluid)
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension and cramps
  • Nasal irritation, nasal ulcer, sinusitis, epistaxis, sore throat, oesophagitis
  • Tube blockage
  • Fluid and electrolyte imbalance, hyperglycaemia, dehydration, refeeding syndrome in severely malnourished patients

J. Removal of the NG tube

  • Explain; place the patient upright; flush the tube with water or air; remove the tape
  • Ask the patient to take a deep breath and hold it; withdraw the tube steadily and quickly, covering it with a towel
  • Give mouth care and nasal care; record the time and the patient's condition

Conclusion Nasogastric intubation is the passing of a tube through the nose into the stomach for feeding, decompression, lavage and medication; correct NEX measurement, confirmation of placement by X-ray or pH, slow gravity feeding in an upright position and careful mouth, nose and tube care prevent aspiration and other complications.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient with nausea and vomiting.
answer_html:
Introduction Nausea is an unpleasant feeling of wanting to vomit. Retching is the attempt to vomit without bringing anything up. Vomiting (emesis) is the forceful ejection of stomach contents through the mouth. Persistent vomiting can cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, aspiration and malnutrition.

1. Common causes

  • Gastrointestinal – gastroenteritis, food poisoning, intestinal obstruction, peptic ulcer
  • Drugs – anticancer drugs, opioids, antibiotics, iron, digoxin toxicity
  • Pregnancy – morning sickness, hyperemesis gravidarum
  • Raised intracranial pressure – head injury, meningitis, brain tumour (often projectile vomiting)
  • Metabolic – uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis
  • Post-operative (anaesthesia), motion sickness, severe pain, anxiety

2. Assessment

  • Frequency, amount, timing (relation to meals), force (projectile)
  • Character of vomitus – undigested food, bile-stained (green), coffee-ground (old blood – upper GI bleeding), fresh blood (haematemesis), faecal smell (low intestinal obstruction)
  • Associated symptoms – pain, fever, diarrhoea, headache
  • Signs of dehydration – thirst, dry mouth, low urine output, tachycardia, hypotension, poor skin turgor
  • Intake–output, weight, serum electrolytes

3. Nursing management

During vomiting

  • Place the patient sitting up or turned to the side (lateral position for unconscious or weak patients) to prevent aspiration
  • Keep a kidney tray and tissues within reach; support the head; stay with the patient
  • Loosen tight clothing; provide privacy

After vomiting

  • Give mouth care – rinse with water or mouthwash
  • Remove the vomitus at once, change soiled linen and ventilate the room to remove odours
  • Observe and record the amount and character of vomitus; save a sample if required; report blood or coffee-ground vomitus

Diet and fluids

  • Nil by mouth during acute vomiting if ordered; then small sips of water, ORS or ice chips
  • Progress to dry toast, biscuits, plain rice; small, frequent meals
  • Avoid fatty, spicy, strong-smelling foods; cold foods have less smell
  • Avoid lying flat immediately after meals

Fluid and electrolyte balance

  • Maintain the intake–output chart
  • Give IV fluids as prescribed; watch for hypokalaemia and alkalosis in prolonged vomiting

Medicines – give antiemetics as prescribed (ondansetron, metoclopramide, domperidone, promethazine), e.g. before chemotherapy or meals

Comfort measures – fresh air, a cool cloth on the forehead, slow deep breathing, distraction, relaxation; avoid sudden movements

Others – NG tube aspiration for intestinal obstruction as ordered; treat the cause; teach the patient and family

Conclusion Care of a patient with nausea and vomiting includes positioning to prevent aspiration, mouth care, removal of vomitus, accurate observation and recording, gradual reintroduction of fluids and food, antiemetics and maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient with dysphagia.
answer_html:
Introduction Dysphagia means difficulty in swallowing. It is common after stroke and in neurological diseases. The main dangers are aspiration pneumonia, choking, dehydration and malnutrition, so feeding these patients needs special care.

1. Causes

  • Neurological – stroke, Parkinson's disease, motor neuron disease, myasthenia gravis, head injury, dementia
  • Local – cancer of the mouth, throat or oesophagus, oesophageal stricture, achalasia, mouth ulcers, tonsillitis
  • Ageing – weak muscles, poor teeth, dry mouth

2. Signs of dysphagia

  • Coughing or choking during or after eating or drinking
  • Wet, gurgly voice after swallowing
  • Drooling, food left in the mouth (pocketing), food coming out of the nose
  • Taking a long time to eat, avoiding certain foods, weight loss
  • Repeated chest infections

3. Assessment

  • Bedside swallow screening (e.g. water swallow test) before giving any oral food or fluid, especially after stroke
  • Referral to the speech and language therapist; videofluoroscopy if needed
  • Assess nutritional and hydration status, weight, chest

4. Nursing management

Positioning

  • Sit the patient upright at 90° for meals and for 30–60 minutes after
  • Chin tuck (head slightly flexed) while swallowing protects the airway

Feeding technique

  • Calm, quiet environment; no talking or TV distraction while swallowing
  • Allow enough time; never rush
  • Give small amounts (half to one teaspoon); check that the mouth is empty before the next spoon
  • Place food on the unaffected side of the mouth in stroke patients; check for pocketing on the weak side
  • Encourage the patient to cough and swallow again after each mouthful
  • Stay with the patient throughout; keep suction ready

Diet modification

  • Thickened fluids and soft, moist or pureed foods as recommended (texture levels such as IDDSI)
  • Avoid thin liquids (if not safe), dry and crumbly foods, sticky foods and mixed textures (soup with pieces)

Other care

  • Mouth care before and after meals – reduces bacteria and risk of pneumonia
  • Medicines in liquid form or crushed (if allowed) in puree
  • Monitor – weight, intake–output, hydration, temperature and chest signs (aspiration)
  • Alternative feeding (NG tube or gastrostomy) if oral feeding is unsafe
  • Swallowing exercises as taught by the therapist; teach the family safe feeding
  • Emotional support – patients may feel embarrassed eating in front of others

Conclusion Care of a patient with dysphagia includes swallow screening before oral intake, upright positioning, slow feeding of small amounts of modified-texture food, mouth care, close observation for aspiration and alternative feeding when oral intake is unsafe.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain gastrostomy and jejunostomy feeding and the care of the stoma.
answer_html:
Introduction When tube feeding is needed for a long period (more than 4–6 weeks), a tube is placed directly into the stomach or small intestine through the abdominal wall. This is more comfortable than an NG tube and is less likely to be displaced.

1. Definitions

  • Gastrostomy – a surgical or endoscopic opening into the stomach through the abdominal wall for feeding; PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) is the most common method
  • Jejunostomy – a feeding tube placed into the jejunum (surgically or as PEJ), used when the stomach must be bypassed

2. Indications

  • Long-term dysphagia – stroke, motor neuron disease, cerebral palsy
  • Cancer of the head, neck or oesophagus; oesophageal obstruction
  • Prolonged unconsciousness
  • Jejunostomy – after gastric or oesophageal surgery, gastric outlet obstruction, gastroparesis, high risk of aspiration

3. Feeding procedure

  • Explain; wash hands; position upright (30–45°)
  • Check the external length mark of the tube; for gastrostomy, check the residual volume as per policy
  • Flush with 30 mL water before and after feeds and medicines
  • Gastrostomy – feeds may be given as bolus (by gravity), intermittent or continuous
  • Jejunostomy – feeds are given continuously by pump, never as a rapid bolus, because the jejunum has no reservoir (bolus can cause dumping syndrome – cramps, diarrhoea, sweating, dizziness)
  • Record the feed, water and tolerance

4. Care of the stoma site

  • First days after insertion – keep the site clean and dry with sterile dressing as advised
  • Later, clean daily with soap and water or saline, dry well; dressing usually not needed once healed
  • Inspect for redness, swelling, pain, discharge, leakage of gastric contents and overgrowth of tissue (granulation)
  • PEG tube – after the tract has healed (as per policy), advance the tube slightly and rotate it 360° daily to prevent the internal bumper from becoming buried in the stomach wall (buried bumper syndrome); keep the external plate not too tight
  • Do not rotate jejunostomy tubes
  • Protect the skin from leakage with barrier cream; secure the tube to avoid pulling

5. Complications

  • Infection of the stoma site, leakage and skin excoriation
  • Tube blockage (flush regularly) or dislodgement – cover the stoma and inform at once, because the opening can close within hours
  • Buried bumper syndrome, bleeding, peritonitis (early)
  • Aspiration, diarrhoea, dumping syndrome (jejunal feeding)

6. Teaching for home care

  • Feeding technique, flushing, stoma care, recognising complications and whom to contact

Conclusion Gastrostomy and jejunostomy provide long-term enteral feeding; the nurse gives feeds in the upright position with regular flushing, uses continuous pump feeding for jejunostomy, keeps the stoma clean and dry, rotates PEG tubes to prevent buried bumper, and watches for infection, blockage and dislodgement.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the procedure of feeding a dependent (helpless) patient.
answer_html:
Introduction Patients who are very weak, paralysed, blind, confused or have injured hands may be unable to feed themselves. Assisted feeding ensures that they receive adequate nutrition while keeping their dignity and independence as far as possible.

1. Purposes

  • To meet the patient's nutritional and fluid needs
  • To make mealtime pleasant and stimulate appetite
  • To promote independence gradually
  • To prevent choking and aspiration

2. Preparation of the patient

  • Offer a bedpan or urinal before the meal; wash the patient's hands and face
  • Give mouth care; fix dentures, spectacles and hearing aids
  • Position – sitting upright in bed or in a chair; support with pillows
  • Relieve pain or nausea beforehand; avoid unpleasant procedures just before meals

3. Preparation of the environment

  • Clean, well-ventilated, odour-free surroundings; remove bedpans, dressing trays and soiled articles
  • Clear the over-bed table; keep it at a comfortable height
  • Protected mealtimes – avoid ward rounds and procedures during meals

4. Preparation of the tray

  • Check the diet order and identify the patient
  • Food should be attractive, at the correct temperature and in suitable portions; cover until served
  • Keep a napkin, spoon, glass or feeding cup, straw and adaptive devices ready

5. Procedure

  1. Wash hands; tell the patient what food is served
  2. Place a napkin under the chin; sit at eye level facing the patient
  3. Ask the patient's preference about the order of food; cut food into small pieces
  4. Feed small amounts at a time; allow enough time to chew and swallow
  5. Alternate solids and liquids; use a straw or feeding cup for fluids
  6. Talk pleasantly; do not hurry the patient
  7. Encourage the patient to help himself – hold bread, use built-up spoons, plate guards, non-slip mats
  8. Blind patients – describe where food is placed using the clock method (e.g. "rice at 6 o'clock, dal at 12 o'clock")
  9. Hemiplegic patients – place food on the unaffected side of the mouth; check for food pocketing
  10. Watch for coughing, choking or breathlessness; stop and seek help if they occur

6. After care

  • Wipe the mouth; give mouth care; wash hands
  • Keep the patient upright for 30 minutes
  • Remove the tray; leave the patient comfortable
  • Record – amount eaten (e.g. "half of meal"), fluid intake on the intake chart; report poor intake or difficulty in swallowing

Conclusion Feeding a dependent patient involves preparing the patient, environment and tray, sitting at eye level, giving small amounts with enough time, encouraging self-feeding with adaptive aids, observing for choking, and recording the intake.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN).
answer_html:
Introduction Total parenteral nutrition supplies all nutrients directly into a central vein when the gastrointestinal tract cannot be used. The solution is concentrated and rich in glucose, so careful nursing care is needed to prevent infection, metabolic complications and catheter problems.

1. Before starting

  • Check the prescription and the bag label – patient's name, contents, volume, rate, expiry
  • Inspect the bag – no leaks; lipid emulsion should be uniformly milky white with no oil separation (cracking)
  • Store bags in a refrigerator and take them out about an hour before use; protect from light if required
  • Confirm the position of the central line (X-ray after insertion)

2. Care of the central line

  • Strict aseptic technique for all handling of the line, bag changes and dressings
  • Dedicated lumen for TPN – no blood sampling, blood transfusion or other drugs through the TPN lumen
  • Transparent dressing; change as per policy or when wet, loose or soiled; inspect the site for redness, swelling or discharge
  • Change administration sets as per policy (usually every 24 hours)

3. Administration

  • Give through an infusion pump at a constant rate
  • Start slowly and increase gradually; at the end, taper off – stopping suddenly can cause rebound hypoglycaemia
  • Never speed up the infusion to "catch up" if it falls behind

4. Monitoring

  • Blood glucose every 4–6 hours at first (risk of hyperglycaemia); insulin may be added as prescribed
  • Daily weight, intake–output chart
  • Vital signs and temperature – fever may indicate catheter infection
  • Blood tests – electrolytes (potassium, phosphate, magnesium), urea, creatinine, liver function, triglycerides, blood counts
  • Signs of fluid overload – oedema, breathlessness, crackles

5. Watch for complications

  • Catheter-related bloodstream infection (sepsis)
  • Air embolism, catheter blockage, thrombosis, displacement
  • Pneumothorax (during insertion of a subclavian line)
  • Hyperglycaemia / hypoglycaemia, electrolyte imbalance, refeeding syndrome
  • Fatty liver, liver dysfunction (long-term)

6. General care

  • Mouth care (no oral intake), skin care
  • Psychological support – explain the purpose; patients miss eating
  • Encourage oral or enteral intake as soon as allowed; TPN is reduced gradually as enteral feeding increases
  • Document – rate, volume infused, glucose values, site condition

Conclusion Nursing care of a patient on TPN centres on strict asepsis of the central line, a dedicated lumen, pump-controlled infusion started and stopped gradually, close monitoring of blood glucose, weight, fluid balance and electrolytes, and early detection of infection and metabolic complications.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is total parenteral nutrition (TPN)?
answer_html:
Definition Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is the intravenous administration of all the nutrients needed by the body – dextrose, amino acids, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins, trace elements and water – usually through a central vein (subclavian, internal jugular or PICC line), when the gastrointestinal tract cannot be used.

Indications

  • Intestinal obstruction, short bowel syndrome, prolonged paralytic ileus
  • Severe pancreatitis, severe malabsorption, enterocutaneous fistula
  • Extensive burns, major trauma or sepsis with inability to feed enterally
  • Preterm or very sick newborns

Note – Peripheral parenteral nutrition (PPN) is a less concentrated solution given through a peripheral vein for short periods.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: List high-protein foods. When is a high-protein diet indicated?
answer_html:
High-protein foods

  • Animal sources – eggs, milk and milk products (paneer, curd, cheese), meat, fish, chicken
  • Plant sources – pulses and dals, soybean and soya chunks, groundnuts, nuts, rajma, chana, sprouts
  • Combinations – cereal–pulse mixtures (khichdi, idli, dal-rice) improve protein quality

Indications for a high-protein diet

  • Burns, wounds, pressure ulcers and after surgery (tissue repair)
  • Fractures, prolonged fever, tuberculosis
  • Protein-energy malnutrition, underweight, recovery from illness
  • Pregnancy, lactation and growing children

Caution – protein is restricted in renal failure and hepatic encephalopathy.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is refeeding syndrome?
answer_html:
Definition Refeeding syndrome is a potentially dangerous shift of fluids and electrolytes that occurs when feeding (oral, enteral or parenteral) is restarted too quickly after a period of starvation or severe malnutrition.

Mechanism – feeding raises insulin, which moves phosphate, potassium and magnesium into the cells, causing low blood levels (hypophosphataemia is the key sign); thiamine deficiency also occurs.

At-risk patients – severe malnutrition, prolonged fasting, chronic alcoholism, cancer, eating disorders.

Features – arrhythmias, heart failure, breathlessness, oedema, confusion, seizures.

Prevention – start feeding slowly, give thiamine before feeding, and monitor and correct electrolytes daily.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the nursing measures to improve appetite in a patient with anorexia.
answer_html:
Anorexia is loss of appetite or desire to eat. Nursing measures:

  1. Find and treat the cause – pain, nausea, fever, constipation, drugs, depression
  2. Give mouth care before meals; treat oral ulcers
  3. Serve small, frequent and attractive meals of the patient's favourite and cultural foods
  4. Provide a clean, pleasant, odour-free environment; encourage eating with family or others
  5. Avoid unpleasant procedures and medicines just before meals
  6. Avoid filling fluids just before meals; offer high-calorie, high-protein snacks and supplements
  7. Encourage light activity and fresh air
  8. Give appetite stimulants or antiemetics as prescribed; record intake and weight

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is an orogastric tube? State its indications.
answer_html:
Definition An orogastric (OG) tube is a tube passed through the mouth and oesophagus into the stomach, used for feeding or for drainage.

Indications

  • Newborns, especially preterm babies – they breathe mainly through the nose, so a nasal tube may obstruct breathing
  • Fracture of the base of the skull or severe facial or nasal injury – a nasal tube may enter the brain
  • Nasal obstruction, nasal surgery or choanal atresia
  • Intubated (ventilated) patients
  • Gastric lavage in poisoning (large-bore tube)

Measurement – from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe and then to the xiphisternum (midway to umbilicus in neonates).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Differentiate between bolus and continuous tube feeding.
answer_html:
Point Bolus (intermittent) feeding Continuous feeding
Method A set volume (e.g. 200–300 mL) given over 15–30 minutes by syringe or gravity, 4–6 times a day Feed given slowly over 16–24 hours by an enteral pump
Tube Gastric tubes (NG, gastrostomy) Gastric or jejunal tubes
Advantages Close to normal mealtimes; patient free between feeds; no pump needed Better tolerated; less risk of aspiration, distension and diarrhoea
Disadvantages Risk of distension, nausea, aspiration in weak patients Patient connected to the pump; needs equipment
Suitable for Stable, mobile patients; home feeding Critically ill, unconscious, jejunostomy feeding

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define pressure ulcer. Explain the causes (risk factors), common sites, stages, prevention and nursing management of pressure ulcers.

diagram.caption: Stages of pressure ulcer (cross-section) with common sites (body outline inset)
labels: stage 3 full-thickness loss with fat visible

answer_html:
Introduction A pressure ulcer (bed sore, decubitus ulcer, now also called pressure injury) is a largely preventable complication of illness and immobility. It causes pain, infection, longer hospital stay and higher cost of care, and its presence is often taken as an indicator of the quality of nursing care.

A. Definition

  • A pressure ulcer is a localised injury to the skin and/or underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by pressure, or pressure combined with shear
  • It may also develop under medical devices (oxygen masks, nasogastric tubes, casts, splints)

B. How it develops (pathophysiology)

  • Sustained pressure greater than the capillary closing pressure (about 32 mmHg) squeezes the small blood vessels between the bone and the surface
  • The tissue becomes ischaemic (deprived of oxygen and nutrients); waste products collect
  • If pressure is not relieved, the cells die (necrosis) and an ulcer forms – deep tissues such as muscle are damaged first and most

C. Causes and risk factors

1. Main (external) causes

  • Pressure – intensity and duration of pressure on one area (lying or sitting in one position for long)
  • Shear – the skin stays fixed while the deeper tissues slide, e.g. when the patient slides down in bed with the head end raised; it stretches and tears blood vessels
  • Friction – rubbing of the skin against the sheet, e.g. dragging the patient up the bed
  • Moisture – urine, faeces, sweat and wound drainage soften the skin (maceration)

2. Patient (internal) risk factors

  • Immobility – paralysis, unconsciousness, sedation, fractures, traction, critical illness
  • Reduced sensation – spinal cord injury, stroke, diabetic neuropathy (cannot feel discomfort)
  • Incontinence of urine or faeces
  • Malnutrition – low protein (low albumin), dehydration, anaemia, vitamin C and zinc deficiency
  • Extremes of weight – emaciation (bones prominent) or obesity
  • Old age – thin, fragile skin with less fat and elastic tissue
  • Poor circulation – diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, heart failure, shock
  • Fever, oedema, steroid therapy, smoking
  • Altered consciousness or confusion
  • Poor nursing care – wrinkled or wet linen, crumbs, infrequent turning, ill-fitting splints and devices

D. Common sites

Position Sites
Supine occiput, scapulae, elbows, sacrum and coccyx, heels
Lateral ear, shoulder (acromion), ribs, greater trochanter (hip), medial and lateral knees, malleoli (ankles)
Prone forehead, cheeks, chin, chest/breasts, genitalia (male), knees, toes
Sitting ischial tuberosities, sacrum, scapulae, heels and soles

The sacrum and heels are the most common sites.

E. Stages (NPIAP classification)

Stage 1 – non-blanchable redness

  • Intact skin with a localised area of redness that does not fade (blanch) when pressed
  • In dark skin the colour may look purple, darker or shiny; the area may be painful, warm or cool, firm or soft

Stage 2 – partial-thickness skin loss

  • Loss of the epidermis and part of the dermis; a shallow open ulcer with a pink or red, moist wound bed
  • May appear as an intact or ruptured blister filled with clear fluid
  • No fat visible, no slough

Stage 3 – full-thickness skin loss

  • Damage extends into the subcutaneous fat, which may be visible
  • Slough (yellow dead tissue) may be present; undermining and tunnelling may occur
  • Bone, tendon and muscle are not exposed

Stage 4 – full-thickness tissue loss

  • Muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone exposed or directly felt
  • Slough or eschar (black, hard dead tissue), undermining and tunnelling often present; risk of osteomyelitis

Unstageable – the base is covered by slough or eschar, so the depth cannot be seen until it is removed

Deep tissue pressure injury – intact or broken skin with a persistent deep red, maroon or purple area or a blood-filled blister, showing damage to deeper tissue

F. Prevention

1. Risk assessment

  • Assess every patient on admission and regularly afterwards with a risk assessment scale (e.g. Braden scale) and clinical judgement
  • Plan preventive care for all patients found to be at risk

2. Skin inspection and care

  • Inspect the skin daily, especially over bony prominences and under devices
  • Keep the skin clean and dry; wash with mild soap and warm water, pat dry
  • Manage incontinence promptly; use barrier creams; avoid excessive moisture
  • Do not massage reddened bony prominences – it damages the tissue further
  • Moisturise dry skin

3. Relieving pressure

  • Change the position at least every 2 hours (more often if needed) using a turning schedule
  • Use the 30° lateral tilt position to keep weight off the sacrum and trochanter
  • Use pressure-redistributing support surfaces – alternating air mattress, water or foam mattress, cushions
  • Off-load the heels by placing a pillow under the calves so the heels "float"
  • Chair-bound patients – reposition every hour and teach them to shift weight every 15 minutes
  • Avoid ring (doughnut) cushions – they reduce blood flow to the centre
  • Check and pad medical devices; re-position tubes and masks regularly

4. Reducing shear and friction

  • Lift, do not drag – use a draw sheet or slide sheet and two persons
  • Keep the head end of the bed at 30° or less unless contraindicated; raise the knee rest slightly to prevent sliding
  • Keep linen dry, clean and free of wrinkles and crumbs

5. Nutrition and hydration

  • Adequate calories, protein, fluids, vitamins (especially vitamin C) and zinc; supplements if intake is poor
  • Monitor weight and intake

6. Mobility and teaching

  • Early mobilisation, active and passive exercises
  • Teach the patient and family about turning, skin inspection, nutrition and early reporting

G. Nursing management of an existing pressure ulcer

1. Assessment and documentation

  • Record site, stage, size (length × width × depth in cm), undermining or tunnelling, wound bed (granulation, slough, eschar), exudate (amount, colour, odour), edges and surrounding skin, signs of infection and pain
  • Re-assess at least weekly; photographs may be used with consent

2. Relieve pressure – keep all weight off the ulcer; continue all preventive measures

3. Wound care according to stage

  • Stage 1 – relieve pressure, protect with a transparent film or hydrocolloid, keep clean and dry
  • Stage 2 – clean with normal saline; use moist wound dressings (hydrocolloid, foam, film); protect blisters
  • Stages 3 and 4 – clean and remove dead tissue (debridement) – surgical (sharp), autolytic (moist dressings), enzymatic or mechanical; fill dead space loosely; dressings according to exudate – alginate or foam for heavy exudate, hydrogel for dry wounds; negative pressure wound therapy for large wounds; surgery (flaps, grafts) for some stage 4 ulcers
  • Avoid harsh antiseptics on clean granulating wounds

4. Treat infection – watch for increasing pain, redness, swelling, foul discharge, fever; send wound swab for culture; give antibiotics as prescribed

5. Nutrition – high-protein, high-calorie diet, fluids, vitamin C and zinc as prescribed; monitor albumin and haemoglobin

6. Pain relief – analgesics before dressing changes and turning

7. Psychological support and teaching – explain the plan; involve the family in prevention and home care

Conclusion A pressure ulcer is a localised injury over a bony prominence caused by pressure, shear and friction, worsened by moisture, immobility and poor nutrition; it is staged from non-blanchable redness to full-thickness tissue loss, and is prevented and managed by risk assessment, regular repositioning, support surfaces, skin care, good nutrition and correct stage-based wound care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the factors influencing personal hygiene. Describe the purposes and the procedure of giving a bed bath.
answer_html:
Introduction Hygiene is the science of health and its maintenance; personal hygiene is the self-care by which people keep their bodies clean and well-groomed – bathing, mouth care, hair, nail and perineal care. When patients are ill or weak, nurses help them meet these needs. A bed bath is given to patients who cannot leave the bed and are unable to bathe themselves.

PART A – FACTORS INFLUENCING PERSONAL HYGIENE

  1. Culture – customs about bathing (daily bath, oil massage, bathing before prayer), body odour and grooming differ between cultures
  2. Religion – rituals of cleanliness (ablution before prayer, bathing before worship), modesty and gender of the caregiver
  3. Socioeconomic status – availability of soap, water, toothpaste, clean clothes and bathroom facilities
  4. Personal preferences – time of bath (morning or evening), type of soap, shower or bucket bath
  5. Body image – people who care about their appearance give more attention to hygiene; low self-esteem or depression may lead to neglect
  6. Knowledge – awareness of the link between hygiene and health (e.g. foot care in diabetes, oral care in heart disease)
  7. Developmental stage (age) – infants and young children depend on others; adolescents become concerned with body odour and acne; the elderly may have less energy, poor vision and stiff joints
  8. Physical condition – illness, pain, fatigue, paralysis, fractures, casts, IV lines and limited mobility reduce the ability to self-care
  9. Cognitive and emotional state – confusion, dementia, mental illness and depression may cause neglect of hygiene
  10. Social practices – family habits learnt in childhood, peer influence
  11. Climate and season – more frequent bathing in hot, humid weather
  12. Environment and facilities – privacy, warm water, safe bathroom, assistive devices

PART B – BED BATH

1. Definition

  • A bed bath (sponge bath) is the cleansing of the whole body of a patient who is confined to bed, by the nurse

Types of bath for patients – complete bed bath, partial bed bath (face, hands, axillae, back and perineum only), assisted bath, tub bath and shower; therapeutic baths (e.g. medicated bath, sitz bath) are given for treatment

2. Purposes

  1. To clean the skin and remove sweat, oil, dirt, dead cells and microorganisms
  2. To prevent skin infection and pressure ulcers
  3. To stimulate blood circulation and give mild exercise to the limbs
  4. To give comfort, relaxation and a sense of well-being; to induce sleep
  5. To remove body odour and improve self-esteem
  6. To observe the skin and the patient's general condition (rashes, pressure areas, oedema)
  7. To reduce body temperature (tepid sponging in fever)
  8. To build a nurse–patient relationship and give health teaching

3. Equipment

  • Two basins or a basin and jug of warm water at about 43–46 °C (110–115 °F), bath thermometer, bucket for used water
  • Soap in a soap dish, two washcloths (face and body), two bath towels, bath blanket
  • Mackintosh, clean gown/clothes, clean linen, laundry bag
  • Comb, nail cutter, lotion or oil, powder (if used), mouth-care tray
  • Clean gloves for perineal care, screen

4. Preparation

  • Check the patient's condition and any restrictions; explain the procedure
  • Offer a bedpan or urinal first
  • Close windows and switch off fans – avoid draughts; ensure privacy with screens
  • Hand hygiene; arrange articles within reach; raise the bed to working height
  • Give mouth care first

5. Procedure

  1. Loosen the top linen; replace it with a bath blanket; remove the gown (from the unaffected arm first; if there is an IV line, remove it from the arm without the line first)
  2. Check the water temperature; keep the patient covered except for the part being washed
  3. Eyes – wipe with a wet cloth without soap, from the inner to the outer canthus, using a different part of the cloth for each eye
  4. Face, ears and neck – wash (soap only if the patient wishes), rinse and pat dry
  5. Arms – place a towel under the far arm; wash with long, firm strokes from the wrist towards the axilla (distal to proximal, which helps venous return); wash the axilla; rinse and dry; soak the hand in the basin, clean the nails; repeat on the near arm
  6. Chest and abdomen – cover with a towel; wash, rinse and dry; in women lift the breasts and clean and dry beneath them; clean the umbilicus
  7. Change the water whenever it is cold, soapy or dirty
  8. Legs and feet – wash from ankle to knee to thigh; soak each foot in the basin; dry well between the toes; check heels and toes for pressure areas
  9. Back – turn the patient to the side facing away; wash the back and buttocks, rinse and dry; give back care (gentle massage with lotion, avoiding reddened bony prominences)
  10. Perineal care – change water and wear gloves; give perineal care or allow the patient to do it if able
  11. Apply lotion to dry skin; dress the patient in a clean gown
  12. Comb the hair; trim nails if needed; change the bed linen
  13. Make the patient comfortable in a suitable position; replace the bed, remove screens

6. After care

  • Clean and replace the articles; send linen to the laundry; wash hands
  • Record the procedure, the condition of the skin and pressure areas, and anything abnormal (rashes, redness, wounds, swelling)

7. Important points

  • Expose only the part being washed; maintain modesty and warmth
  • Wash, rinse and dry each part well, especially skin folds
  • Encourage the patient to do as much as possible (promotes independence)
  • Never leave the patient alone; keep side rails up when stepping away
  • Use good body mechanics; perform range-of-motion exercises during the bath
  • Stop and report if the patient becomes breathless, tired, faint or in pain

8. Special considerations

  • Elderly patients – skin is thin and dry; use less soap, warm (not hot) water and moisturiser; bathe every other day if the skin is very dry
  • IV lines, drains, casts and dressings – keep them dry; protect with plastic covers; do not disconnect lines
  • Breathless patients – keep in a sitting position; give rest periods; oxygen continued
  • Patients with paralysis – support the affected limbs; check skin carefully for pressure areas
  • Isolation patients – use dedicated equipment and protective clothing

9. Observations during the bath

  • Colour, temperature and moisture of the skin; pressure areas; rashes, bruises, swelling, wounds
  • Range of movement and muscle strength; level of fatigue or breathlessness
  • The patient's mood, understanding and any complaints (pain, itching)

Conclusion Personal hygiene is influenced by culture, religion, socioeconomic status, preferences, body image, knowledge, age and physical and mental condition; a bed bath cleans the skin, prevents infection and pressure ulcers, stimulates circulation and gives comfort, and must be given systematically with privacy, warmth and observation of the skin.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain oral care (mouth care) for an unconscious patient.
answer_html:
Introduction An unconscious patient cannot eat, drink or clean the mouth, and often breathes through the mouth. Saliva dries, bacteria multiply and sordes, stomatitis, parotitis and aspiration pneumonia may develop. Mouth care every 2–4 hours is therefore an essential nursing responsibility.

1. Purposes

  • To keep the mouth, teeth, gums and tongue clean and moist
  • To prevent infection – stomatitis, gingivitis, parotitis, candidiasis and aspiration pneumonia (ventilator-associated pneumonia in intubated patients)
  • To remove sordes, plaque and odour (halitosis)
  • To observe the condition of the mouth

2. Solutions used

  • Normal saline or clean water
  • Chlorhexidine mouthwash 0.12–0.2% (especially for ventilated patients)
  • Sodium bicarbonate solution (dissolves mucus and crusts)
  • Diluted hydrogen peroxide for crusts (rinse well afterwards)
  • Petroleum jelly or lip balm for the lips

3. Equipment

  • Tray with soft toothbrush or foam swabs, gauze swabs, artery forceps, padded tongue depressor or mouth gag
  • Prescribed solution in a gallipot, kidney tray, towel and mackintosh, gloves, torch
  • Suction apparatus ready, lip balm, paper bag for waste

4. Procedure

  1. Explain to the patient (hearing may be present); hand hygiene; wear gloves
  2. Position – side-lying (lateral) with the head turned to the side and slightly lowered, so that fluid drains out of the mouth and is not aspirated
  3. Place a towel and mackintosh under the chin and a kidney tray against the cheek
  4. Open the mouth gently with a padded tongue depressor or mouth gag – never put fingers between the teeth (the patient may bite)
  5. Inspect the mouth with a torch
  6. Clean the teeth with a soft brush or a swab held in artery forceps, moistened but not dripping – outer, inner and biting surfaces, from gums towards the crown
  7. Clean the gums, palate, inner cheeks and tongue (from back to front); use one swab for each stroke
  8. Suction secretions and fluid as needed
  9. Clean and dry the lips; apply petroleum jelly or lip balm
  10. Remove dentures if any; clean and store them in a labelled container (unconscious patients should not wear dentures)

5. After care

  • Leave the patient comfortable in a safe position; clean the equipment
  • Record – time, solution used, condition of the mouth (coated tongue, ulcers, bleeding, sordes, white patches of thrush); report abnormalities

6. Precautions

  • Use small amounts of fluid; never pour fluid into the mouth
  • Count the swabs; make sure no swab is left in the mouth
  • Clamp the swab firmly in the forceps so it does not slip
  • In intubated patients follow the ventilator care bundle (head end raised 30–45°, oral care with chlorhexidine, subglottic suction)

Conclusion Mouth care for an unconscious patient is given every 2–4 hours in the lateral position with suction ready, using a padded gag, moist (not wet) swabs or a soft brush and a suitable solution; it keeps the mouth clean and moist and prevents infection and aspiration.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain hair care. Add a note on the treatment of pediculosis.
answer_html:
Introduction Clean, well-groomed hair is important for comfort, appearance and self-esteem. Patients confined to bed need help with combing and washing hair, and nurses must recognise and treat pediculosis (lice infestation), which spreads easily.

A. Hair care

1. Purposes

  • To keep the hair and scalp clean, prevent dandruff and infection
  • To stimulate circulation of the scalp
  • To prevent matting and tangling
  • To detect lice, nits, lesions and hair loss
  • To improve appearance, comfort and morale

2. Brushing and combing

  • Daily; comb in small sections from the ends towards the scalp to remove tangles; braid long hair loosely (tight braids pull the scalp)
  • Use the patient's own comb; respect cultural practices (e.g. oiling, covering the hair)

3. Shampoo in bed (main points)

  • Explain; close windows; position the patient diagonally with the head at the edge of the bed
  • Place a mackintosh trough (Kelly's pad) draining into a bucket; plug the ears with cotton and cover the eyes with a folded towel
  • Wet the hair with warm water (about 40–43 °C), apply shampoo, massage the scalp with fingertips, rinse thoroughly
  • Dry quickly with a towel or dryer; comb; make the patient comfortable and warm
  • Contraindicated or done with care in head injury, neck injury, high fever and very weak patients

B. Pediculosis

1. Definition – infestation of the hair or body with lice; eggs are called nits – small, white, oval and firmly attached to the hair shaft near the scalp (unlike dandruff, they do not brush off)

2. Signs – itching, scratch marks, live lice, nits, secondary infection, enlarged neck lymph nodes

3. Treatment

  • Isolate personal articles; the nurse wears gloves and a gown
  • Apply a pediculicide as prescribed – e.g. 1% permethrin cream rinse or lotion (or malathion lotion); leave on for the recommended time, then rinse
  • Wet combing with a fine-toothed (nit) comb to remove lice and nits
  • Repeat after 7–10 days to kill newly hatched lice
  • Wash clothes, linen, towels and combs in hot water and dry in hot sun or dryer; seal items that cannot be washed in a plastic bag for two weeks
  • Examine and treat family members and close contacts
  • Do not use kerosene or other unsafe home remedies – they burn the skin and are flammable
  • Teach the patient not to share combs, caps, towels and pillows

Conclusion Hair care keeps the hair and scalp clean and the patient comfortable through daily combing and shampoo in bed when needed; pediculosis is treated with a pediculicide, nit combing, repeat treatment after a week, hot washing of articles and treatment of contacts.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain perineal and meatal care.
answer_html:
Introduction Perineal care is cleaning of the external genitalia and the surrounding skin (perineum). Meatal care is cleaning of the urinary meatus, especially in patients with an indwelling urinary catheter. Patients who are bedridden, incontinent, post-operative or after childbirth need this care.

1. Purposes

  • To remove secretions, discharge, urine and faeces and odour
  • To prevent infection – urinary tract infection, perineal wound infection
  • To promote healing after childbirth (episiotomy) or perineal surgery
  • To give comfort and maintain skin integrity
  • To observe the area for redness, discharge, lesions or swelling

2. Indications – catheterised patients, incontinence, after delivery, perineal or rectal surgery, unconscious and bedridden patients, patients with vaginal or penile discharge

3. Equipment

  • Clean gloves, jug of warm water, mild soap or prescribed solution, cotton swabs or washcloths
  • Bedpan, mackintosh and towel, sterile perineal pad (after delivery), kidney tray, screen

4. Procedure – female patient

  1. Explain; ensure privacy; hand hygiene; wear gloves
  2. Position in dorsal recumbent position with knees flexed; drape the legs; place the bedpan
  3. Separate the labia with the non-dominant hand
  4. Clean from front to back (pubis towards the anus) using one swab for one stroke – labia majora, labia minora, then the vestibule and urinary meatus
  5. Pour warm water gently over the perineum (from above downward); dry with a towel from front to back
  6. Turn the patient to the side and clean the anal area last
  7. Apply a clean perineal pad if needed

5. Procedure – male patient

  1. Supine position; drape
  2. Hold the penis; retract the foreskin (if uncircumcised)
  3. Clean the glans in a circular motion from the meatus outwards
  4. Replace the foreskin at once (to prevent paraphimosis)
  5. Clean the shaft downwards, then the scrotum (lifting it to clean underneath) and finally the anal area

6. Meatal (catheter) care

  • Clean the meatus and the first few centimetres of the catheter, wiping away from the meatus, with soap and water at least once daily and after every bowel movement
  • Do not pull the catheter; keep it secured to the thigh
  • Avoid powders and lotions around the meatus
  • Observe for redness, discharge, encrustation and leakage

7. After care – remove the bedpan, make the patient comfortable, discard swabs, wash hands, record the condition of the perineum and any discharge

Conclusion Perineal and meatal care removes secretions and prevents infection by cleaning from the cleanest to the dirtiest area – front to back in females and from the meatus outwards in males – with one swab per stroke, with special daily meatal care for catheterised patients.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the care of feet and nails, with special reference to diabetic foot care.
answer_html:
Introduction Feet carry the body's weight and are easily injured. Poor foot and nail care leads to corns, calluses, fungal infection and ingrown nails. In diabetic patients, nerve damage and poor circulation mean that a small injury can become an ulcer, gangrene or amputation, so foot care is vital.

1. Assessment

  • Skin – dryness, cracks (especially heels), corns, calluses, blisters, wounds, redness
  • Between the toes – maceration, fungal infection (athlete's foot)
  • Nails – length, thickness, discolouration, ingrown toenail, fungal nails
  • Circulation – colour, temperature, pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial), oedema
  • Sensation – with a monofilament or cotton wisp
  • Footwear and deformities (bunion, hammer toes)

2. Routine foot care

  1. Wash the feet daily in warm (not hot) water with mild soap; check water temperature with the elbow or thermometer
  2. Dry thoroughly, especially between the toes
  3. Apply moisturising lotion on dry skin, but not between the toes
  4. Wear clean, dry socks and well-fitting footwear
  5. Do not walk barefoot

3. Nail care

  • Trim nails after a bath when they are soft
  • Fingernails – cut following the curve of the fingertip; file rough edges
  • Toenails – cut straight across, not too short, and file the edges – this prevents ingrown toenails
  • Clean under the nails with an orange stick, not a sharp instrument
  • Patients with diabetes, poor circulation or thick nails should have nails cut by a trained person (or only filed)

4. Special foot care in diabetes

  • Inspect the feet every day (use a mirror for the soles) for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling
  • Never walk barefoot, even at home
  • Avoid hot water bottles, heating pads and soaking feet for long periods (risk of burns and maceration)
  • Do not cut corns or calluses or use corn plasters; see a doctor or podiatrist
  • Wear soft, closed, well-fitting shoes; check inside shoes for stones before wearing
  • Keep blood sugar well controlled; stop smoking
  • Report any wound, colour change or loss of sensation immediately
  • Have feet examined at every clinic visit

5. Exercises – foot and ankle exercises, walking; avoid crossing legs and tight socks (improve circulation)

Conclusion Care of the feet and nails includes daily inspection, washing and thorough drying, moisturising, cutting toenails straight across and wearing proper footwear; diabetic patients need special daily inspection, protection from injury and burns, and prompt reporting of wounds to prevent ulcers and amputation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the care of assistive devices – dentures, spectacles, contact lenses, artificial eye and hearing aids.
answer_html:
Introduction Many patients use assistive devices for chewing, seeing and hearing. When they are ill, nurses must care for these devices so that they stay clean, safe and undamaged, and are returned to the patient – losing or breaking them causes great distress and expense.

1. Dentures

  • Removal – wear gloves; hold the upper denture with gauze and break the suction by moving it gently up and down; remove the upper first, then the lower (lift up and rotate out)
  • Cleaning – over a basin lined with a towel or partly filled with water (prevents breakage if dropped); brush all surfaces with a soft brush and denture cleaner; rinse in cool or lukewarm water (hot water warps them)
  • Storage – in a labelled denture cup with water or soaking solution when not in use (e.g. at night); never wrap in tissue (may be thrown away)
  • Clean the patient's gums and tongue; inspect for sores; reinsert moist dentures
  • Remove dentures from unconscious patients and before surgery

2. Spectacles (eyeglasses)

  • Clean with warm water and a soft cloth (or lens cleaner); dry with a soft tissue
  • Hold by the frame, not the lenses; store in a labelled case within the patient's reach
  • Never place lenses face down on a surface

3. Contact lenses

  • Hand hygiene before handling; use only the prescribed sterile lens solution – never tap water or saliva
  • Remove before sleep and surgery, and from unconscious patients (can cause corneal damage)
  • Store in a labelled case marked left (L) and right (R)
  • Watch for redness, pain, watering – remove and report

4. Artificial eye (ocular prosthesis)

  • Removal – pull the lower eyelid down and press gently below the eye; the prosthesis slides out
  • Clean with warm water or normal saline; dry with soft gauze
  • Clean the socket and eyelids with saline swabs from inner to outer canthus; observe for discharge or redness
  • Reinsert (lift the upper lid, slide in, then pull the lower lid down) or store in a labelled container with saline

5. Hearing aids

  • Check that the battery works and the device is switched on; adjust volume
  • Remove before bathing, shampooing, sleeping and X-rays; switch off and store in a labelled case (open the battery compartment)
  • Clean the earmould with a dry soft cloth; keep away from water, heat and hair spray
  • Clean the ear canal of wax as advised; observe for soreness
