6. General principles

  • Record all devices on admission; label containers with the patient's name
  • Keep devices within reach and return them promptly (communication, orientation and nutrition depend on them)
  • Encourage the patient to care for the device independently where possible

Conclusion Care of assistive devices involves correct removal, gentle cleaning with suitable solutions, safe storage in labelled containers and prompt return to the patient, so that the devices last and the patient can eat, see, hear and communicate.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain back care (back massage).
answer_html:
Introduction Back care is cleaning and gentle massage of the back. It is given to bedridden patients usually after the bath and at bedtime and is a valuable nursing comfort measure.

1. Purposes

  • To stimulate circulation to the skin and muscles
  • To relieve muscle tension, promote relaxation and sleep
  • To inspect the skin for redness or breakdown over pressure areas
  • To give comfort and a chance for communication

2. Contraindications and precautions

  • Do not massage reddened areas over bony prominences – it can damage the tissue
  • Avoid in fractured ribs or spine, back surgery or wounds, burns of the back, and when the patient cannot tolerate turning
  • Caution in severe cardiac or respiratory distress
  • Never massage the legs (risk of dislodging a clot in deep vein thrombosis)

3. Equipment

  • Basin of warm water, soap, towel, washcloth, lotion or oil, powder (optional), gloves if needed, clean linen

4. Procedure

  1. Explain; ensure privacy; hand hygiene; check the room is warm
  2. Position the patient prone or side-lying; expose the back from shoulders to sacrum; drape the rest
  3. Wash, rinse and dry the back
  4. Warm the lotion in your hands before applying
  5. Effleurage – long, smooth, gliding strokes from the sacrum up to the shoulders and back down the sides, without lifting the hands from the skin
  6. Petrissage – gentle kneading of the large muscles (shoulders, sides) by lifting and squeezing
  7. Friction – small circular movements with the palms or fingertips over muscle (not over bony points)
  8. Finish with effleurage for 2–3 minutes; total massage about 3–5 minutes
  9. Wipe off excess lotion; straighten and tighten the linen; replace the gown
  10. Make the patient comfortable; dispose of articles; wash hands

5. Observation and recording

  • Note the condition of the skin – redness that does not fade, blisters, dryness, rashes
  • Record the time, the care given and the patient's response; report early signs of pressure injury

Conclusion Back care – washing and gentle massage using effleurage, petrissage and friction – improves circulation, relaxes the patient and allows inspection of pressure areas, but massage is never done over reddened bony prominences.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Name the types of pediculi.
answer_html:
Pediculi (lice) are small, wingless, blood-sucking insects. Their eggs are called nits.

Type Common name Where found Condition
Pediculus humanus capitis Head louse Scalp hair, behind the ears, nape of neck Pediculosis capitis
Pediculus humanus corporis Body louse Lives in the seams of clothing, feeds on the body Pediculosis corporis – can spread epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, trench fever
Pthirus pubis Crab (pubic) louse Pubic hair, axillary hair, eyelashes Pediculosis pubis – spread by close (sexual) contact

Signs – itching, scratch marks and nits stuck firmly to the hair shafts.

Prevention – regular hair washing and combing; do not share combs, caps, towels or bedding.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: List the causes of pressure sores.
answer_html:
Main causes

  1. Pressure – prolonged pressure over bony prominences
  2. Shear – sliding of deep tissues while the skin stays fixed
  3. Friction – rubbing or dragging the skin on the sheet
  4. Moisture – urine, faeces, sweat

Contributing factors

  • Immobility – paralysis, unconsciousness, sedation, fractures
  • Reduced sensation (spinal cord injury, neuropathy)
  • Incontinence
  • Malnutrition, dehydration, anaemia, low albumin
  • Old age, emaciation or obesity
  • Poor circulation (diabetes, heart failure), fever, oedema
  • Wrinkled or wet linen, crumbs, infrequent turning, ill-fitting devices

Common sites – sacrum, heels, hips (greater trochanter), elbows, shoulder blades and back of the head.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define the following: halitosis, stomatitis, gingivitis, sordes.
answer_html:
• Halitosis – foul-smelling breath; caused by poor oral hygiene, dental caries, gum disease, infections, some foods and systemic disease
  • Stomatitis – inflammation of the mucous membrane of the mouth, with redness, ulcers and pain; caused by infection, vitamin B deficiency, chemotherapy, poor oral hygiene
  • Gingivitis – inflammation of the gums, with redness, swelling and bleeding on brushing; caused mainly by plaque
  • Sordes – dried crusts of mucus, food particles and bacteria on the teeth and lips, seen in patients with fever, dehydration, mouth breathing or unconsciousness who do not receive mouth care

Other terms – glossitis (inflammation of the tongue), cheilosis (cracks at the corners of the mouth), pyorrhoea (pus from the gums), parotitis (inflammation of the parotid gland).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Differentiate between shear and friction.
answer_html:
Point Shear Friction
Meaning Skin stays fixed while the deeper tissues slide over the bone Rubbing of the skin surface against another surface
Example Patient slides down in bed with the head end raised above 30° Dragging the patient up the bed on the sheet
Damage Stretches and tears deep blood vessels – deep tissue injury Abrasion of the epidermis – superficial injury
Prevention Keep the head end at 30° or less, raise the knee rest, use slide sheets Lift, do not drag; use a draw sheet; keep linen smooth; protective films

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is xerostomia? State the nursing measures.
answer_html:
Definition Xerostomia is dryness of the mouth due to reduced or absent saliva.

Causes – drugs (antihistamines, anticholinergics, diuretics, antidepressants), dehydration, mouth breathing, oxygen therapy, radiotherapy to the head and neck, Sjögren's syndrome, old age.

Nursing measures

  • Frequent sips of water and adequate fluid intake
  • Regular mouth care; avoid alcohol-based mouthwashes
  • Saliva substitutes, sugar-free chewing gum or sour sweets to stimulate saliva
  • Lip balm; humidified oxygen
  • Avoid caffeine, smoking and dry, spicy foods

Complications – difficulty in chewing, swallowing and speaking, altered taste, dental caries and oral candidiasis.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD)?
answer_html:
Definition Incontinence-associated dermatitis is inflammation and erosion of the skin caused by prolonged contact with urine or faeces.

Features – diffuse redness, moist and shiny skin, superficial erosions in the perineum, buttocks, groins and inner thighs; burning or itching; often with fungal infection. Unlike a pressure ulcer, it is not limited to a bony prominence and is not deep.

Prevention and care

  • Clean promptly after each episode with a gentle, pH-balanced cleanser; pat dry
  • Apply a barrier cream or film
  • Use absorbent pads and change them often; treat the cause of incontinence
  • Treat fungal infection as prescribed

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define urinary catheterisation. Explain the types of catheters, indications, equipment, procedure of catheterisation and the care of a patient with an indwelling catheter.

diagram.caption: Indwelling (Foley) catheter in the bladder
labels: inflated balloon in the bladder neck
closed drainage bag below bladder level

answer_html:
Introduction Urinary catheterisation is a common but invasive nursing procedure. It relieves retention and allows accurate measurement of urine, but it is also the leading cause of hospital-acquired urinary tract infection. It must therefore be done only when truly needed, with strict aseptic technique, and the catheter must be removed as early as possible.

A. Definition

  • Urinary catheterisation is the introduction of a sterile catheter through the urethra into the urinary bladder to drain urine
  • Intermittent (straight) catheterisation – the catheter is removed as soon as the bladder is emptied
  • Indwelling catheterisation – the catheter is left in place, held by an inflated balloon, and connected to a closed drainage system

B. Types of catheters

1. According to duration and design

  • Straight (Nelaton) catheter – single lumen, no balloon; for intermittent catheterisation and specimen collection
  • Foley (indwelling) catheter – two-way (one lumen for drainage, one for inflating the balloon)
  • Three-way Foley catheter – an extra lumen for continuous bladder irrigation (after prostate surgery)
  • Coudé catheter – curved, firm tip; for men with an enlarged prostate or strictures
  • Suprapubic catheter – inserted through the abdominal wall into the bladder (urethral injury, long-term use)
  • External (condom) catheter – a sheath worn over the penis for incontinent men

2. According to material

  • Latex (short-term; risk of allergy), PTFE-coated latex, silicone (long-term, less encrustation), hydrogel-coated, silver-alloy coated

3. Sizes

  • Measured in French (Fr) or Charrière (Ch) units – 1 Fr = 0.33 mm of outer diameter
  • Adult female 12–14 Fr, adult male 14–16 Fr, children 6–10 Fr; use the smallest size that drains well
  • Standard balloon 10 mL, inflated with sterile water

C. Indications

  1. Acute urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction
  2. Accurate measurement of urine output in critically ill patients
  3. Before, during and after certain surgeries – urological, gynaecological, long operations, spinal or epidural anaesthesia
  4. To help heal open sacral or perineal wounds in incontinent patients
  5. Prolonged immobilisation – unstable spinal or pelvic fractures
  6. Comfort in end-of-life care
  7. To obtain a sterile urine specimen, measure residual urine, irrigate the bladder or instil medicine
  8. Diagnostic tests – cystogram, urodynamic studies

Contraindications – suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus after pelvic trauma); caution in urethral stricture and acute prostatitis

D. Equipment

  • Sterile catheterisation pack – sterile towels (drapes), gallipot, cotton balls or gauze, forceps, kidney tray
  • Sterile gloves, antiseptic solution or sterile normal saline for meatal cleaning
  • Sterile lubricant – 2% lignocaine gel (especially for men)
  • Catheter of correct size (and a spare), 10 mL syringe with sterile water
  • Sterile closed drainage bag with tubing, bag holder, catheter securement device or tape
  • Specimen container, mackintosh, bath blanket, torch, screen, clean gloves for perineal care

E. Procedure – female patient

  1. Check the order; identify the patient; explain and obtain consent; ensure privacy
  2. Hand hygiene; give perineal care with clean gloves; remove gloves and wash hands
  3. Position – dorsal recumbent with knees flexed and separated (or Sims' lateral position if she cannot abduct the hips); drape the legs; ensure good light
  4. Open the sterile pack; put on sterile gloves; arrange the drape under the buttocks
  5. Lubricate the catheter tip; attach the drainage bag (if not pre-connected)
  6. With the non-dominant hand, separate the labia and keep them apart – this hand is now not sterile
  7. Clean the meatus with the dominant hand using forceps and swabs, from front to back, one swab per stroke – far labium, near labium, then down the centre over the meatus
  8. Ask the patient to take a deep breath; insert the catheter gently into the meatus about 5–7.5 cm until urine flows, then advance a further 2.5–5 cm
  9. If the catheter enters the vagina by mistake, leave it there as a landmark and insert a new sterile catheter into the urethra
  10. Inflate the balloon with the recommended volume of sterile water; then pull back gently until resistance is felt
  11. Secure the catheter to the inner thigh, leaving slack to avoid pulling
  12. Hang the bag below the level of the bladder and off the floor

F. Procedure – male patient (differences)

  • Supine position with legs slightly apart
  • Retract the foreskin; clean the glans in a circular motion from the meatus outwards
  • Instil about 10 mL of lignocaine gel into the urethra and wait 3–5 minutes for it to act
  • Hold the penis upright (about 90° to the body) with gentle traction; insert 17–22 cm until urine flows, then advance up to the Y-junction (bifurcation) before inflating the balloon – this prevents inflating the balloon in the urethra
  • If resistance is felt at the prostate, ask him to breathe deeply; never force the catheter
  • Replace the foreskin (to prevent paraphimosis); secure the catheter to the upper thigh or lower abdomen

G. After the procedure

  • Note the amount, colour and appearance of the urine; send a specimen if ordered
  • If a very large volume drains in retention, follow hospital policy and watch for haematuria and hypotension
  • Make the patient comfortable; dispose of waste; wash hands
  • Record – date, time, reason, catheter type and size, balloon volume, amount and nature of urine, and the patient's response

H. Care of a patient with an indwelling catheter

  1. Keep the drainage system closed – do not disconnect the catheter from the tubing
  2. Unobstructed flow – no kinks or loops; the patient should not lie on the tubing
  3. Bag below bladder level at all times (also during transport) and never on the floor
  4. Empty the bag when about two-thirds full into a separate clean container for each patient; the drainage tap must not touch the container
  5. Meatal care with soap and water daily and after bowel movements
  6. Secure the catheter to prevent pulling and urethral injury
  7. Fluid intake 2–3 litres a day (unless restricted) to flush the bladder
  8. Collect specimens from the sampling port with aseptic technique, never from the bag
  9. Hand hygiene and gloves for every handling
  10. Monitor urine output, colour, clarity and odour; watch for fever, cloudy or foul-smelling urine, suprapubic pain, blood, leakage around the catheter or blockage
  11. Review the need every day and remove as early as possible
  12. Change the catheter only when indicated or as advised by the manufacturer

I. Removal of an indwelling catheter

  • Explain; empty the bag; deflate the balloon completely with a syringe (never cut the catheter)
  • Withdraw the catheter gently while the patient breathes out
  • Encourage fluids; monitor the first voiding – the patient should pass urine within 6–8 hours; measure volumes and watch for retention, burning or frequency

J. Complications of catheterisation

  • Catheter-associated urinary tract infection – the most common
  • Trauma to the urethra, false passage, haematuria
  • Paraphimosis (foreskin not replaced)
  • Bladder spasms, leakage around the catheter (bypassing), blockage and encrustation
  • Urethral stricture, bladder stones (long-term)
  • Failure of the balloon to deflate; latex allergy

Conclusion Urinary catheterisation is the aseptic introduction of a catheter into the bladder for drainage; correct choice of catheter, careful technique for male and female patients, a closed and unobstructed drainage system, meatal care and early removal reduce trauma and catheter-associated infection.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the factors affecting micturition.
answer_html:
Introduction Micturition (urination, voiding) is the process of emptying the urinary bladder. Normal adults pass about 1–2 litres of urine a day, voiding 5–6 times. Many physical, psychological and social factors affect how often and how well a person passes urine.

1. Developmental factors (age)

  • Infants and young children – voiding is reflex; voluntary control develops at about 2–3 years
  • Pregnancy – pressure of the uterus on the bladder causes frequency
  • Elderly – smaller bladder capacity, weak muscles, nocturia; enlarged prostate in men causes hesitancy and retention; weak pelvic floor in women after menopause causes stress incontinence

2. Food and fluid intake

  • More fluid → more urine; less fluid, sweating, vomiting and diarrhoea → less urine
  • Caffeine (tea, coffee) and alcohol increase urine output (diuretic effect)
  • High-salt foods cause water retention

3. Psychological factors

  • Anxiety and stress cause urgency and frequency
  • Lack of privacy, embarrassment or fear of pain may cause retention
  • The sound of running water may help a person to void

4. Activity and muscle tone

  • Immobility leads to incomplete emptying and stasis of urine (infection, stones)
  • Weak pelvic floor and abdominal muscles (childbirth, obesity, ageing) reduce control

5. Personal habits and position

  • Most people void at fixed times (on waking, before sleep) and need privacy
  • Normal position – men usually stand and women sit or squat; bedpans and lying positions make voiding difficult

6. Socio-cultural factors

  • Cultural norms of privacy, availability of toilet facilities (schools, workplaces, travel) – people may hold urine for long periods

7. Pathological conditions

  • Kidney disease, heart failure, shock – reduced output
  • Diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus – polyuria
  • Spinal cord injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis – neurogenic bladder
  • Prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, stones – obstruction and retention
  • Urinary tract infection – frequency, urgency, dysuria
  • Dementia – incontinence

8. Surgical and diagnostic procedures

  • Anaesthesia, especially spinal anaesthesia, and opioid analgesia cause retention
  • Pelvic and abdominal surgery; cystoscopy may cause swelling, haematuria and retention

9. Medications

  • Diuretics increase urine output
  • Anticholinergics, antihistamines, opioids, some antidepressants cause retention
  • Some drugs change urine colour – rifampicin (orange-red), vitamin B complex (bright yellow), methylene blue (blue-green)

10. Climate

  • Hot weather → more sweating → less urine; cold weather → more urine

Conclusion Micturition is affected by age, fluid and food intake, psychological state, muscle tone and activity, habits and privacy, culture, diseases, surgery, drugs and climate; the nurse considers these factors while assessing and helping patients with urinary elimination.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the alterations in urinary elimination.
answer_html:
Introduction Alterations in urinary elimination are problems in the production, storage or emptying of urine. Nurses must recognise them early, record them correctly and give appropriate care.

1. Urinary retention

  • Accumulation of urine in the bladder because of inability to empty it
  • Acute (sudden, painful) or chronic (gradual, painless, with overflow dribbling)
  • Causes – enlarged prostate, urethral stricture, anaesthesia, opioids, pain after surgery, anxiety, lack of privacy, spinal cord injury
  • Signs – distended bladder felt above the symphysis, suprapubic discomfort, restlessness, frequent passing of small amounts (overflow)
  • Care – privacy, normal position, running water, warm water over the perineum, analgesia; catheterisation if these fail

2. Urinary incontinence – involuntary leakage of urine

  • Stress – leakage on coughing, sneezing, lifting (weak pelvic floor)
  • Urge – sudden strong urge followed by leakage (overactive bladder)
  • Overflow – dribbling from an over-full bladder (obstruction, neurogenic bladder)
  • Functional – normal bladder but unable to reach the toilet in time (immobility, dementia)
  • Reflex – emptying without awareness (spinal cord injury)
  • Total – continuous unpredictable loss; mixed – combination

3. Enuresis

  • Involuntary passing of urine after the age at which control is expected (about 5 years); nocturnal enuresis = bed-wetting at night

4. Changes in the amount of urine

  • Polyuria – excessive urine output (more than about 3 litres/day) – diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, diuretics
  • Oliguria – reduced output (less than 400 mL/day or less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour) – dehydration, shock, kidney failure
  • Anuria – less than 100 mL/day – acute kidney failure, complete obstruction

5. Changes in the pattern of voiding

  • Frequency – voiding more often than usual (infection, pregnancy, anxiety)
  • Urgency – sudden strong need to void
  • Nocturia – waking at night to void (prostate enlargement, heart failure, elderly)
  • Dysuria – painful or burning urination (infection, stones)
  • Hesitancy – difficulty in starting the stream (prostate enlargement)

6. Changes in the character of urine

  • Haematuria – blood in urine (stones, injury, tumour, infection)
  • Pyuria – pus in urine (infection); proteinuria, glycosuria, ketonuria
  • Cloudy, foul-smelling or dark urine

7. Urinary tract infection – frequency, urgency, dysuria, suprapubic pain, fever, cloudy urine

Nurse's role

  • Accurate intake–output charting; observation of urine; bladder palpation
  • Prompt reporting of oliguria or anuria (less than 30 mL/hour in an adult)
  • Toileting assistance, catheter care, skin care for incontinent patients, health teaching

Conclusion Alterations in urinary elimination include retention, the various types of incontinence, enuresis, changes in urine volume (polyuria, oliguria, anuria), changes in voiding pattern and in the character of urine; early recognition and accurate recording guide nursing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define urinary diversion. Explain its types and the nursing care of a patient with urinary diversion.

diagram.caption: Ileal conduit urinary diversion
labels: ureters implanted into an isolated segment of ileum
stoma on the right lower abdomen

answer_html:
Introduction When the bladder is removed (as in bladder cancer) or cannot be used, urine must leave the body by a new route. This is called urinary diversion. Patients need skilled nursing care and teaching to live normally with it.

1. Definition

  • Urinary diversion is a surgical procedure that re-routes the flow of urine from the kidneys to a new exit, usually a stoma (urostomy) on the abdominal wall or a newly made reservoir

2. Indications

  • Cancer of the bladder (after cystectomy), pelvic cancers
  • Severe trauma to the bladder or urethra
  • Neurogenic bladder, congenital defects (e.g. bladder exstrophy), obstruction, fistulae

3. Types

a. Incontinent diversions (urine drains continuously into a bag)

  • Ileal conduit – the most common; the ureters are joined to an isolated segment of ileum, one end of which is brought out as a stoma, usually on the right lower abdomen
  • Cutaneous ureterostomy – the ureters are brought directly out to the skin
  • Nephrostomy – a tube placed through the skin directly into the renal pelvis (often temporary, for obstruction)
  • Suprapubic cystostomy – a catheter into the bladder through the abdominal wall

b. Continent diversions

  • Continent cutaneous reservoir (e.g. Kock pouch, Indiana pouch) – an internal pouch made of bowel with a valve; the patient drains it with a catheter 4–6 times a day; no external bag
  • Orthotopic neobladder – a pouch of bowel joined to the urethra; the patient passes urine through the urethra by relaxing the pelvic muscles and straining

4. Nursing care

Before surgery

  • Explanation and counselling; stoma site marking (flat area, visible to the patient, away from skin folds and belt line); bowel preparation as ordered

After surgery

  • Stoma assessment – a healthy stoma is red or pink, moist and shiny; a pale, dusky or black stoma (poor blood supply) must be reported at once
  • Urine output – measure hourly at first; ureteric stents may be in place; report output less than 30 mL/hour
  • Mucus in the urine is normal with an ileal conduit (from the bowel lining)
  • Appliance care – use a urostomy pouch with an anti-reflux valve and drain tap; cut the opening to fit the stoma; empty when one-third to half full; connect to a night drainage bag; change every 3–5 days or if leaking
  • Peristomal skin care – clean with warm water, dry, use skin barrier; check for irritation and crystals
  • Fluid intake 2–3 litres a day to prevent infection and stones
  • Watch for complications – infection, leakage, stoma stenosis or retraction, stones, electrolyte imbalance (metabolic acidosis)
  • Continent pouches – teach clean intermittent self-catheterisation and pouch irrigation to clear mucus

Teaching and support

  • Self-care of the stoma and appliance, diet and fluids, recognising complications
  • Body image and sexuality concerns; referral to a stoma nurse and support groups; return to normal activities

Conclusion Urinary diversion re-routes urine through an ileal conduit, ureterostomy, nephrostomy, continent reservoir or neobladder; nursing care focuses on stoma and skin care, accurate output monitoring, appliance management, prevention of infection and complications, and teaching and emotional support.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the procedure of giving a bedpan and urinal.
answer_html:
Introduction Patients who cannot walk to the toilet use a bedpan (for defecation and, in women, urination) or a urinal (for urination). Giving them correctly maintains dignity, comfort, hygiene and skin integrity.

1. Types

  • Regular bedpan – for patients who can raise their hips
  • Fracture (slipper) pan – flat, with one shallow end; for patients with hip fractures, casts, spinal injury, the elderly and those who cannot raise the hips
  • Male urinal – bottle with an angled neck; female urinal – wider opening shaped to fit the perineum

2. Equipment

  • Clean, dry, warmed bedpan with cover, toilet paper, mackintosh, clean gloves
  • Bowl of water, soap and towel for the patient's hand washing; air freshener; screen

3. Procedure – giving the bedpan

  1. Respond promptly when the patient asks; explain; ensure privacy
  2. Hand hygiene; wear gloves; warm the bedpan with water and dry it
  3. Lower the head end; fold back the top linen; place a mackintosh under the buttocks
  4. If the patient can help – ask him to flex the knees and lift the hips; slide the bedpan under the buttocks with the wide rounded end under the buttocks
  5. If the patient cannot lift – turn him on the side away from you, place the bedpan firmly against the buttocks, then roll him back onto it
  6. Use the fracture pan with the flat end under the buttocks for patients who must not move
  7. Raise the head end to a sitting position (if allowed) – this is the natural position for elimination
  8. Check the position; cover the patient; keep toilet paper and the call bell within reach
  9. Leave the patient alone if safe; return promptly

4. Removing the bedpan

  1. Wear gloves; lower the head end
  2. Ask the patient to lift the hips (or roll him to the side) while you hold the bedpan steady to avoid spilling
  3. Clean the perineum from front to back if the patient cannot do it
  4. Remove the mackintosh; offer water for hand washing
  5. Observe the urine or stool – amount, colour, consistency, odour, blood; measure if on intake–output; collect a specimen if ordered
  6. Empty, clean and disinfect the bedpan; ventilate the room
  7. Record the output and observations

5. Giving a urinal

  • Male – place the urinal between the legs and position the penis inside it, or let the patient do it; he may stand at the bedside if allowed
  • Female – place the female urinal firmly against the perineum
  • Remove promptly; empty, measure and clean; do not leave urinals on the bed for long

6. Precautions

  • Never leave a patient on a bedpan for too long – risk of pressure injury and discomfort
  • Check the skin for redness; keep the patient covered; maintain dignity

Conclusion Giving a bedpan or urinal requires prompt response, privacy, a warm dry pan, correct placement (rolling the patient if necessary), a sitting position where allowed, careful removal, perineal hygiene, observation of output and accurate recording.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain condom (external) catheter drainage.
answer_html:
Introduction A condom catheter is a soft sheath that fits over the penis and is connected to a drainage bag. It is a non-invasive alternative to an indwelling catheter for incontinent men, with a lower risk of infection.

1. Indications

  • Male urinary incontinence – elderly, dementia, stroke, spinal cord injury – when the bladder empties completely
  • To keep the skin dry and protect pressure areas and wounds

2. Contraindications

  • Urinary retention or incomplete emptying (needs catheterisation)
  • Injury, ulcers, rash or swelling of the penis; very retracted penis
  • Latex allergy (use silicone sheaths)

3. Equipment

  • Condom catheter of correct size (use the sizing guide), skin protectant, drainage bag (leg bag or bedside bag), gloves, basin of warm water, soap, towel, scissors (to clip hair), screen

4. Procedure

  1. Explain; ensure privacy; hand hygiene; wear gloves
  2. Position the patient supine; give perineal care – wash the penis with soap and water, dry thoroughly; clip (do not shave) long pubic hair near the base
  3. Apply a skin protectant and let it dry
  4. Hold the penis and roll the sheath on, leaving 2.5–5 cm (1–2 inches) of space between the tip of the penis and the end of the sheath – prevents irritation and allows free drainage
  5. Secure with the self-adhesive layer or the strap provided – firm but not tight; never use ordinary adhesive tape around the penis (it can cut off blood supply)
  6. Connect to the drainage bag placed below the level of the bladder; check that the tubing is not twisted
  7. Make the patient comfortable; dispose of waste; record

5. Care

  • Check the penis within 30 minutes of application and then every few hours for swelling, colour change, irritation or maceration
  • Change the sheath every 24 hours (or as per manufacturer); wash and dry the penis each time and allow the skin to air
  • Keep the drainage system free-flowing; empty the bag regularly
  • Measure urine output and observe its character

6. Complications – skin irritation and breakdown, swelling and restricted circulation if too tight, leakage, sheath twisting or falling off, urinary infection (less common)

Conclusion A condom catheter provides non-invasive drainage for incontinent men who empty the bladder completely; correct size, a gap at the tip, secure but loose fixing, daily changing and frequent skin checks prevent complications.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain bladder irrigation.
answer_html:
Introduction Bladder irrigation is the washing out of the bladder with a sterile solution through a catheter. It is mainly used after prostate and bladder surgery to prevent blood clots from blocking the catheter.

1. Purposes

  • To prevent clot formation and catheter blockage after transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) or bladder surgery
  • To remove clots, mucus or debris
  • To instil medicines into the bladder (e.g. anticancer drugs)

2. Types

  • Continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) – sterile fluid flows continuously into the bladder through a three-way Foley catheter and drains out through the drainage lumen
  • Intermittent irrigation – a set volume is instilled with a syringe or bag through a closed system and then allowed to drain
  • Bladder washout – done when a catheter is blocked, only as ordered

3. Solution – sterile normal saline at room temperature (or as prescribed), usually in 3-litre bags

4. Procedure of continuous bladder irrigation

  1. Check the order; explain; hand hygiene; maintain aseptic technique
  2. Hang the irrigation bag on a stand; prime the tubing to remove air
  3. Clean the irrigation port of the three-way catheter and connect the tubing
  4. Regulate the flow to keep the drainage light pink or clear – increase the rate if the drainage becomes red or contains clots
  5. Make sure the outflow is free and the drainage bag is below bladder level; empty it often (it fills quickly)

5. Monitoring and nursing care

  • Intake–output chart – true urine output = total drainage minus the irrigation fluid used
  • Colour of drainage – bright red with clots suggests bleeding; report
  • Signs of blockage – drainage stops or decreases, lower abdominal pain, bladder distension, spasms, leakage around the catheter – stop the irrigation, check the tubing for kinks, and do a washout or inform the doctor as ordered
  • Bladder spasms – give antispasmodics/analgesics as prescribed
  • Vital signs; watch for signs of fluid absorption and low sodium after TURP (confusion, nausea, hypertension then hypotension)
  • Catheter care, fluids by mouth 2–3 litres if allowed
  • Irrigation is usually stopped when the drainage stays clear for some time

Conclusion Bladder irrigation washes out the bladder with sterile saline, usually continuously through a three-way catheter after prostate or bladder surgery; the nurse adjusts the flow to keep drainage light pink, calculates true urine output and watches for clots, blockage, spasms and bleeding.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing management of urinary incontinence, including bladder training.
answer_html:
Introduction Urinary incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine. It is common in the elderly, after childbirth, in neurological disease and in dementia. Besides skin problems and infection, it causes embarrassment, isolation and depression, so management must be both physical and emotional.

1. Assessment

  • Type of incontinence (stress, urge, overflow, functional, reflex, mixed)
  • Bladder diary – times of voiding and leaking, amount, fluid intake, activities for 3 days
  • Mobility, cognition, medicines, bowel habits (constipation worsens incontinence), skin condition, urine test for infection, post-void residual urine

2. Bladder training (bladder retraining)

  • Aim – to increase the interval between voidings and the bladder's capacity, mainly for urge incontinence
  • Start with voiding at fixed intervals (e.g. every hour by the clock) whether or not there is an urge
  • Gradually increase the interval by 15–30 minutes each week until the patient can wait 3–4 hours
  • Teach urge suppression – when the urge comes, stand still, contract the pelvic muscles, breathe slowly and distract the mind until it passes
  • Needs a motivated, alert patient; keep a record

3. Other toileting programmes

  • Timed (scheduled) voiding – taking the patient to the toilet at fixed times (every 2–3 hours); for confused or dependent patients
  • Prompted voiding – asking the patient regularly whether he needs to void and praising success

4. Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises – strengthen the muscles for stress incontinence; done several times daily for at least 2–3 months

5. Fluid and diet

  • Adequate fluids (1.5–2 litres) – restricting fluids concentrates urine and irritates the bladder
  • Reduce tea, coffee, alcohol and carbonated drinks; limit fluids 2 hours before bedtime
  • Prevent constipation; weight reduction if obese

6. Environment

  • Commode or urinal near the bed, call bell within reach, night light, clear path to the toilet
  • Clothing that is easy to remove (elastic waist, Velcro)

7. Devices and skin care

  • Absorbent pads, condom catheter for men; intermittent catheterisation for overflow; indwelling catheter only as a last resort
  • Skin care – clean and dry promptly, barrier cream

8. Medical and surgical treatment – drugs for overactive bladder, treatment of infection or prostate enlargement, surgery (sling procedures) for stress incontinence

9. Emotional support – privacy, respect, reassurance; avoid scolding or labelling the patient

Conclusion Management of urinary incontinence includes assessment with a bladder diary, bladder training with gradually increasing intervals, timed and prompted voiding, pelvic floor exercises, sensible fluid intake, a supportive environment, appropriate devices, skin care and emotional support.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the normal characteristics of urine.
answer_html:
Characteristic Normal
Amount about 1–2 litres/day in adults; at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour (about 30 mL/hour)
Colour pale yellow to amber (due to urochrome); darker when concentrated
Clarity clear, transparent
Odour faintly aromatic; ammonia smell on standing
pH 4.6–8 (average about 6 – slightly acidic)
Specific gravity 1.010–1.025
Constituents no glucose, ketones, blood or pus; protein only in traces
Frequency 5–6 times a day; seldom at night

Abnormal findings – dark, concentrated urine (dehydration), red or cola-coloured (blood), deep yellow-brown with froth (jaundice), cloudy and foul-smelling (infection), fruity odour (ketones).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC)?
answer_html:
Definition Clean intermittent self-catheterisation is a method in which the patient (or carer) passes a catheter into the bladder at regular intervals to empty it, then removes it, using a clean (not sterile) technique.

Indications – neurogenic bladder (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida), chronic urinary retention, continent urinary diversions.

Frequency – usually 4–6 times a day, keeping each volume below about 400–500 mL.

Advantages – lower infection risk than an indwelling catheter, independence, no bag, normal sexual activity.

Teaching – hand washing, cleaning the meatus, lubrication, positioning, catheter care, fluid intake and signs of infection.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What are Kegel (pelvic floor) exercises?
answer_html:
Definition Kegel exercises are exercises that strengthen the pelvic floor muscles (which support the bladder, uterus and rectum).

Method

  1. Identify the muscles – those used to hold back urine or wind (stopping urine midstream is used only to learn, not as practice)
  2. Tighten the muscles for 3–10 seconds, then relax for the same time
  3. Repeat 10–15 times, three times a day, in lying, sitting and standing positions; breathe normally and do not tighten the abdomen, thighs or buttocks

Uses – stress and urge incontinence, after childbirth and prostate surgery, preventing pelvic organ prolapse. Improvement is seen in 6–12 weeks of regular practice.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is residual urine? How is it measured?
answer_html:
Definition Residual urine (post-void residual) is the amount of urine left in the bladder immediately after voiding.

Normal – less than 50 mL; a residual of more than 100–150 mL suggests incomplete emptying (retention), as in prostate enlargement or neurogenic bladder.

Measurement – within 10–15 minutes after the patient voids:

  • Bladder scanner (portable ultrasound) – non-invasive, preferred
  • Straight (in-and-out) catheterisation – measures exactly but carries a risk of infection

Importance – residual urine causes infection and stones; it guides the decision for catheterisation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define enema. Explain the types, purposes, contraindications and the procedure of giving a cleansing enema, with precautions and complications.

diagram.caption: Position and height for giving an enema
labels: patient in left lateral (Sims') position with right knee flexed
rectal tube directed towards the umbilicus
enema can 30-45 cm above the anus

answer_html:
Introduction An enema is one of the oldest nursing procedures. Although bowel preparation is now often done with oral solutions, enemas are still used to relieve constipation and impaction, prepare the bowel and give some medicines. Done carelessly, an enema can cause discomfort, injury and fluid–electrolyte imbalance, so the nurse must know the correct solution, amount, temperature and technique.

A. Definition

  • An enema is the introduction of a solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon through the anus, to stimulate peristalsis and evacuate the bowel, or to give medicine or soften faeces

B. Types of enema

1. Cleansing (evacuant) enemas – given to empty the bowel

  • Tap water enema – hypotonic; repeated use can cause water intoxication – avoid repeating
  • Normal saline enema – isotonic; the safest, especially for children and the elderly
  • Soap solution enema – mild soap in warm water; irritates the bowel lining and stimulates peristalsis; may irritate the mucosa
  • Hypertonic enema – small volume (e.g. ready-made sodium phosphate enema, about 120 mL); draws fluid into the bowel; avoid in kidney failure, dehydration and small children
  • High enema – reaches higher into the colon (larger volume, can held higher, patient turned from side to side)
  • Low enema – cleans only the rectum and sigmoid colon

2. Retention enemas – retained in the bowel for a period

  • Oil retention enema – 90–150 mL of warm mineral or olive oil, retained for 1–3 hours; softens hard faeces and lubricates (used in faecal impaction, before a cleansing enema)
  • Medicated enema – e.g. lactulose or neomycin in hepatic encephalopathy (reduces ammonia), steroid enema in ulcerative colitis, ion-exchange resin in hyperkalaemia

3. Carminative enema – relieves gas (flatus) and distension, e.g. MGW enema (magnesium sulphate, glycerine and water)

4. Return-flow enema – small volumes run in and out repeatedly to expel flatus

5. Diagnostic enema – barium enema for X-ray of the colon

C. Purposes

  1. To relieve constipation and faecal impaction
  2. To clean the bowel before surgery, colonoscopy and some X-ray examinations
  3. To help in bowel training programmes
  4. To give medicines (local or systemic)
  5. To relieve flatulence and distension
  6. To reduce ammonia in hepatic coma and potassium in hyperkalaemia

D. Contraindications

  • Acute abdomen – suspected appendicitis, peritonitis, intestinal obstruction (risk of perforation)
  • Recent rectal or colon surgery, rectal bleeding, severe haemorrhoids or rectal tumour
  • Paralytic ileus, active inflammatory bowel disease (cleansing enemas)
  • Pregnancy complications – threatened preterm labour, antepartum haemorrhage
  • Raised intracranial pressure and some heart conditions (straining and vagal stimulation)
  • Hypertonic enemas – kidney failure, dehydration

E. Amount, temperature and tube

Point Adults Children
Amount (cleansing) 500–1000 mL infant 150–250 mL; toddler 250–350 mL; school age 300–500 mL; adolescent 500–700 mL
Temperature 40.5–43 °C (105–110 °F) about 37.7 °C (100 °F)
Rectal tube size 22–30 Fr 12–18 Fr
Length inserted 7.5–10 cm 5–7.5 cm (infant 2.5–3.75 cm)
Height of can 30–45 cm above the anus lower (about 7.5 cm for infants)

F. Equipment

  • Enema can or bag with tubing and clamp (or disposable enema set), rectal tube or nozzle
  • Prepared solution at the correct temperature, bath thermometer, jug
  • Water-soluble lubricant, gauze, tissue paper, kidney tray
  • Mackintosh and towel, bath blanket, bedpan or commode, clean gloves, screen, air freshener

G. Procedure (cleansing enema)

Preparation

  1. Check the doctor's order; identify the patient; explain the procedure and the need to retain the solution
  2. Ensure privacy; keep a bedpan or commode ready (or check the toilet is free)
  3. Hand hygiene; prepare the solution and check its temperature with a thermometer

Position

  1. Place the patient in the left lateral (Sims') position with the right knee flexed – the solution flows down into the rectum and sigmoid colon, which lie on the left side
  2. If the patient cannot control the sphincter, give the enema in the dorsal recumbent position on a bedpan
  3. Place the mackintosh and towel under the buttocks; cover with a bath blanket, exposing only the anal area

Administration

  1. Wear gloves; lubricate the tip of the rectal tube (5 cm); run some solution through the tubing to expel air and clamp
  2. Separate the buttocks; ask the patient to take slow deep breaths through the mouth (relaxes the anal sphincter)
  3. Insert the tube gently, pointing towards the umbilicus, 7.5–10 cm in adults; never force it
  4. Raise the can to 30–45 cm above the anus; open the clamp and let the solution flow slowly (about 5–10 minutes for 1 litre)
  5. If the patient complains of cramps or the urge to defecate, lower the can or clamp the tube for a short time and encourage deep breathing, then continue
  6. Clamp the tubing before the can is empty (to prevent air entering); withdraw the tube gently into a kidney tray
  7. Ask the patient to retain the solution for 5–10 minutes (cleansing) – press tissue against the anus if needed
  8. Help the patient to the toilet, commode or bedpan; keep the call bell within reach

After care

  1. Observe the result – amount, colour, consistency of faeces, flatus, worms, blood or mucus
  2. Clean the perineal area; help the patient wash hands; make him comfortable
  3. Clean and replace equipment; ventilate the room; wash hands
  4. Record – type and amount of enema, time, result, the patient's tolerance

"Enemas until clear" – ordered before some investigations; no more than three enemas are given; inform the doctor if the return is still not clear.

H. Precautions

  • Check the temperature – too hot burns the mucosa; too cold causes cramps
  • Use correct amount and height – too high or too fast causes cramps and early expulsion
  • Never force the tube against resistance
  • Stop if the patient has pain, bleeding, sudden abdominal rigidity, dizziness or slowing of pulse
  • Do not give repeated tap-water enemas; prefer saline for children
  • Stay nearby with the call bell available; elderly patients may feel faint

I. Complications

  • Rectal or colon perforation, mucosal injury, bleeding
  • Vagal stimulation – bradycardia, fainting
  • Fluid and electrolyte imbalance – water intoxication (repeated tap water), dehydration and high phosphate (hypertonic enemas)
  • Abdominal cramps, rectal irritation (soap), fatigue
  • Dependence on enemas for bowel movement (habitual use)

J. Special groups

  • Children – use normal saline only, smaller volumes, lower height and a smaller tube; a parent may hold and comfort the child
  • Elderly – often cannot retain the solution; give it on a bedpan in the dorsal recumbent position; watch for fatigue, dizziness and fluid imbalance
  • Pregnant women – only when ordered; avoid hypertonic enemas; stop if contractions or bleeding occur

Conclusion An enema is the introduction of a solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon to evacuate the bowel, soften faeces, relieve flatus or give medicine; a cleansing enema is given in the left lateral position with the correct solution, volume, temperature and height, inserting the tube gently towards the umbilicus and observing and recording the result.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define colostomy. Explain the types of colostomy, the characteristics of a healthy stoma, the procedure of changing a colostomy appliance, and the nursing care and teaching of a patient with a colostomy.

diagram.caption: Sites of colostomy and character of faeces

answer_html:
Introduction An ostomy is a surgically created opening that brings a part of the bowel or urinary tract to the abdominal surface. A colostomy changes the way a person passes stool, and affects diet, skin, clothing, body image, relationships and work. Good nursing care and teaching help the patient return to a normal life.

A. Definitions

  • Stoma – the opening of the bowel (or ureter) on the abdominal wall
  • Colostomy – a surgical opening of the colon onto the abdominal wall, through which faeces and flatus are passed into an external pouch
  • Ileostomy – an opening of the ileum onto the abdominal wall (liquid output)

B. Indications

  • Cancer of the colon or rectum – a permanent colostomy after abdominoperineal resection
  • Intestinal obstruction, perforated diverticulitis, trauma (gunshot or stab wounds)
  • To rest a diseased bowel or protect an anastomosis (temporary)
  • In children – Hirschsprung's disease, anorectal malformations (imperforate anus)
  • Ileostomy – ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, familial polyposis

C. Types of colostomy

1. According to duration

  • Temporary – closed later (weeks or months) after the bowel heals
  • Permanent – when the rectum or anus is removed

2. According to site

Site Stool Notes
Ascending (right side) liquid irritating to skin; drainable pouch
Transverse (upper abdomen) semi-liquid / mushy often temporary, loop type
Descending (left side) semi-formed
Sigmoid (left lower abdomen) formed most common; bowel can be regulated by irrigation

3. According to construction

  • End (single-barrel) colostomy – one stoma from the cut end of the colon
  • Loop colostomy – a loop of colon is brought out and supported by a rod or bridge for 7–10 days; has two openings in one stoma; usually temporary
  • Double-barrel colostomy – two separate stomas: the proximal (functioning) one passes faeces; the distal one passes only mucus (mucous fistula)

D. Characteristics of a healthy stoma

  • Colour red or pink, moist and shiny (like the inside of the mouth)
  • Slightly raised (1–2.5 cm) above the skin; round or oval
  • Painless (no pain nerve endings) – it may bleed slightly when cleaned
  • Swelling (oedema) is normal in the first few weeks and gradually decreases
  • Abnormal – pale (anaemia), dusky blue, purple or black (poor blood supply, necrosis – report at once), retraction below skin level, prolapse, narrowing (stenosis), excessive bleeding

E. Ostomy appliances

  • One-piece pouch (skin barrier and bag joined) or two-piece system (separate baseplate/flange and pouch that clips on)
  • Drainable pouches (with clip or tap) for liquid or semi-liquid output; closed pouches for formed stool (changed once or twice daily)
  • Skin barrier (wafer), stoma paste, powder, adhesive remover, deodorising filters, belts

F. Procedure of changing a colostomy appliance

Equipment – new pouch and baseplate, stoma measuring guide, scissors, adhesive remover, skin barrier film or paste, warm water, soft gauze or cloth, towel, disposable bag, clean gloves, mirror (for teaching)

Steps

  1. Explain; ensure privacy; involve the patient (teaching opportunity); hand hygiene; wear gloves
  2. Position supine or standing so the skin around the stoma is flat; protect clothing
  3. Empty the pouch if it contains stool
  4. Remove the old appliance gently, from top to bottom, pushing the skin away from the adhesive (use adhesive remover); discard in a disposable bag
  5. Clean the stoma and surrounding skin with warm water and soft gauze (no soap with oils or perfumes, no alcohol); pat dry
  6. Inspect the stoma (colour, swelling, bleeding) and peristomal skin (redness, rash, excoriation)
  7. Measure the stoma with the guide and cut the barrier opening about 1.5–3 mm larger than the stoma – a larger opening exposes skin to stool; a smaller one injures the stoma
  8. Apply barrier film or paste if the skin is irritated; let it dry
  9. Remove the backing; centre the barrier over the stoma and press it on; hold your hand over it for 30–60 seconds (warmth improves adhesion)
  10. Attach the pouch (two-piece) and close the end (drainable); check it is secure
  11. Dispose of waste; wash hands; record the stoma and skin condition and the output

Frequency – empty when the pouch is one-third to half full; change the appliance every 3–5 days (or as recommended) and at once if it leaks

G. Colostomy irrigation

  • Used to regulate bowel action in descending and sigmoid colostomies (formed stool) so that the patient can wear a small cap instead of a pouch
  • 500–1000 mL of lukewarm water introduced slowly through a cone-tipped irrigation set, at the same time each day; the return takes about 45–60 minutes
  • Not used for ileostomies or in patients with prolapse, stenosis or during chemotherapy/radiotherapy unless advised

H. Nursing care after surgery

  • Monitor the stoma colour every few hours in the first days; vital signs, fluid balance, wound care
  • Output – the colostomy usually starts working in 2–4 days (flatus first)
  • Diet – clear fluids, then low-residue diet, gradually returning to a normal balanced diet; fluids 2–3 litres a day
  • Peristomal skin care – prevent leakage and excoriation
  • Pain relief, early ambulation, prevention of complications
  • Psychological support – encourage the patient to look at and touch the stoma; involve the family

I. Teaching for self-care

  • Appliance change and emptying; obtaining supplies
  • Diet – eat regularly and chew well; limit gas-forming foods (beans, cabbage, onions, fizzy drinks) and odour-causing foods (eggs, fish, garlic); curd and parsley reduce odour; ileostomy patients avoid high-fibre foods that can block the stoma (nuts, popcorn, raw fibrous vegetables) and drink extra fluids
  • Bathing – can bathe or shower with or without the pouch
  • Clothing – normal clothes; avoid tight belts over the stoma
  • Activity and work – return to normal activities; avoid heavy lifting for about 6–8 weeks (risk of hernia)
  • Sexuality and body image – open discussion; referral to a stoma nurse and ostomy support groups
  • Report – change in stoma colour, bleeding, severe skin irritation, no output with pain and vomiting, prolapse, very watery output

J. Complications

  • Peristomal skin irritation and excoriation (commonest)
  • Stoma necrosis, retraction, prolapse, stenosis, parastomal hernia
  • Bleeding, leakage, obstruction
  • Dehydration and electrolyte loss (ileostomy, ascending colostomy)
  • Psychological problems – altered body image, depression, social isolation

K. Pre-operative preparation

  • Explanation and counselling about the stoma, the appliance and life afterwards; meeting a person living well with a stoma helps acceptance
  • Stoma site marking by the stoma nurse or surgeon – on a flat area of the abdomen, within the rectus muscle, visible to the patient, away from skin folds, scars, bony prominences and the belt line, checked in sitting, standing and lying positions
  • Bowel preparation, consent and routine pre-operative care as ordered

Conclusion A colostomy is a surgical opening of the colon on the abdomen, temporary or permanent, at the ascending, transverse, descending or sigmoid colon; a healthy stoma is red, moist and slightly raised, and nursing care involves correct appliance fitting and change, skin protection, diet and fluid advice, irrigation where suitable, prevention of complications and teaching with emotional support.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the factors affecting bowel elimination.
answer_html:
Introduction Defecation is the expulsion of faeces from the rectum through the anus. The normal frequency varies widely – from three times a day to three times a week. Many factors influence the pattern and the consistency of stools.

1. Age

  • Infants – frequent, soft, unformed stools; no voluntary control until about 2–3 years
  • Elderly – slower peristalsis, weak abdominal and pelvic muscles, poor teeth, less fibre and fluid intake, less activity → constipation; reduced sphincter control may cause incontinence

2. Diet

  • Fibre (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, pulses) adds bulk and promotes regular movements
  • Low-fibre, refined foods cause constipation
  • Irregular meals, spicy foods, food intolerance (e.g. lactose intolerance – diarrhoea, gas)
  • Gas-forming foods cause flatulence

3. Fluid intake – inadequate fluid makes stools hard and dry

4. Physical activity – exercise stimulates peristalsis; immobility causes constipation

5. Psychological factors

  • Anxiety and stress can cause diarrhoea (rapid peristalsis) or constipation
  • Depression slows peristalsis

6. Personal habits

  • Regular time (often after breakfast – gastrocolic reflex), privacy, familiar toilet
  • Ignoring the urge repeatedly weakens the reflex and causes constipation

7. Position during defecation

  • Squatting or sitting with the thighs flexed increases abdominal pressure and helps defecation; lying on a bedpan makes it difficult

8. Pain – haemorrhoids, anal fissure, abdominal or perineal surgery – the person suppresses the urge to avoid pain

9. Pregnancy – hormones slow peristalsis, and the growing uterus presses on the bowel → constipation, haemorrhoids

10. Surgery and anaesthesia – handling of the bowel and anaesthetics cause paralytic ileus for 24–48 hours

11. Medications

  • Constipation – opioids, iron, anticholinergics, aluminium and calcium antacids, some antidepressants
  • Diarrhoea – antibiotics, laxatives, magnesium antacids
  • Colour change – iron → black stools; barium → white stools

12. Diagnostic tests – bowel preparation, fasting and barium studies alter bowel habits

13. Pathological conditions – spinal cord injury, stroke, hypothyroidism, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, colon cancer, intestinal obstruction, infections

Nurse's role

  • Assess the usual bowel pattern and the factors above on admission
  • Encourage fibre, fluids and activity; provide privacy and a normal position
  • Review medicines that cause constipation or diarrhoea, and report changes in bowel habit

Conclusion Bowel elimination is influenced by age, diet and fibre, fluid intake, activity, psychological state, habits, position, pain, pregnancy, surgery, medicines, tests and diseases; assessing these factors helps the nurse prevent and manage constipation, diarrhoea and incontinence.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define constipation. Explain its causes and nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Constipation is a common problem, especially in the elderly, immobile, post-operative and pregnant patients. Straining at stool can be dangerous for patients with heart disease, raised intracranial pressure or recent surgery.

1. Definition

  • Constipation is the infrequent passage (fewer than three times a week) of hard, dry stools, with straining, difficulty or a feeling of incomplete evacuation

2. Causes

  • Low-fibre diet, inadequate fluid intake
  • Inactivity, bed rest, immobility
  • Ignoring the urge, irregular habits, lack of privacy, use of bedpans
  • Medicines – opioids, iron, antacids, anticholinergics; laxative abuse (bowel loses tone)
  • Ageing, pregnancy
  • Diseases – hypothyroidism, diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord injury, depression, colon cancer, haemorrhoids and fissures (pain)

3. Signs and symptoms

  • Hard, small stools; straining; abdominal distension, discomfort or cramps
  • Feeling of fullness in the rectum, loss of appetite, headache, flatulence

4. Complications

  • Faecal impaction, haemorrhoids, anal fissure, rectal prolapse
  • Straining (Valsalva manoeuvre) – can cause bradycardia and arrhythmias in heart patients and raise intracranial pressure

5. Nursing management

Assessment – usual bowel pattern, last bowel movement, diet, fluids, activity, medicines, abdominal distension and bowel sounds

Diet and fluids

  • High-fibre diet – fruits (guava, papaya, banana), green leafy vegetables, whole grains, pulses, salads, bran (about 25–30 g fibre daily)
  • Fluids 2–3 litres a day (unless restricted); a warm drink in the morning helps

Activity – encourage walking and exercise; abdominal exercises for bedridden patients

Habit and environment

  • Respond to the urge promptly; set a regular time, preferably after breakfast (gastrocolic reflex)
  • Provide privacy and enough time; sitting or squatting position; a footstool to raise the knees; commode rather than bedpan if possible

Medicines and procedures (as prescribed)

  • Bulk-forming laxatives (ispaghula/isabgol), stool softeners (docusate), osmotic laxatives (lactulose), stimulant laxatives (bisacodyl, senna)
  • Suppositories (glycerine, bisacodyl) or an enema if needed; oil retention enema and digital removal for impaction (as ordered)

Teaching

  • Avoid regular use of laxatives; follow diet, fluid and exercise advice
  • Patients with heart disease should avoid straining; stool softeners may be prescribed

Conclusion Constipation is the infrequent and difficult passage of hard stools; it is managed by finding the cause, high-fibre diet, adequate fluids, exercise, regular toilet habits with privacy, laxatives, suppositories or enemas as prescribed and teaching to avoid laxative dependence.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the administration of a rectal suppository.
answer_html:
Introduction A suppository is a solid, cone-shaped medicine that melts at body temperature after insertion into a body cavity. Rectal suppositories are used for local effect (to cause bowel movement) or for systemic effect when the oral route cannot be used.

1. Purposes

  • Local – to stimulate bowel evacuation (glycerine, bisacodyl); to relieve haemorrhoids and local inflammation
  • Systemic – to give paracetamol (fever in children), antiemetics, anticonvulsants (diazepam), anti-inflammatory drugs, when the patient is vomiting, unconscious or cannot swallow

2. Contraindications

  • Recent rectal or prostate surgery, rectal bleeding, severe haemorrhoids
  • Cardiac arrhythmias or recent heart attack (vagal stimulation)
  • Low platelet count; diarrhoea (for systemic drugs)

3. Equipment – prescribed suppository, water-soluble lubricant, clean gloves, gauze or tissue, mackintosh, bedpan (for laxative suppository), medicine chart

4. Procedure

  1. Check the prescription and follow the rights of medication administration; identify the patient
  2. Explain; ensure privacy; ask the patient to empty the bladder
  3. Hand hygiene; position the patient in the left lateral (Sims') position with the upper knee flexed
  4. Wear gloves; remove the wrapper; lubricate the suppository tip and the gloved index finger
  5. Separate the buttocks; ask the patient to breathe slowly through the mouth (relaxes the anal sphincter)
  6. Insert the suppository, usually tapered end first (or as the manufacturer directs), gently beyond the internal sphincter along the rectal wall – about 10 cm (the length of the index finger) in adults and about 5 cm in children (use the little finger)
  7. Place it against the rectal wall, not into faeces (it will not be absorbed)
  8. Withdraw the finger; wipe the anal area; press the buttocks together for a moment
  9. Ask the patient to remain lying for 15–20 minutes and to retain the suppository – a laxative suppository usually acts in 15–60 minutes; keep the bedpan and call bell within reach
  10. Remove gloves; wash hands

5. After care and recording

  • Observe the result (bowel movement – amount, consistency) or the effect of the drug (e.g. fall in temperature)
  • Record the drug, dose, time and effect

6. Precautions

  • Store suppositories in a cool place (they melt at body temperature)
  • Do not cut a suppository unless ordered
  • Watch for dizziness or a slow pulse during insertion

Conclusion A rectal suppository is inserted with gloved lubricated finger beyond the internal sphincter against the rectal wall, with the patient in the left lateral position, for local or systemic effect; the patient is asked to retain it and the effect is observed and recorded.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient with diarrhoea.
answer_html:
Introduction Diarrhoea is the passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours. It is a major cause of dehydration and death in children, and in hospital it may spread from patient to patient. The nurse's aims are to replace fluids, find and treat the cause, prevent spread and protect the skin.

1. Causes

  • Infections – viruses (rotavirus, norovirus), bacteria (E. coli, cholera, shigella, salmonella, Clostridioides difficile), parasites (amoeba, giardia)
  • Food – food poisoning, food intolerance (lactose)
  • Drugs – antibiotics, laxatives, chemotherapy, enteral feeds given too fast
  • Diseases – inflammatory bowel disease, malabsorption, irritable bowel syndrome, thyrotoxicosis
  • Anxiety and stress

2. Complications

  • Dehydration, hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis, shock and kidney failure
  • Perianal skin excoriation, malnutrition, weakness

3. Assessment

  • Number, amount, consistency, colour and odour of stools; blood or mucus
  • Signs of dehydration – thirst, dry mouth, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, low urine output, rapid pulse, low BP; in infants sunken fontanelle
  • Fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, recent food, travel, antibiotics
  • Weight, intake–output, serum electrolytes

4. Nursing management

Fluid replacement

  • Oral rehydration solution (ORS) – small, frequent sips; extra fluids after each loose stool
  • IV fluids (e.g. Ringer's lactate) for severe dehydration as prescribed
  • Strict intake–output chart; daily weight

Diet

  • Continue feeding – soft, easily digested foods (rice, khichdi, banana, curd, boiled potato); breastfeeding continued in infants
  • Avoid fatty, spicy, fried foods, caffeine and very sugary drinks; temporarily avoid milk if lactose intolerance is suspected
  • Zinc supplements for children as per national guidelines

Infection control

  • Hand washing with soap and water (alcohol rubs do not kill some organisms such as C. difficile spores)
  • Contact (enteric) precautions for infectious diarrhoea; separate toilet or commode; safe disposal of stools; disinfection of bedpans and surfaces

Comfort and skin care

  • Keep the bedpan or commode within easy reach; respond quickly
  • Gentle perianal cleaning after each stool, pat dry, apply barrier cream
  • Rest; keep the room ventilated and odour-free

Medicines and investigations

  • Send a stool sample for examination and culture
  • Give antidiarrhoeal and antimicrobial drugs only as prescribed (antimotility drugs are not used in infectious diarrhoea in children)
  • Review medicines that may be causing diarrhoea; slow down tube feeds

Teaching – safe drinking water, food hygiene, hand washing, preparation and use of ORS, warning signs of dehydration

Conclusion Care of a patient with diarrhoea centres on early recognition and correction of dehydration with ORS or IV fluids, continued suitable feeding, strict hand hygiene and enteric precautions, perianal skin care, accurate recording and treatment of the cause.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the normal characteristics of faeces.
answer_html:
Characteristic Normal
Amount about 100–400 g/day (depends on diet)
Frequency from three times a day to three times a week
Colour brown (due to stercobilin); infants – yellow
Consistency soft, formed, cylindrical (Bristol types 3–4)
Odour characteristic (indole, skatole), affected by diet
Composition about 75% water, 25% solids – bacteria, undigested fibre, fat, dead cells, bile pigments

Abnormal – black tarry (melaena – upper GI bleeding), clay-coloured (obstructive jaundice), fresh blood (haemorrhoids, lower GI bleeding), pale bulky greasy (steatorrhoea), rice-water (cholera).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is faecal impaction? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Definition Faecal impaction is a mass of hard, dry stool in the rectum (or colon) that the patient cannot pass.

Signs – no bowel movement for several days; oozing of liquid stool around the mass (false diarrhoea); rectal pain and fullness; abdominal distension; loss of appetite, nausea; hard mass felt on rectal examination.

Management

  • Oil retention enema to soften the stool, followed by a cleansing enema
  • Digital removal of faeces, only on order and with gloved lubricated finger, gently in small pieces – watch for slowing of the pulse (vagal stimulation)
  • Prevent recurrence – fibre, fluids, activity, regular toileting, stool softeners

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is a rectal (flatus) tube? State the procedure.
answer_html:
Definition A rectal (flatus) tube is a soft tube inserted into the rectum to relieve flatulence and abdominal distension.

Procedure

  1. Explain; privacy; left lateral position
  2. Use a 22–30 Fr tube for adults; lubricate the tip
  3. Insert gently about 10–15 cm into the rectum, pointing towards the umbilicus
  4. Place the open end in a container of water or a bag (to see the bubbles of flatus and prevent soiling)
  5. Leave in place for not more than 20 minutes (longer use damages the sphincter); reinsert after 2–3 hours if needed

Note – encourage walking and avoid gas-forming foods.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is bowel training?
answer_html:
Definition Bowel training (bowel programme) is a planned method of establishing a regular, controlled pattern of bowel evacuation, used in spinal cord injury, stroke, chronic constipation and faecal incontinence.

Main steps

  1. Choose a fixed time daily, usually 20–30 minutes after a meal (gastrocolic reflex)
  2. Ensure adequate fibre and fluids and regular exercise
  3. Help the patient to the toilet or commode in a sitting position with privacy; allow enough time
  4. Use digital stimulation or a suppository if prescribed, at the same time each day
  5. Record the results; gradually reduce laxatives as a regular pattern develops (takes several weeks)

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the phases of diagnostic testing and the role of the nurse in each phase. Describe the collection of urine specimens for various investigations.
answer_html:
Introduction Doctors depend on laboratory and imaging tests to diagnose disease and monitor treatment, but the accuracy and safety of these tests depend largely on the nurse – on how the patient is prepared, how the specimen is collected, labelled and sent, and how the patient is cared for afterwards. A wrongly collected specimen gives a wrong result and may lead to wrong treatment.

PART A – PHASES OF DIAGNOSTIC TESTING

1. Pre-test phase (before the test)

  • Check the order and the type of test; know its purpose and requirements
  • Assess the patient – allergies (especially iodine/contrast, latex, drugs), pregnancy, kidney function (for contrast studies), bleeding tendency and anticoagulants (for invasive tests), diabetes and medicines such as metformin or insulin (dose adjustment during fasting as advised)
  • Explain the test in simple words – what will happen, how long it takes, what the patient will feel; reduce anxiety
  • Obtain informed consent for invasive procedures (endoscopy, biopsy, angiography)
  • Physical preparation – fasting (nil by mouth) as required, bowel preparation, full or empty bladder, removal of metal objects, dentures and jewellery, IV access, premedication
  • Arrange timing – e.g. fasting blood sugar early morning, specimens before antibiotics, peak and trough drug levels

2. Intra-test phase (during the test)

  • Identify the patient with two identifiers; check that preparation is complete
  • Position the patient correctly and support him; maintain privacy and comfort
  • Use correct technique – aseptic for sterile specimens, correct containers and amounts
  • Monitor – vital signs, oxygen saturation and level of consciousness during sedation; watch for reactions
  • Assist the doctor; keep emergency drugs and equipment ready
  • Label specimens at the bedside and handle them safely (standard precautions)

3. Post-test phase (after the test)

  • Observe for complications – bleeding from puncture sites, allergic reactions, perforation after endoscopy, delayed contrast reactions
  • Aftercare – rest, diet resumed when safe (e.g. after the gag reflex returns), extra fluids after contrast (unless restricted)
  • Send specimens promptly with a complete request form; store correctly if delayed
  • Compare results with normal values, report abnormal or critical results at once
  • Teach the patient about results and follow-up as appropriate
  • Document – test done, time, specimen sent, patient's condition and any problems

General principles of specimen collection

  • Right patient, right specimen, right container, right amount, right time
  • Collect before starting antibiotics whenever possible (cultures)
  • Use sterile containers and aseptic technique for cultures; do not touch the inside of containers or lids
  • Label with name, ID number, ward, date, time of collection, type of specimen, test required (and antibiotics given)
  • Send in a leak-proof container in a biohazard bag with the request form, as soon as possible
  • Follow standard precautions; dispose of waste correctly

PART B – COLLECTION OF URINE SPECIMENS

1. Routine (random) urine specimen

  • Purpose – routine urine examination (physical, chemical, microscopic)
  • Collected at any time, preferably the first morning specimen (most concentrated – best for protein, pregnancy test and microscopy)
  • Procedure – explain; the patient washes hands and the perineum; passes urine into a clean, dry container (about 30–50 mL); avoid contamination with stool, toilet paper or menstrual blood; label and send within an hour
  • In women during menstruation, note it on the form

2. Midstream clean-catch urine (MSU) – for culture and sensitivity

  1. Explain; give a sterile container; the patient washes hands
  2. Female – separate the labia and clean the meatus from front to back with soap and water or sterile swabs; keep the labia apart while voiding
  3. Male – retract the foreskin and clean the glans from the meatus outwards
  4. Pass the first part of the stream into the toilet, then collect the middle portion (about 15–30 mL) in the sterile container without stopping the stream, and finish voiding in the toilet
  5. Do not touch the inside of the container or lid; close it at once
  6. Label and send within 1–2 hours, or refrigerate at about 4 °C if there is a delay - First part of the stream washes out bacteria from the urethra – so the midstream sample shows the true bladder urine

3. Catheter specimen of urine (CSU)

  • Never take urine from the drainage bag, and never disconnect the catheter from the tubing
  • If no urine is in the tubing, clamp the tubing below the sampling port for a short time (15–30 minutes)
  • Wear gloves; disinfect the sampling port with alcohol and let it dry
  • Aspirate the required volume with a sterile syringe (or needle-free adaptor); transfer to a sterile container
  • Unclamp the tubing; label and send

4. 24-hour (timed) urine collection

  • Purpose – measurement of creatinine clearance, protein, electrolytes, calcium, uric acid, cortisol, catecholamines (VMA) etc.
  • Procedure:
    1. Explain to the patient and all staff; place a sign on the bed and in the toilet
    2. Obtain a large labelled container with the preservative required by the laboratory
    3. At the start time (e.g. 8 a.m.), ask the patient to empty the bladder and discard this urine; note the time – the collection starts now
    4. Collect every voiding for the next 24 hours in the container; keep it cool (on ice or in a refrigerator) as advised
    5. At the end time (8 a.m. next day), ask the patient to void and add this final urine to the container
    6. Label with start and finish times and send
  • If any urine is discarded or lost, the test must be restarted
  • Patients with catheters – collect from the drainage bag into the container at intervals (the bag is changed or emptied at the start time)

5. Urine specimen from infants and young children

  • Clean and dry the perineum; apply a sterile adhesive urine collection bag around the genitalia; check frequently; remove when urine is collected; for culture, catheter or suprapubic samples may be needed

6. Other urine tests at the bedside

  • Dipstick (reagent strip) testing – dip a strip in fresh urine and read colour changes at the stated time for glucose, protein, ketones, blood, pH, specific gravity, nitrites, leucocytes
  • Pregnancy test – first morning specimen
  • Specific gravity with a urinometer

PART C – Common errors in specimen collection and their prevention

Error Effect Prevention
Wrong patient or unlabelled specimen wrong result, wrong treatment two identifiers, label at the bedside
Contamination (skin, perineum, saliva, toilet water) false-positive culture correct cleaning, sterile container, midstream technique
Specimen after antibiotics started false-negative culture collect before antibiotics
Delay in sending, wrong storage bacteria multiply or cells die send promptly, refrigerate urine if delayed, warm stool for amoebae
Wrong container or preservative test cannot be done check laboratory requirements
Incomplete timed collection wrong calculation restart the 24-hour collection if any urine is lost

Conclusion Diagnostic testing has pre-test, intra-test and post-test phases, and the nurse prepares and explains, collects specimens correctly, monitors the patient, observes for complications, reports results and documents; urine specimens include routine, midstream clean-catch, catheter, 24-hour and paediatric specimens, each collected by a specific technique to give accurate results.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nurse's role in the preparation and care of patients undergoing radiological and endoscopic investigations.
answer_html:
Introduction Radiological (imaging) investigations – X-rays, contrast studies, CT, MRI and ultrasound – and endoscopic procedures allow doctors to see inside the body. Many need special preparation (fasting, bowel preparation, full bladder), carry risks (allergy to contrast, radiation, perforation, sedation) and need aftercare. The nurse ensures the patient is safe, prepared and comfortable throughout.

PART A – GENERAL ROLE OF THE NURSE

  • Explain the procedure, its purpose, duration and sensations; obtain consent for invasive and contrast procedures
  • Assess – allergies (contrast, iodine, latex), pregnancy (radiation), kidney function (contrast), bleeding tendency, diabetes and medicines, implants and pacemakers (MRI), claustrophobia
  • Physical preparation – fasting, bowel preparation, bladder preparation, removal of metal objects, jewellery, dentures; IV line; premedication as ordered
  • Safety – correct patient identification, emergency drugs and oxygen ready, monitoring during sedation, radiation protection (lead apron, distance, minimum exposure for staff and patient)
