  • Aftercare – monitoring vital signs and complications, diet and fluids, specimen (biopsy) handling and documentation

PART B – RADIOLOGICAL INVESTIGATIONS

1. Plain X-ray

  • Usually no special preparation; remove metal, jewellery and clothing over the area; give a gown
  • Ask women about pregnancy; use a lead shield where possible
  • Chest X-ray – take a deep breath and hold it; abdominal X-ray – may need an empty bowel
  • Help with positioning; protect fractured limbs

2. Barium studies (barium swallow, meal, follow-through, enema)

  • Before – nil by mouth for 6–8 hours (swallow/meal); for barium enema, low-residue diet, laxatives and cleansing enemas to empty the colon
  • During – the patient drinks barium (or it is given rectally) while X-rays are taken in different positions
  • After – plenty of fluids and a laxative to remove barium (it can cause constipation and impaction); tell the patient that stools will be white for 1–3 days

3. Contrast studies with iodinated dye (IVP/IVU, CT with contrast, angiography)

  • Before – history of contrast allergy, asthma or previous reaction; serum creatinine/kidney function; adequate hydration; fasting for a few hours; consent; withhold metformin as per hospital policy; IV access
  • During – the patient may feel warmth, flushing or a metallic taste when the dye is injected; watch for itching, rashes, breathlessness, low BP (allergic reaction) and keep emergency drugs ready
  • After – encourage fluids to flush out the dye (unless restricted); watch for delayed reactions and reduced urine output (contrast-induced kidney injury)
  • Angiography additionally – check peripheral pulses before and after; after the test, bed rest, pressure dressing, keep the limb straight, check the puncture site for bleeding or haematoma and the distal pulses, colour and warmth regularly

4. CT scan (computed tomography)

  • Remove metal; fasting 4 hours if contrast is to be used; contrast precautions as above
  • Explain that the scanner is noisy but open; the patient must lie still and may be asked to hold the breath
  • Oral contrast may be given for abdominal CT

5. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)

  • Uses a strong magnet – screen for pacemakers, defibrillators, cochlear implants, metallic aneurysm clips, metal fragments (especially in the eye) and other implants
  • Remove all metal objects – jewellery, hair pins, watches, credit cards, hearing aids, medicine patches; no metal equipment (oxygen cylinders, wheelchairs) in the scanner room
  • Explain that it is noisy (give ear plugs) and enclosed; claustrophobic patients may need sedation; must lie still for 30–60 minutes
  • Gadolinium contrast – check kidney function

6. Ultrasound (USG)

  • Abdominal USG (liver, gallbladder) – nil by mouth for 6–8 hours (gallbladder is distended and less gas)
  • Pelvic USG (uterus, ovaries, bladder, early pregnancy) – full bladder: drink about 1 litre of water an hour before and do not pass urine
  • Painless and without radiation; clean off the gel afterwards

7. Nuclear (radioisotope) scans

  • Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding; explain that the dose of radiation is small; encourage fluids and frequent voiding afterwards; follow precautions for handling urine as per policy

PART C – ENDOSCOPIC INVESTIGATIONS

1. Upper GI endoscopy (oesophagogastroduodenoscopy)

  • Before – nil by mouth for 6–8 hours; consent; remove dentures; local anaesthetic throat spray; sedation as ordered; left lateral position with a mouth guard
  • After – nothing by mouth until the gag (swallowing) reflex returns (about 1–2 hours) – test with sips of water; monitor vital signs and sedation
  • Watch for perforation – severe pain, fever, difficulty swallowing, vomiting of blood, swelling of the neck (surgical emphysema)
  • Sore throat – warm saline gargles or lozenges

2. Colonoscopy and sigmoidoscopy

  • Before – bowel preparation – clear liquid diet for 1–2 days and an oral bowel-cleansing solution (e.g. polyethylene glycol) as ordered, or enemas for sigmoidoscopy; consent; stop iron tablets as advised
  • During – left lateral position with knees flexed; sedation; monitor vital signs and comfort
  • After – cramps and passing of flatus are normal; watch for rectal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, distension and fever (perforation); resume diet as allowed

3. Bronchoscopy

  • Before – nil by mouth 6–8 hours; consent; remove dentures; local anaesthetic and sedation; oxygen and suction ready
  • After – nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns; semi-Fowler's position; watch for breathlessness, stridor (laryngeal oedema), haemoptysis (slight blood-streaked sputum is normal after biopsy), fever and pneumothorax

4. Cystoscopy

  • Before – consent; fluids; sedation or anaesthesia as ordered
  • After – pink urine and burning are common for a day or two; encourage fluids; watch for retention, frank bleeding and signs of infection

5. Care of biopsy specimens – place in the correct fixative (usually 10% formalin) in a labelled container, with the request form; send promptly

PART D – Care during and after procedural sedation

  • Before – fasting confirmed, IV access, baseline vital signs and SpO₂, removal of dentures, emergency drugs, oxygen and suction ready
  • During – continuous monitoring of pulse, BP, respiration, SpO₂ and level of consciousness; watch for respiratory depression and low BP
  • After – recovery position until awake; observe vital signs every 15 minutes until stable; nothing by mouth until fully awake and the gag reflex returns
  • Discharge (day-care) – only when fully alert, vital signs stable and able to walk; must go home with a responsible adult; no driving, machine operation or important decisions for 24 hours; written instructions about warning signs (pain, bleeding, fever, breathlessness) and whom to contact

PART E – Radiation safety for nurses

  • Follow time, distance and shielding – spend minimum time near the source, stand as far away as possible, wear a lead apron and thyroid shield when staying in the room
  • Pregnant staff should avoid exposure; wear dosimeter (TLD) badges where required
  • Never hold a patient during an X-ray unless essential (then wear lead protection)

Conclusion For radiological and endoscopic investigations the nurse explains, obtains consent and assesses allergies, pregnancy, kidney function and implants; prepares the patient with fasting, bowel or bladder preparation and removal of metal; ensures safety and monitoring during the test; and gives aftercare – fluids after contrast, nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns after endoscopy, and observation for bleeding, perforation and reactions.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain capillary blood glucose monitoring with a glucometer.
answer_html:
Introduction Capillary blood glucose (CBG) monitoring is a quick bedside test of the blood sugar level using a drop of blood from a finger prick and a glucometer. It is used many times a day in hospitals and by diabetic patients at home.

1. Purposes

  • To monitor blood glucose in diabetes and adjust insulin or diet
  • To detect hypoglycaemia (in confused, sweating or unconscious patients) and hyperglycaemia quickly
  • To monitor patients on steroids, TPN or enteral feeds, critically ill patients and newborns at risk

2. Equipment

  • Glucometer (checked with control solution as per policy), test strips (check expiry date and code)
  • Single-use lancet or lancing device, alcohol swab or soap and warm water, dry cotton, clean gloves
  • Sharps container, record chart

3. Procedure

  1. Check the order and the timing (fasting, before meals, 2 hours after meals, bedtime); identify the patient; explain
  2. Ask the patient to wash hands with soap and warm water (removes sugar residues and improves blood flow); dry well
  3. Hand hygiene; wear gloves; insert a strip into the meter
  4. Choose the side of the fingertip (middle or ring finger) – less painful than the pad; rotate sites
  5. If alcohol is used, let it dry completely (wet alcohol dilutes the blood and stings)
  6. Hold the hand below heart level; prick the side of the fingertip with the lancet
  7. Wipe away the first drop if the hospital policy says so; gently squeeze from the base of the finger to form a drop – do not milk hard (tissue fluid dilutes the sample)
  8. Touch the drop to the strip so that it fills the test area
  9. Apply pressure with dry cotton to stop bleeding
  10. Read the result; dispose of the lancet in the sharps container and the strip as clinical waste
  11. Record the value and time; report values outside the prescribed limits – e.g. below 70 mg/dL (hypoglycaemia) or very high values

4. Sources of error

  • Sugar or food residue on the fingers, alcohol not dry, expired or damp strips, wrong code
  • Too little blood or squeezing hard
  • Poor peripheral circulation (shock, cold hands), very high or low haematocrit – capillary results may be inaccurate; a venous sample is taken to confirm doubtful readings

5. Teaching (home use) – technique, times of testing, keeping a record, recognising and treating hypoglycaemia, care of the meter and safe disposal of lancets

Conclusion Capillary blood glucose monitoring is a quick finger-prick test using a glucometer; clean, dry hands, a prick on the side of the fingertip, gentle formation of the drop, correct strips and prompt recording and reporting give reliable results for adjusting diabetic treatment.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the procedure of collecting a venous blood sample (venepuncture).
answer_html:
Introduction Venepuncture is the puncture of a vein with a needle to obtain a blood sample for laboratory tests. Correct technique gives accurate results and prevents injury and infection.

1. Sites

  • Antecubital fossa – median cubital vein (first choice: large, superficial, well anchored), cephalic and basilic veins
  • Veins on the back of the hand when others are not available
  • Avoid – the arm with an IV infusion (above the site), AV fistula, the side of a mastectomy, areas with haematoma, infection, burns or scars

2. Equipment

  • Tourniquet, 70% alcohol swab (or chlorhexidine), clean gloves
  • Vacutainer holder and needle (usually 21 G) or syringe and needle, correct blood collection tubes
  • Dry cotton, adhesive plaster, sharps container, labels and request form, kidney tray

3. Procedure

  1. Check the order; identify the patient with two identifiers; explain; check fasting status if required
  2. Hand hygiene; wear gloves; position the patient with the arm extended and supported
  3. Apply the tourniquet 7–10 cm above the site – not for more than 1 minute (prolonged use changes results)
  4. Palpate the vein; ask the patient to make a fist (no pumping)
  5. Clean the site and let it dry completely; do not touch it again
  6. Anchor the vein below the site with the thumb
  7. Insert the needle bevel up at 15–30° in the direction of blood flow
  8. Attach the tubes in the correct order of draw; allow each to fill to the mark
  9. Release the tourniquet as soon as blood flows (and always before removing the needle)
  10. Place cotton over the site, withdraw the needle and apply firm pressure for 2–3 minutes with the arm straight (bending the elbow causes bruising)
  11. Activate the safety device; discard the needle in the sharps container at once – never recap
  12. Gently invert tubes with additives (do not shake)
  13. Label at the bedside; send with the request form promptly
  14. Apply a plaster; record

4. Complications

  • Haematoma (bruise), pain
  • Haemolysis of the sample – small needle, vigorous shaking, prolonged tourniquet, wet alcohol – gives wrong results (e.g. falsely high potassium)
  • Vasovagal fainting – lay the patient down
  • Accidental arterial puncture, nerve injury, infection
  • Needle-stick injury to the nurse

Conclusion Venepuncture is done in a suitable vein, usually the median cubital, with correct patient identification, a tourniquet applied for less than a minute, aseptic technique, the correct order of tubes, firm pressure after withdrawal, safe sharps disposal and labelling at the bedside.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the collection of blood for culture.
answer_html:
Introduction A blood culture detects bacteria or fungi in the blood (bacteraemia, septicaemia) and identifies the organism and the antibiotics it is sensitive to. A contaminated sample gives false results and leads to unnecessary antibiotics, so strict asepsis is essential.

1. Indications

  • Fever with chills, suspected sepsis, infective endocarditis, enteric fever, pneumonia, meningitis, osteomyelitis
  • Fever in patients with central lines, low immunity or newborns

2. Timing

  • Before starting antibiotics (or just before the next dose)
  • As soon as sepsis is suspected; ideally around a fever spike if possible
  • Usually two sets from two different sites (each set = one aerobic and one anaerobic bottle)

3. Equipment

  • Blood culture bottles (check expiry; paediatric bottles for children), 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol (or povidone-iodine), 70% alcohol swabs for bottle tops
  • Sterile gloves or a "no-touch" technique, tourniquet, needle and syringe or blood culture collection set, sharps box, labels, request form

4. Procedure

  1. Identify the patient; explain; hand hygiene
  2. Remove the bottle caps; disinfect the rubber tops with alcohol and let them dry
  3. Apply the tourniquet; select the vein
  4. Clean the skin with chlorhexidine–alcohol with friction for 30 seconds and allow it to dry completely (povidone-iodine needs about 2 minutes)
  5. Do not touch the cleaned site again (if palpation is necessary, wear sterile gloves)
  6. Collect 8–10 mL per bottle in adults (1–3 mL in children, as per the bottle); volume is the most important factor in detecting organisms
  7. Inoculate the bottles – with a collection set, fill the aerobic bottle first; with a syringe, the anaerobic first; do not let air into the anaerobic bottle
  8. Release the tourniquet, remove the needle, apply pressure; dispose of sharps safely
  9. Mix the bottles gently; label (site, date, time, antibiotics received)
  10. Send immediately to the laboratory at room temperature – do not refrigerate

5. Precautions

  • Do not take blood from an existing IV cannula (unless line infection is suspected and ordered, together with a peripheral sample)
  • Do not take blood above an IV infusion
  • Record the temperature and any antibiotics given

Conclusion Blood for culture is collected before antibiotics, usually as two sets from different sites, with thorough skin and bottle-top disinfection, adequate volume in aerobic and anaerobic bottles, correct labelling and immediate dispatch at room temperature.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the collection of a sputum specimen.
answer_html:
Introduction Sputum is the mucus coughed up from the lungs and airways. It is examined to diagnose tuberculosis, pneumonia, lung abscess and lung cancer. A specimen of saliva is useless, so the patient must be taught how to bring up true sputum.

1. Purposes

  • Microscopy for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and molecular tests (e.g. NAAT) for tuberculosis
  • Gram stain, culture and sensitivity – organism and antibiotic choice in chest infections
  • Cytology – cancer cells

2. Best time – early morning, before eating or drinking (secretions collect overnight and are most concentrated); for TB, specimens are collected as per national programme guidelines (e.g. a spot specimen and an early-morning specimen)

3. Equipment – sterile, wide-mouthed, screw-capped container, tissues, gloves, mask (N95 for staff in suspected TB), label, request form, biohazard bag

4. Procedure

  1. Explain the difference between sputum and saliva
  2. Ask the patient to rinse the mouth with plain water – no toothpaste or mouthwash (they may kill organisms)
  3. Position the patient sitting upright; collect in a well-ventilated area, away from others (or a sputum collection booth or open air for TB)
  4. Ask the patient to take 2–3 deep breaths and then cough deeply from the chest
  5. Expectorate directly into the container without touching the inside or the rim; about 3–5 mL is needed
  6. Close the lid tightly; clean the outside; remove gloves; wash hands
  7. Label and send promptly (within 1–2 hours) or refrigerate as advised
  8. Give mouth care; record the amount, colour, consistency and odour of sputum

5. If the patient cannot produce sputum

  • Steam inhalation or nebulisation with hypertonic saline (induced sputum), postural drainage and chest percussion
  • Suction with a sterile sputum trap (mucus extractor) in unconscious or intubated patients
  • Gastric aspirate for TB in young children

6. Infection control – staff wear masks during collection; the patient covers the mouth while coughing; safe disposal of tissues

Conclusion Sputum is collected early in the morning after rinsing the mouth with plain water, by deep coughing into a sterile container, with attention to infection control; induced sputum, postural drainage or suction are used when the patient cannot cough it up.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the collection of stool specimens for various investigations.
answer_html:
Introduction Stool (faecal) specimens are examined to detect parasites, infections, hidden blood and malabsorption. The specimen must be fresh, uncontaminated and of adequate amount.

1. Types of stool examination

  • Routine examination – colour, consistency, ova, cysts and parasites, pus cells, red cells
  • Culture and sensitivity – bacterial diarrhoea (cholera, shigella, salmonella)
  • Occult blood test – hidden bleeding (ulcers, colorectal cancer)
  • Fat estimation – malabsorption (steatorrhoea)
  • Toxin tests – e.g. Clostridioides difficile in antibiotic-associated diarrhoea

2. Equipment – clean, dry bedpan or commode liner, specimen container with spoon/spatula (sterile for culture), gloves, tongue depressor, label, request form, biohazard bag

3. Procedure

  1. Explain; ask the patient to pass urine first (urine mixed with stool destroys some parasites and alters results)
  2. Ask the patient to pass stool into a clean, dry bedpan or a container placed in the toilet – not into toilet water; no toilet paper in the specimen
  3. Wear gloves; with the spatula take about 2–3 teaspoons (a walnut-sized piece) of formed stool or 15–30 mL of liquid stool, choosing parts with blood, mucus or pus
  4. Place it in the container and close the lid tightly; do not soil the outside
  5. Label and send promptly – warm stool within 30 minutes for amoebic trophozoites (they die when cool)
  6. Empty and clean the bedpan; wash hands; record

4. Special points

  • Stool culture – sterile container, before antibiotics; a rectal swab may be used in infants or acutely ill patients
  • Occult blood – usually three specimens on three different days; for the guaiac test, avoid red meat, certain vegetables, vitamin C and aspirin/NSAIDs for about 3 days as advised (immunochemical tests need no diet change)
  • Fat estimation – 72-hour collection on a fixed-fat diet
  • Infants – scrape stool from the nappy

5. Observation and recording – note and record the colour, consistency, amount, odour and the presence of blood, mucus, pus or worms, the time of collection and the time the specimen was sent; report abnormal findings such as black tarry or blood-stained stools at once.

Conclusion Stool specimens for routine examination, culture, occult blood and other tests are collected fresh into a clean dry bedpan without urine or toilet paper, in adequate amounts from abnormal-looking parts, and sent promptly with correct labelling.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the colour codes of blood collection tubes and the order of draw.
answer_html:
Order Tube cap colour Additive Common tests
1 Blood culture bottles broth culture and sensitivity
2 Light blue sodium citrate coagulation (PT/INR, aPTT)
3 Red / gold (SST) none or clot activator with gel serum – biochemistry, LFT, RFT, serology
4 Green heparin plasma chemistry, ammonia
5 Lavender / purple EDTA CBC, blood grouping, HbA1c
6 Grey sodium fluoride / potassium oxalate blood glucose, lactate

Reason – following this order prevents carry-over of additives from one tube to the next (e.g. EDTA contamination falsely raises potassium).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is an occult blood test?
answer_html:
Definition An occult blood test detects hidden (microscopic) blood in the stool that cannot be seen with the naked eye.

Uses – screening for colorectal cancer and polyps; detecting slow bleeding from ulcers, inflammatory bowel disease; investigating iron-deficiency anaemia.

Types

  • Guaiac test (gFOBT) – needs diet restrictions for about 3 days (red meat, turnip, radish, vitamin C, aspirin/NSAIDs); usually 3 samples on 3 days
  • Faecal immunochemical test (FIT) – detects human haemoglobin; no diet restriction

A positive result is followed by colonoscopy.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the nursing precautions before and after the use of contrast media.
answer_html:
Before

  • Ask about previous contrast reaction, iodine allergy, asthma
  • Check kidney function (serum creatinine); ensure good hydration
  • Check pregnancy; withhold metformin as per policy; consent; IV access
  • Keep emergency drugs (adrenaline, hydrocortisone, antihistamine) and oxygen ready

During / after

  • Watch for reactions – mild (warmth, nausea, itching, urticaria) or severe (bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, hypotension, anaphylaxis)
  • Encourage fluids afterwards (unless restricted) to flush out the dye
  • Monitor urine output for contrast-induced kidney injury and watch for delayed reactions

Higher-risk patients – those with kidney disease, diabetes, dehydration, heart failure, old age or multiple myeloma; they need special care and hydration as advised.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the safety precautions for an MRI scan.
answer_html:
MRI uses a very strong magnet, so:

  1. Screen for pacemakers, defibrillators, cochlear implants, metallic aneurysm clips, metal fragments in the eye and other implants (only MRI-safe devices allowed)
  2. Remove all metal – jewellery, hair pins, watches, credit cards, hearing aids, metal-backed medicine patches
  3. No ferromagnetic equipment (oxygen cylinders, wheelchairs, trolleys) in the scanner room
  4. Explain the loud noise (give ear plugs) and the enclosed space; sedation for claustrophobic or restless patients
  5. The patient must lie still for 30–60 minutes
  6. Check kidney function before gadolinium contrast; take care in early pregnancy

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the collection of a throat swab.
answer_html:
Purpose – to identify organisms causing pharyngitis, tonsillitis or diphtheria (culture and sensitivity), before antibiotics.

Procedure

  1. Explain; patient sitting with the head tilted back; good light (torch)
  2. Wear gloves and a mask; depress the tongue with a tongue depressor; ask the patient to say "ah"
  3. Swab the tonsils and posterior pharyngeal wall, especially areas of redness, exudate or membrane, with a sterile swab – without touching the tongue, cheeks, teeth or lips
  4. Place the swab in the sterile tube or transport medium; label and send promptly
  5. The patient may gag – work quickly and gently

labels: oxygen diffusing from alveolus to blood
carbon dioxide diffusing from blood to alveolus
partial pressures PO2 100 and PCO2 40 in alveolus

answer_html:
Introduction Oxygen is the most basic physiological need – brain cells begin to die within 4–6 minutes without it. Oxygenation depends on the respiratory system (to take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide), the blood (to carry it) and the cardiovascular system (to deliver it to the tissues). Any disturbance in these systems produces hypoxia, and nurses play a key role in recognising it and promoting oxygenation.

PART A – PHYSIOLOGY OF OXYGENATION (5 marks)

1. Ventilation – movement of air into and out of the lungs

  • Inspiration (active) – the diaphragm contracts and moves down, the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs; the chest enlarges, pressure in the lungs falls and air flows in
  • Expiration (passive) – the muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil; air flows out
  • Depends on open airways, lung compliance (stretchability), elastic recoil, surfactant (keeps alveoli open) and intact respiratory muscles and nerves

2. Diffusion – exchange of gases across the alveolar–capillary membrane

  • Oxygen moves from the alveoli (PO₂ about 100 mmHg) into the blood (venous PO₂ about 40 mmHg)
  • Carbon dioxide moves from the blood (PCO₂ about 46 mmHg) into the alveoli (about 40 mmHg)
  • Diffusion is reduced when the membrane is thickened (oedema, fibrosis) or the surface area is reduced (emphysema, removal of a lung)

3. Perfusion – blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries

  • Good gas exchange needs matching of ventilation and perfusion (V/Q); a blocked airway or a clot in the pulmonary artery (embolism) disturbs this

4. Transport of gases

  • Oxygen – about 97–98% is carried bound to haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin), the rest dissolved in plasma; therefore haemoglobin level, cardiac output and the affinity of Hb for oxygen are important
  • Carbon dioxide – mostly as bicarbonate (about 70%), some bound to haemoglobin and some dissolved

5. Regulation of respiration

  • Neural – the respiratory centres in the medulla and pons control rate and depth
  • Chemical – central chemoreceptors respond to rising CO₂ (and H⁺); peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to low O₂, high CO₂ and low pH

6. Cardiovascular physiology

  • Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (about 5 litres/minute in an adult)
  • Stroke volume depends on preload (filling), afterload (resistance) and contractility
  • The conduction system – SA node (pacemaker, 60–100/min) → atria → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres – keeps the heart pumping in rhythm
  • The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself; systemic circulation carries oxygen to all tissues

PART B – ALTERATIONS IN OXYGENATION (5 marks)

1. Alterations in respiratory functioning

a. Hyperventilation

  • Ventilation more than needed to remove CO₂ → low PaCO₂ (respiratory alkalosis)
  • Causes – anxiety, fever, infection, pain, aspirin poisoning, compensation for metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis)
  • Signs – rapid deep breathing, sighing, light-headedness, palpitations, tingling and numbness of fingers and around the mouth, muscle cramps

b. Hypoventilation

  • Inadequate alveolar ventilation → CO₂ retention (hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis) and low oxygen
  • Causes – atelectasis, COPD, sedatives and opioids, head injury, neuromuscular diseases, severe obesity, giving high-concentration oxygen to some COPD patients
  • Signs – drowsiness, headache, confusion, flushed warm skin, irregular pulse, convulsions, coma

c. Hypoxia

  • Inadequate oxygen at the tissue level
  • Causes – low inspired oxygen (high altitude), low haemoglobin (anaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning), impaired diffusion (pneumonia, pulmonary oedema), poor perfusion (shock, heart failure), impaired ventilation (chest injury, airway obstruction), inability of cells to use oxygen (cyanide)
  • Early signs – restlessness, anxiety, inability to concentrate, confusion, increased pulse, respiration and BP, dizziness, pallor
  • Late signs – cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, decreased consciousness – cyanosis is a late sign and may be absent in anaemia

2. Alterations in cardiac functioning

  • Disturbances in conduction (arrhythmias) – tachycardia, bradycardia, atrial fibrillation, heart blocks – reduce effective cardiac output
  • Altered cardiac output – heart failure:
    • left-sided failure – blood backs up into the lungs: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, crackles, cough, fatigue
    • right-sided failure – blood backs up into the systemic veins: peripheral oedema, weight gain, raised jugular venous pressure, enlarged liver
  • Impaired valvular function – stenosis or regurgitation of valves (e.g. rheumatic heart disease) – murmurs, heart failure
  • Myocardial ischaemia – reduced coronary blood flow – angina and myocardial infarction (chest pain)

3. Other factors – anaemia, pregnancy, obesity, smoking, air pollution, immobility, chest deformities and lifestyle

PART C – NURSING INTERVENTIONS TO PROMOTE OXYGENATION (5 marks)

1. Health promotion

  • Vaccination – influenza, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccines
  • Avoid smoking and exposure to smoke, indoor air pollution (chulha smoke), dust and occupational hazards
  • Regular exercise, weight control, balanced diet, early treatment of chest infections

2. Acute care

  • Positioning – semi-Fowler's or high Fowler's to allow full lung expansion; orthopnoeic position (leaning forward on a pillow on the over-bed table) for severe breathlessness; frequent turning of bedridden patients; in one-sided lung disease, lie with the healthy lung down
  • Airway maintenance – head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust, removal of secretions by suctioning, artificial airways when needed
  • Mobilisation of secretions – adequate hydration (unless restricted), humidification and nebulisation, effective coughing, chest physiotherapy and postural drainage
  • Deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry – prevent atelectasis, especially after surgery
  • Oxygen therapy as prescribed, aiming at the target oxygen saturation
  • Care of chest drains, monitoring of SpO₂, respiration, pulse, colour and level of consciousness
  • Medicines as prescribed – bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics, diuretics
  • Reduce oxygen demand – rest, relieve anxiety, treat fever and pain

3. Restorative and continuing care

  • Breathing exercises – pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing in COPD
  • Pulmonary and cardiac rehabilitation – graded exercise, energy conservation, respiratory muscle training
  • Home oxygen teaching, inhaler technique, recognition of warning signs, regular follow-up

4. Monitoring and documentation

  • Respiratory rate, depth and effort, SpO₂, breath sounds, sputum, colour, pulse, BP, mental status; arterial blood gases when ordered; record and report changes promptly

PART D – Assessment and nursing diagnoses related to oxygenation

Assessment

  • History – cough, sputum (amount, colour), breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain, fatigue, smoking and exposure to smoke or dust, previous lung or heart disease, medicines
  • Physical examination – respiratory rate, rhythm and effort, chest shape and movement, SpO₂, colour, clubbing, breath sounds, pulse, BP, jugular veins, oedema, level of consciousness
  • Investigations – arterial blood gases, haemoglobin, chest X-ray, ECG, pulmonary function tests, sputum examination

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Ineffective airway clearance r/t thick secretions
  • Impaired gas exchange r/t alveolar consolidation or fluid
  • Ineffective breathing pattern r/t pain, fatigue or anxiety
  • Decreased cardiac output r/t altered heart rate or contractility
  • Activity intolerance r/t imbalance between oxygen supply and demand

  • Risk for aspiration r/t reduced level of consciousness

  • Fatigue and Anxiety r/t breathlessness – common companions of the above problems

Conclusion Oxygenation depends on ventilation, diffusion, perfusion and transport of gases controlled by neural and chemical mechanisms, and on adequate cardiac output; it is disturbed by hyperventilation, hypoventilation, hypoxia and cardiac alterations, and nurses promote it through health promotion, positioning, airway clearance, breathing exercises, oxygen therapy and rehabilitation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define oxygen therapy. Explain the indications, devices used, procedure, precautions, hazards and the nursing care of a patient receiving oxygen.

diagram.caption: Oxygen delivery devices
labels: non-rebreather mask with reservoir bag (10-15 L/min)

answer_html:
Introduction Oxygen is a drug. It must be prescribed, given in the correct dose (flow rate or concentration) by the correct device, monitored, and stopped when no longer needed. Too little oxygen causes hypoxia; too much can cause CO₂ retention, oxygen toxicity and fire.

A. Definition

  • Oxygen therapy is the administration of oxygen at a concentration higher than that of room air (21%) to prevent or treat hypoxaemia and hypoxia

B. Purposes

  • To correct hypoxaemia and relieve tissue hypoxia
  • To reduce the work of breathing and the work of the heart
  • To improve oxygen delivery in shock, anaemia and poisoning

C. Indications

  • Low oxygen saturation – generally SpO₂ below 94% (target 94–98% for most patients; 88–92% for patients at risk of CO₂ retention, such as severe COPD, as per guidelines)
  • Cardiac or respiratory arrest, shock, sepsis, severe trauma, major bleeding
  • Pneumonia, acute asthma, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism, COPD exacerbation
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning (high-concentration oxygen)
  • Severe anaemia, heart failure, myocardial infarction with hypoxaemia
  • After anaesthesia and surgery, during sedation, in unconscious patients
  • Newborns with respiratory distress (with careful monitoring)

D. Sources of oxygen

  • Central pipeline (wall outlet) with flowmeter
  • Oxygen cylinders – stored upright and chained; medical oxygen cylinders in India are black with a white shoulder
  • Oxygen concentrators – for home and low-flow use

E. Oxygen delivery devices

1. Low-flow devices (concentration varies with the patient's breathing)

Device Flow rate Approximate FiO₂ Points
Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min 24–44% comfortable; patient can eat and talk; drying above 4 L/min
Simple face mask 5–10 L/min 40–60% at least 5 L/min to flush out exhaled CO₂
Partial rebreather mask 6–10 L/min 50–70% reservoir bag; patient rebreathes some exhaled air
Non-rebreather mask 10–15 L/min 60–90% one-way valves; reservoir bag must stay inflated; for emergencies

2. High-flow devices (deliver a fixed, precise concentration)

  • Venturi mask – fixed FiO₂ of 24–60% using colour-coded adaptors with a stated flow rate; ideal for COPD
  • High-flow nasal cannula – heated, humidified oxygen up to 60 L/min, FiO₂ up to 100%
  • CPAP / BiPAP (non-invasive ventilation) and mechanical ventilation in severe failure

3. Other devices – face tent, tracheostomy mask/collar, T-piece; for infants – oxygen hood (head box), incubator

F. Equipment

  • Oxygen source and flowmeter, humidifier bottle filled with sterile water to the mark (when required)
  • Prescribed delivery device and tubing, pulse oximeter
  • "No smoking – oxygen in use" sign; gauze and cream for skin protection

G. Procedure

  1. Check the prescription – device, flow rate or FiO₂, target SpO₂; identify the patient
  2. Explain the purpose; reassure (masks can make patients anxious); remove sources of fire
  3. Hand hygiene; record baseline respiratory rate, pulse, SpO₂, colour and level of consciousness
  4. Position the patient in semi-Fowler's or high Fowler's, if not contraindicated
  5. Check the oxygen supply; attach the humidifier and flowmeter; connect the tubing and device
  6. Set the prescribed flow rate and check that oxygen is flowing (bubbling in the humidifier or flow felt at the prongs)
  7. Nasal cannula – place the prongs in the nostrils (curving downwards), loop the tubing over the ears and adjust under the chin
  8. Mask – cover the nose and mouth, mould the metal strip over the nose, adjust the elastic strap for a snug but comfortable fit; for a non-rebreather, fill the reservoir bag before applying
  9. Monitor SpO₂, respiration, pulse, colour, mental status and comfort; arterial blood gases as ordered
  10. Document – time, device, flow rate/FiO₂, SpO₂ and the patient's response

H. Precautions (safety)

  • No smoking, no naked flames, matches or lighters near the patient; display warning signs
  • No oil, grease or alcohol-based products on the cylinder fittings or on the patient's face (use water-based creams)
  • Check electrical equipment for sparks; avoid static-producing woollen or synthetic blankets
  • Cylinders – secure upright, away from heat; open the valve slowly; keep a spare full cylinder; transport on a trolley
  • Give oxygen only as prescribed; do not increase the flow on your own in COPD patients – use controlled oxygen (Venturi) and monitor for drowsiness

I. Hazards and complications

  • Oxygen toxicity – high concentrations (above about 50–60%) for more than 24–48 hours damage the lungs: substernal discomfort, dry cough, breathlessness, worsening hypoxaemia
  • CO₂ retention (hypercapnia, CO₂ narcosis) in some COPD patients – drowsiness, headache, confusion, warm flushed skin
  • Absorption atelectasis – high oxygen washes out nitrogen from the alveoli, which then collapse
  • Retinopathy of prematurity – in preterm infants given too much oxygen (can cause blindness)
  • Drying of mucous membranes, nosebleeds, thick secretions (if not humidified)
  • Pressure sores on the ears, nose and face from tubing and masks
  • Infection from contaminated humidifiers
  • Fire – oxygen supports combustion

J. Nursing care of a patient on oxygen

  • Keep the device in the correct position and the tubing free of kinks; check the flow rate every hour
  • Humidifier – keep at the correct water level with sterile water; change as per policy; drain condensate away from the patient
  • Mouth and nose care – frequent mouth care, moisten lips, clean the nostrils
  • Skin care – pad the tubing behind the ears; check the bridge of the nose and cheeks
  • Monitor against the target saturation; report falling SpO₂, rising respiratory rate, drowsiness or confusion
  • Allow the patient to eat and drink (change a mask to nasal cannula during meals if ordered)
  • Wean oxygen gradually as ordered when saturation is stable
  • Teach the patient and family about safety and home oxygen use

K. Weaning from oxygen

  • Reduce the flow or concentration gradually, as ordered, when the patient's condition improves and SpO₂ stays in the target range
  • Change from a mask to a nasal cannula, then to room air; check SpO₂, respiratory rate and comfort after each change
  • Restart or increase oxygen if saturation falls or the patient becomes breathless

L. Teaching for home oxygen

  • Use the prescribed flow and hours only; do not change the flow without advice
  • No smoking by the patient or family, no cooking flames or lamps near the oxygen; keep cylinders or concentrators 2 metres away from heat
  • Care of the concentrator (filter cleaning), cannula and humidifier; keep a spare cylinder for power cuts
  • Recognise warning signs – increasing breathlessness, drowsiness, confusion, blue lips – and seek help

M. Infants and children

  • Use oxygen hood (head box), nasal prongs or incubator oxygen; monitor SpO₂ continuously; avoid excess oxygen in preterm babies (risk of retinopathy of prematurity)

Conclusion Oxygen therapy is the prescribed administration of oxygen above 21% to correct hypoxaemia, using low-flow devices (nasal cannula, masks) or high-flow devices (Venturi, high-flow cannula); safe practice requires the correct device and flow, target-based monitoring, humidification where needed, strict fire safety and watching for CO₂ retention, toxicity and skin damage.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a client with dyspnoea.
answer_html:
Introduction Dyspnoea is the subjective feeling of difficult, uncomfortable or laboured breathing. It is frightening for the patient and is a sign of serious heart or lung disease. Types include exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea (breathlessness on lying flat), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (sudden breathlessness at night) and breathlessness at rest.

1. Causes

  • Respiratory – asthma, COPD, pneumonia, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, airway obstruction
  • Cardiac – heart failure, myocardial infarction, valvular disease
  • Others – severe anaemia, obesity, anxiety and panic, metabolic acidosis, neuromuscular weakness, pregnancy (late)

2. Assessment

  • Respiratory rate, depth, rhythm; use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, retractions
  • SpO₂, colour (cyanosis), pulse, BP, temperature, level of consciousness
  • Ability to speak – in full sentences, phrases or only words
  • Breath sounds – wheeze, crackles, reduced air entry; cough and sputum; chest pain
  • Onset, triggers and position that relieves it; severity on a dyspnoea scale

3. Nursing management

Position

  • High Fowler's or orthopnoeic position – sitting up, leaning forward with the arms supported on pillows on an over-bed table; this lets the diaphragm descend and uses accessory muscles

Oxygen and medicines

  • Give oxygen as prescribed to the target saturation
  • Nebulised or inhaled bronchodilators, steroids, diuretics, antibiotics as prescribed; check inhaler technique

Airway and secretions

  • Encourage effective coughing; suction if needed; adequate fluids (unless restricted) and humidification to loosen secretions

Breathing techniques

  • Pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing – slow the breathing and prevent airway collapse

Comfort and anxiety

  • Stay with the patient; speak calmly; anxiety worsens breathlessness
  • Loosen tight clothing; keep the room well ventilated and cool; a fan directed at the face can reduce the sensation of breathlessness
  • Remove irritants – smoke, strong smells, dust

Energy conservation

  • Rest periods, help with activities of daily living, keep articles within reach
  • Small, frequent meals; avoid large meals and gas-forming foods (pressure on the diaphragm)

Monitoring and emergency readiness

  • Monitor SpO₂, respiratory rate, pulse and mental status; ABG as ordered
  • Keep emergency equipment (suction, bag-valve mask, non-invasive ventilation) ready; report worsening at once

Teaching

  • Avoid triggers; stop smoking; correct use of inhalers; breathing exercises; when to seek help

Conclusion Care of a client with dyspnoea involves careful assessment, upright or orthopnoeic positioning, oxygen and prescribed medicines, airway clearance, breathing techniques, reduction of anxiety and energy demand, close monitoring and teaching.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the procedure of oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal suctioning.
answer_html:
Introduction Suctioning is the removal of secretions from the airway with a catheter connected to a suction source. It keeps the airway clear in patients who cannot cough effectively – unconscious, weak, post-operative or neurological patients.

1. Indications

  • Visible or audible secretions (gurgling, rattling)
  • Coarse crackles, ineffective cough
  • Falling SpO₂, restlessness, increased respiratory rate due to secretions
  • Vomitus or blood in the mouth of an unconscious patient

2. Equipment

  • Suction machine or wall suction with collection bottle and tubing
  • Sterile suction catheters of suitable size (adults about 12–14 Fr) and a Yankauer (tonsil) tip for the mouth
  • Sterile water or saline in a container for rinsing, gloves (sterile for nasopharyngeal suction), goggles/mask, water-soluble lubricant
  • Towel, pulse oximeter, oxygen supply

3. Suction pressure

  • Adults – 100–150 mmHg; children – 100–120 mmHg; infants – 60–100 mmHg

4. Procedure

  1. Assess the need (listen to breath sounds); identify the patient; explain even if unconscious
  2. Hand hygiene; position – semi-Fowler's for a conscious patient, lateral (facing the nurse) for an unconscious patient
  3. Pre-oxygenate if SpO₂ is low or as ordered; place a towel under the chin
  4. Switch on suction and check the pressure by occluding the tubing
  5. Wear gloves (sterile hand handles the catheter for nasopharyngeal suction); connect the catheter
  6. Nasopharyngeal – measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe; lubricate; insert gently along the floor of the nostril during inspiration without applying suction
  7. Oropharyngeal – insert the Yankauer or catheter along the side of the mouth to the pharynx, without suction
  8. Apply intermittent suction while withdrawing the catheter with a rotating motion
  9. Each pass must not exceed 10–15 seconds; allow 20–30 seconds (and oxygen) between passes; usually not more than 2–3 passes
  10. Rinse the catheter with sterile water between passes
  11. Suction the nose before the mouth, or use a new catheter – never use a catheter from the mouth in the nose
  12. Discard the catheter; switch off suction; give mouth care; reposition the patient
  13. Assess – breath sounds, SpO₂, pulse, colour

5. Documentation – time, route, amount, colour, consistency and odour of secretions, patient's tolerance

6. Complications

  • Hypoxia, bradycardia and arrhythmias (vagal stimulation)
  • Trauma and bleeding of the mucosa
  • Laryngospasm, bronchospasm, gagging and vomiting with aspiration
  • Infection; raised intracranial pressure

Conclusion Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal suctioning removes secretions when the patient cannot cough; correct position, safe pressure, insertion without suction, intermittent suction on withdrawal for no more than 10–15 seconds, oxygenation between passes and observation of the patient prevent complications.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain chest physiotherapy and postural drainage.

diagram.caption: Postural drainage positions
labels: upper lobes sitting upright or leaning
middle lobe and lingula side-lying with head down 15 degrees
lower lobes head down 30 degrees prone or side-lying

answer_html:
Introduction Chest physiotherapy (CPT) is a group of techniques – postural drainage, percussion, vibration and coughing – that help loosen and remove secretions from the lungs. It is used in patients with excess or retained secretions.

1. Definitions

  • Postural drainage – placing the patient in positions that allow gravity to drain secretions from particular lung segments into the larger airways, from where they are coughed up or suctioned
  • Percussion (clapping) – rhythmic striking of the chest wall with cupped hands to loosen secretions
  • Vibration – fine shaking movement of the hands on the chest wall during expiration

2. Indications

  • Bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess
  • COPD with excessive sputum, atelectasis due to mucus plugs
  • Patients unable to clear secretions – weak, post-operative or neuromuscular patients

3. Contraindications

  • Haemoptysis, recent chest injury, rib fractures, osteoporosis, chest wall pain
  • Raised intracranial pressure (head-down position), recent eye or brain surgery
  • Unstable heart condition, uncontrolled hypertension, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism
  • Immediately after meals (risk of vomiting)

4. Positions (examples)

  • Upper lobes – sitting upright or leaning forward/backward at different angles
  • Middle lobe (right) and lingula (left) – lying on the opposite side, rotated slightly backwards, with the foot end raised about 15°
  • Lower lobes – lying prone or on the side with the foot end raised about 30° (head down)
  • The patient's chest X-ray and breath sounds show which segment needs drainage

5. Procedure

  1. Check the order; plan before meals (or 1–2 hours after) – often on waking and at bedtime; give bronchodilator nebulisation first if ordered
  2. Explain; hand hygiene; check vital signs, SpO₂ and breath sounds
  3. Place the patient in the required position and keep him there for 5–15 minutes per position (as tolerated)
  4. Percussion – with cupped hands, over a thin towel or gown, clap the chest wall over the segment for 1–2 minutes; avoid the spine, sternum, kidneys, breasts and below the ribs
  5. Vibration – flat hands on the chest wall, shake gently while the patient breathes out slowly, for several breaths
  6. Help the patient to sit up and cough (or huff); suction if he cannot cough; provide tissues and a sputum cup
  7. Total session usually 20–30 minutes; stop if he becomes breathless, cyanosed, dizzy, or has chest pain
  8. Give mouth care; make him comfortable

6. Observation and recording

  • Amount, colour and consistency of sputum, breath sounds before and after, SpO₂ and tolerance

Conclusion Chest physiotherapy combines postural drainage, percussion, vibration and coughing to clear secretions; it is given before meals in positions that drain the affected segments, avoiding contraindicated conditions, and its effect is judged by the sputum produced, breath sounds and oxygen saturation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient with an underwater seal chest drainage.

diagram.caption: Underwater seal drainage system
labels: long tube 2 cm under water in the water-seal bottle
fluctuation (tidalling) of water in the tube

answer_html:
Introduction An intercostal chest drain connected to an underwater seal drainage (UWSD) system removes air, blood or fluid from the pleural space and allows the lung to re-expand. The water seal acts as a one-way valve – air and fluid can leave the chest but cannot enter it.

1. Indications

  • Pneumothorax, haemothorax, haemopneumothorax
  • Pleural effusion, empyema
  • After chest (thoracic) and heart surgery

2. Principle

  • The end of the long tube is kept about 2 cm under water – this forms the water seal
  • The bottle is kept below the level of the chest so that gravity helps drainage and water is not sucked back into the chest

3. Nursing care

Maintaining the system

  • Keep the bottle below chest level at all times (also when moving or transporting the patient); never lift it above the chest
  • Keep the bottle upright and the water seal at the correct level; check that connections are airtight and taped
  • Keep the tubing free of kinks and loops; coil it on the bed so that the patient can move
  • Milking or stripping the tube is done only if ordered (e.g. to clear clots)

Observing the drainage

  • Tidalling (fluctuation) – the water in the tube rises on inspiration and falls on expiration; it shows the system is working; it stops when the lung has re-expanded or the tube is blocked or kinked
  • Bubbling – intermittent bubbling (especially on coughing or expiration) shows air leaking from the pleural space (expected in pneumothorax); continuous bubbling may mean a leak in the system – check connections
  • Drainage – measure and mark the level with the time on the bottle; note colour and amount; report sudden heavy bleeding (e.g. more than about 100–200 mL/hour of bloody drainage) or a sudden stop of drainage with breathlessness

Patient care

  • Semi-Fowler's position; encourage deep breathing, coughing and incentive spirometry
  • Arm and shoulder exercises on the affected side; early ambulation with the bottle held below the chest
  • Pain relief – the drain site is painful
  • Inspect the insertion site – dressing dry and secure; feel for crepitus (surgical emphysema)
  • Monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂, breath sounds, pulse, BP and temperature

Safety measures

  • Keep two padded artery forceps (clamps) at the bedside; clamp only briefly (changing the bottle, finding a leak) and as per policy – prolonged clamping can cause tension pneumothorax
  • If the bottle breaks – put the end of the tube under sterile water (in a new bottle) at once
  • If the tube comes out of the chest – cover the site immediately with a sterile occlusive dressing and call the doctor
  • Change the bottle with aseptic technique

4. Removal

  • Done when the lung has re-expanded and drainage is minimal (confirmed by X-ray)
  • Give analgesia; ask the patient to take a deep breath and hold it (or perform the Valsalva manoeuvre) while the tube is pulled out; cover with an airtight dressing; follow-up chest X-ray; watch for breathlessness

Conclusion Care of a patient with an underwater seal drainage involves keeping the system airtight and below chest level, maintaining the water seal, observing tidalling, bubbling and drainage, encouraging breathing exercises and mobility, relieving pain, and knowing the emergency steps if the bottle breaks or the tube comes out.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain deep breathing and coughing exercises and incentive spirometry.
answer_html:
Introduction Breathing exercises help to expand the lungs, improve ventilation, move secretions and prevent atelectasis and pneumonia, especially after surgery and in chronic lung disease. They are simple, cheap and very effective when taught well.

1. Purposes

  • Prevent atelectasis and pneumonia after surgery and during bed rest
  • Improve lung expansion and oxygenation
  • Loosen and remove secretions
  • Reduce breathlessness and the work of breathing in COPD
  • Promote relaxation

2. Diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing

  1. Semi-Fowler's or sitting position with knees slightly bent
  2. Place one hand on the chest and one on the abdomen
  3. Breathe in slowly through the nose – the abdomen should rise while the chest moves little
  4. Breathe out slowly through pursed lips – the abdomen falls
  5. Repeat 5–10 times, several times a day

3. Pursed-lip breathing

  • Breathe in through the nose for about 2 counts; breathe out slowly through pursed lips (as if whistling or blowing out a candle) for about 4 counts
  • Keeps the small airways open, slows breathing and relieves breathlessness in COPD

4. Coughing exercises

  • Sit upright, lean slightly forward
  • Splint the incision with a pillow or folded hands (after chest or abdominal surgery)
  • Take 2–3 deep breaths, then cough 2–3 times forcefully from the chest (not the throat)
  • Huff coughing – a series of forced exhalations with an open mouth ("ha-ha-ha") – less tiring for COPD patients
  • Give tissues and a sputum cup; mouth care afterwards

5. Incentive spirometry

  • An incentive spirometer is a device that gives visual feedback (a rising ball or piston) to encourage slow, deep inspiration
  • Procedure:
    1. Sit upright; hold the device upright
    2. Breathe out normally, then seal the lips around the mouthpiece
    3. Breathe in slowly and deeply to raise the ball or piston to the target level
    4. Hold the breath for 3–5 seconds, then breathe out slowly
    5. Rest; repeat 10 times every hour while awake
    6. Cough after each set to clear secretions
  • Record the volume or level reached; clean the mouthpiece and keep it covered

6. Nurse's role

  • Teach before surgery (pre-operative teaching), when the patient is free of pain
  • Relieve pain before exercises; encourage and supervise; record progress and sputum
  • Stop if the patient becomes dizzy (hyperventilation) and let him rest

Conclusion Diaphragmatic and pursed-lip breathing, effective coughing with splinting and hourly incentive spirometry expand the lungs, clear secretions and prevent post-operative atelectasis and pneumonia, and relieve breathlessness in chronic lung disease.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain nebulisation and steam inhalation.
answer_html:
Introduction Both nebulisation and steam inhalation deliver moisture or medicine directly to the airways. Nebulisation is used mainly to give bronchodilators and other drugs; steam inhalation is a simple home remedy to moisten and loosen secretions.

A. Nebulisation

1. Definition – the conversion of a liquid medicine into a fine mist (aerosol) that the patient inhales through a mouthpiece or mask

2. Purposes

  • Bronchodilation – salbutamol, ipratropium in asthma and COPD
  • Loosening secretions – normal or hypertonic saline, mucolytics
  • Anti-inflammatory – budesonide; antibiotics in some conditions

3. Equipment – nebuliser chamber with mouthpiece or mask, compressor (or oxygen/air source at 6–8 L/min), prescribed drug, normal saline, syringe, tissues

4. Procedure

  1. Check the prescription; identify the patient; explain
  2. Hand hygiene; check pulse, respiratory rate, SpO₂ and breath sounds before treatment
  3. Sit the patient upright
  4. Put the drug and diluent (usually a total of 3–5 mL) into the chamber; attach the mouthpiece or mask
  5. Connect to the compressor (or gas source); a fine mist should appear
  6. Ask the patient to breathe slowly and deeply through the mouth, holding the breath briefly if able
  7. Continue until the mist stops (about 10–15 minutes); tap the chamber near the end
  8. Encourage coughing; rinse the mouth after steroid nebulisation (prevents oral thrush)
  9. Reassess pulse, respiration, SpO₂ and breath sounds; note side effects – tachycardia, tremor, nausea
  10. Wash, dry and store the nebuliser parts; record the drug, dose, time and response - In COPD with CO₂ retention, drive the nebuliser with air rather than high-flow oxygen as advised

B. Steam inhalation

1. Purposes – to moisten and loosen thick secretions, relieve nasal and sinus congestion, soothe the throat

2. Methods – electric steam inhaler or vaporiser; traditionally a bowl of hot water with a towel draped over the head (now discouraged because of scalds); medicated additives such as menthol or tincture benzoin may be used if prescribed

3. Procedure

  • Explain; sit the patient upright in a stable position with the device on a firm surface
  • Keep the face about 20–30 cm from the steam; inhale through the nose and mouth for 10–15 minutes
  • Cover the eyes if irritants are added; dry the face afterwards; avoid going out into cold air immediately

4. Precautions

  • Risk of burns and scalds – never leave the patient alone; not recommended for young children
  • Not for patients who are confused or unable to hold steady
  • Check water temperature and keep the device away from the edge of the table

Conclusion Nebulisation delivers inhaled medicines as a fine mist through a mouthpiece or mask with monitoring before and after; steam inhalation moistens and loosens secretions but must be given carefully to prevent scalds.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain airway maintenance, including the use of artificial airways.
answer_html:
Introduction A clear airway is the first priority in every patient – A (airway) comes before B (breathing) and C (circulation). Unconscious patients lose muscle tone, and the tongue falls back and blocks the pharynx; secretions, vomit and blood may also obstruct the airway.

1. Signs of airway obstruction – snoring, gurgling, stridor, see-saw breathing, absent air movement, restlessness, cyanosis, falling SpO₂

2. Simple measures

  • Head tilt–chin lift – opens the airway in patients without neck injury
  • Jaw thrust – lifts the jaw forward without moving the neck – used when cervical spine injury is suspected
  • Recovery (lateral) position for unconscious patients who are breathing – allows secretions to drain
  • Suctioning of the mouth and pharynx; removal of loose dentures or foreign bodies

3. Artificial airways

a. Oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway

  • A curved plastic airway that holds the tongue away from the back of the pharynx
  • For unconscious patients without a gag reflex (causes gagging and vomiting in conscious patients)
  • Size – from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw (or earlobe)
  • Insertion in adults – insert with the curve upside down, then rotate 180° as it reaches the soft palate; in children insert the right way up using a tongue depressor

b. Nasopharyngeal airway

  • A soft tube passed through the nostril into the pharynx; better tolerated by semi-conscious patients with a gag reflex
  • Size – tip of the nose to the earlobe; lubricate and insert along the floor of the nostril
  • Avoid in suspected base-of-skull fracture, nasal injury and bleeding disorders

c. Endotracheal tube

  • Inserted into the trachea by a doctor/anaesthetist for ventilation and airway protection
  • Nurse's role – prepare equipment (laryngoscope, tubes of correct size, stylet, 10 mL syringe for the cuff, lubricant, suction, bag-valve mask, oxygen, tube holder); help confirm placement (chest rise on both sides, breath sounds, end-tidal CO₂, chest X-ray); secure the tube and note the length at the lips
  • Care – check cuff pressure (about 20–30 cmH₂O), suction as needed, mouth care with chlorhexidine, head end raised 30–45°, prevent accidental extubation

d. Tracheostomy

  • A surgical opening into the trachea with a tube in place – for long-term ventilation, upper airway obstruction or clearing secretions
  • Care – humidified oxygen, suctioning, cleaning the inner cannula, sterile stoma dressing and tie changes (two persons), keep a spare tube, obturator and tracheal dilator at the bedside, provide a means of communication (writing board)

e. Supraglottic devices – laryngeal mask airway or similar devices used in emergencies and anaesthesia

4. General nursing responsibilities

  • Keep suction, oxygen and a bag-valve mask ready for every patient with an artificial airway
  • Humidify inspired gases (the nose is bypassed)
  • Monitor breathing, SpO₂, secretions and position of the airway; document

Conclusion Airway maintenance starts with head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust, positioning and suction, and may need oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal, endotracheal or tracheostomy airways; the nurse sizes and inserts simple airways correctly, assists with advanced airways and gives safe ongoing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Name the types of hypoxia with examples.
answer_html:
Hypoxia – inadequate supply or use of oxygen at the tissue level.

Type Cause Examples
Hypoxic (hypoxaemic) hypoxia low oxygen in arterial blood high altitude, hypoventilation, pneumonia, asthma, airway obstruction
Anaemic hypoxia reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood anaemia, haemorrhage, carbon monoxide poisoning
Stagnant (circulatory) hypoxia reduced blood flow to tissues shock, heart failure, arterial blockage
Histotoxic hypoxia cells cannot use oxygen cyanide poisoning

Signs of hypoxia – early: restlessness, anxiety, tachycardia, tachypnoea, confusion; late: cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension, drowsiness.

Treatment depends on the type – oxygen for hypoxic hypoxia, blood transfusion for anaemia, restoring circulation in shock, and antidotes in cyanide poisoning.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is oxygen toxicity?
answer_html:
Definition Oxygen toxicity is damage to the lungs (and other organs) caused by breathing high concentrations of oxygen (above about 50–60%) for a prolonged period (more than 24–48 hours), due to the formation of harmful free radicals.

Signs – substernal discomfort or chest pain, dry cough, breathlessness, tingling of the extremities, fatigue, restlessness and progressive hypoxaemia; may lead to lung injury similar to ARDS.

Prevention – give the lowest concentration that achieves the target saturation; monitor SpO₂ and arterial blood gases; reduce oxygen as soon as possible.

Related problems – absorption atelectasis; retinopathy of prematurity in preterm babies.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Why is oxygen humidified?
answer_html:
Oxygen from cylinders and pipelines is completely dry. Humidification adds water vapour to prevent:

  1. Drying and irritation of the nose, mouth and throat
  2. Thick, sticky secretions that are hard to cough up
  3. Nosebleeds, discomfort and damage to the airway lining

When used – usually for flows above 4 L/min by cannula, for masks (as per policy), and always for patients with tracheostomy or endotracheal tubes (the nose, which normally warms and moistens air, is bypassed).

Care – use sterile water filled to the mark; change it regularly (stagnant water grows bacteria); drain condensed water from tubing away from the patient.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is a Venturi mask?
answer_html:
Definition A Venturi mask is a high-flow oxygen mask that delivers a precise, fixed concentration of oxygen (usually 24–60%), regardless of the patient's breathing pattern.

Principle – oxygen passes through a narrow jet in the adaptor, which draws in (entrains) a fixed amount of room air through side ports (Venturi effect).

Features – colour-coded adaptors (e.g. 24%, 28%, 35%, 40%, 60%), each requiring a stated oxygen flow rate.

Use – patients who need controlled oxygen, especially COPD patients at risk of CO₂ retention.

Care – set the correct flow for the adaptor; keep the side ports uncovered by sheets or clothing.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)? How is it measured?
answer_html:
Definition PEFR is the maximum speed of air a person can blow out forcefully after a full inspiration, measured in litres per minute with a peak flow meter. It reflects narrowing of the large airways.

Procedure

  1. Stand or sit upright; set the pointer to zero
  2. Take a deep breath, seal the lips around the mouthpiece
  3. Blow out as hard and fast as possible
  4. Note the reading; repeat three times and record the highest value

Uses – monitoring asthma (morning and evening), judging response to treatment; asthma action plans use zones – green 80–100% of personal best, yellow 50–80%, red below 50% (seek urgent help).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the distribution and regulation of body fluids. Describe fluid volume deficit and fluid volume excess – causes, clinical features and nursing management.

diagram.caption: Body fluid compartments in an adult
labels: total body water about 60% of body weight

answer_html:
Introduction Water is the largest component of the body. Fluid and electrolyte balance is essential for cell function, circulation, temperature control and the removal of wastes. Imbalances are common in vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, surgery, heart, kidney and liver disease, and nurses are often the first to recognise them through intake–output records, daily weights and observation.

PART A – DISTRIBUTION OF BODY FLUIDS

1. Total body water

  • About 60% of body weight in adult men, about 55% in women (more fat), 70–80% in infants and about 45–50% in the elderly – infants and the elderly are more easily dehydrated

2. Compartments

  • Intracellular fluid (ICF) – fluid inside the cells – two-thirds of body water (about 40% of body weight)
  • Extracellular fluid (ECF) – one-third (about 20% of body weight):
    • interstitial fluid – between the cells (about 15%)
    • intravascular fluid (plasma) – in the blood vessels (about 5%)
    • transcellular fluid – CSF, pleural, peritoneal, synovial fluid, digestive juices

3. Electrolytes

  • ECF – main cation sodium (Na⁺), main anions chloride and bicarbonate
  • ICF – main cation potassium (K⁺), main anions phosphate and proteins

4. Movement of fluids and solutes

  • Diffusion – movement of particles from higher to lower concentration
  • Osmosis – movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane from a less concentrated to a more concentrated solution
  • Filtration – movement of fluid by hydrostatic pressure (e.g. from capillaries to tissues)
  • Active transport – movement against a concentration gradient using energy (e.g. sodium–potassium pump)

5. Daily intake and output (approximate, adult)

Intake mL Output mL
Drinks 1,300–1,500 Urine 1,400–1,500
Water in food 700–800 Skin (insensible) 500–600
Water from metabolism 200–300 Lungs (insensible) 400
Faeces 100–200
Total about 2,500 Total about 2,500

PART B – REGULATION OF FLUID BALANCE

  1. Thirst – osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect increased concentration of plasma and stimulate thirst
  2. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) – released from the posterior pituitary when plasma becomes concentrated or blood volume falls; makes the kidneys reabsorb water – less, concentrated urine
  3. Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – low blood volume or pressure → kidneys release renin → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, thirst) → aldosterone from the adrenal cortex → sodium and water retention, potassium excretion
  4. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) – released when the atria are stretched by excess volume → sodium and water excretion
  5. Kidneys – the main regulators; filter about 180 litres a day and adjust urine volume and composition
  6. Other organs – lungs and skin (insensible loss), GI tract (absorption and secretion), heart (circulation)

PART C – FLUID VOLUME DEFICIT (HYPOVOLAEMIA)

1. Definition – a loss of both water and electrolytes from the extracellular fluid (isotonic loss); when only water is lost the term dehydration is used

2. Causes

  • Gastrointestinal losses – vomiting, diarrhoea, nasogastric suction, fistulas
  • Haemorrhage, burns, excessive sweating, fever
  • Renal losses – diuretics, uncontrolled diabetes (polyuria), diabetes insipidus, Addison's disease
  • Inadequate intake – unconscious, confused, elderly, nausea, inability to swallow
  • Third-space shifts – ascites, burns, peritonitis, intestinal obstruction, pancreatitis

3. Clinical features

  • Thirst, acute weight loss (1 kg ≈ 1 litre of fluid)
  • Dry mouth and tongue, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor; in infants, sunken fontanelle and no tears
  • Oliguria, concentrated urine (high specific gravity)
  • Tachycardia, weak thready pulse, low BP and postural hypotension, flat neck veins, delayed capillary refill
  • Cold clammy skin, weakness, dizziness, confusion; severe loss → hypovolaemic shock
  • Laboratory – raised haematocrit (haemoconcentration), raised blood urea

4. Nursing management

  • Monitor – vital signs including postural BP, hourly urine output (report less than 30 mL/hour), level of consciousness, skin turgor, mucous membranes
  • Strict intake–output chart and daily weight (same time, same scale, same clothing)
  • Fluid replacement – oral rehydration solution in mild deficit; IV isotonic fluids (normal saline, Ringer's lactate) or blood as prescribed; watch for overload during rapid replacement
  • Treat the cause – antiemetics, control of bleeding, treatment of diarrhoea
  • Mouth care and skin care; fall prevention (dizziness on standing – help the patient to rise slowly)
  • Monitor electrolytes; teach the patient and family about ORS and early signs of dehydration

PART D – FLUID VOLUME EXCESS (HYPERVOLAEMIA)

1. Definition – excess retention of water and sodium in the extracellular fluid

2. Causes

  • Heart failure, kidney failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
  • Excessive IV fluids (especially saline) or blood, given too fast
  • High salt intake, corticosteroid therapy, excess aldosterone

3. Clinical features

  • Weight gain, oedema (pitting oedema of feet, sacral oedema in bedridden patients), puffy eyelids
  • Distended neck veins, bounding pulse, hypertension
  • Crackles in the lungs, breathlessness, orthopnoea, cough; in severe cases pulmonary oedema with frothy pink sputum
  • Ascites; laboratory – low haematocrit (haemodilution)

4. Nursing management

  • Restrict sodium and fluids as prescribed; give diuretics as ordered and watch for low potassium
  • Daily weight, strict intake–output; monitor breath sounds, oedema, neck veins and BP
  • Position – semi-Fowler's or high Fowler's for breathlessness; oxygen as prescribed
  • IV fluids only by infusion pump at the ordered rate
  • Skin care – oedematous skin is fragile; turn every 2 hours; elevate oedematous limbs
  • Prepare for dialysis if ordered; teach a low-salt diet and daily weighing at home

PART E – Nursing assessment of fluid balance

  • History – fluid intake, thirst, vomiting, diarrhoea, urine pattern, sweating, bleeding, medicines (diuretics, steroids), heart, kidney or liver disease
  • Daily weight – the most reliable indicator of short-term fluid change
  • Vital signs – pulse rate and volume, BP lying and standing, respiration, temperature
  • Skin and mucous membranes – turgor, moisture of the tongue and mouth, sunken eyes, oedema (site and grade)
  • Neck veins – flat in deficit, distended in excess
  • Lungs – crackles and breathlessness in excess
  • Urine – volume, colour and specific gravity
  • Laboratory – haematocrit, blood urea, creatinine, serum electrolytes and osmolality, urine specific gravity

PART F – Common nursing diagnoses

  • Deficient fluid volume r/t active fluid loss (vomiting, diarrhoea) AEB dry mucosa, tachycardia and oliguria
  • Excess fluid volume r/t compromised regulatory mechanisms (heart or kidney failure) AEB oedema, weight gain and crackles
  • Risk for imbalanced fluid volume r/t major surgery
  • Impaired oral mucous membrane r/t dehydration; Risk for impaired skin integrity r/t oedema

PART G – Special groups

  • Infants and young children – higher body water, faster turnover and immature kidneys; they become dehydrated quickly with diarrhoea and fever; watch the fontanelle, tears, nappies and weight

  • Elderly – reduced thirst sensation, less body water, weaker kidney concentrating ability and frequent use of diuretics – risk of both dehydration and overload; offer fluids regularly and monitor closely

  • Pregnant women – blood volume rises by about 40–50%; mild oedema of the feet is common, but sudden swelling of the face and hands with high BP must be reported (pre-eclampsia)

Conclusion Body water is distributed between the intracellular and extracellular compartments and is regulated by thirst, ADH, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, ANP and the kidneys; fluid volume deficit and excess have typical causes and signs, and are managed by careful monitoring, intake–output, daily weights, correct fluid replacement or restriction and treatment of the cause.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define intravenous therapy. Explain the purposes, sites, equipment, procedure of starting an IV infusion, calculation of flow rate, complications and nursing care.

diagram.caption: Common sites for peripheral IV cannulation
labels: median cubital vein in antecubital fossa

answer_html:
Introduction Intravenous (IV) therapy is one of the most common procedures in hospitals. It can save lives in shock and dehydration, but it also carries risks – infection, phlebitis, fluid overload and air embolism. Nurses start, maintain and monitor IV infusions and are responsible for their safety.

A. Definition

  • Intravenous therapy is the administration of fluids, electrolytes, nutrients, medicines or blood directly into a vein

B. Purposes

  1. To restore and maintain fluid and electrolyte balance
  2. To give medicines that need rapid action or cannot be given by other routes
  3. To give nutrients (dextrose, parenteral nutrition)
  4. To transfuse blood and blood products
  5. To keep venous access open for emergencies
  6. To monitor central venous pressure (central lines)

C. Sites

  • Peripheral veins of the arm – dorsal metacarpal veins of the hand, cephalic and basilic veins of the forearm, median cubital vein (antecubital fossa – used for emergencies and sampling, but movement of the elbow disturbs the flow)
  • Start distally (hand/forearm) and move upwards for later cannulations; prefer the non-dominant arm
  • Infants – scalp veins, dorsum of hand or foot
  • Central veins – subclavian, internal jugular, femoral and PICC lines (inserted by doctors or trained nurses)
  • Avoid – leg veins in adults (risk of thrombosis), the arm with an AV fistula or on the side of mastectomy, injured, infected, bruised or phlebitic areas, joints, and sites below a recent puncture

D. Cannula sizes (colour codes)

Gauge Colour Use
14 G / 16 G orange / grey trauma, major surgery, rapid fluids
18 G green blood transfusion, surgery
20 G pink routine adult infusions
22 G blue small veins, elderly, children
24 G yellow neonates, infants

E. Equipment

  • Prescribed IV fluid, IV administration set (macro-drip 15 or 20 drops/mL; micro-drip 60 drops/mL), extension set or three-way stopcock
  • IV cannula of correct size, tourniquet, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol (or as per policy), sterile gauze, clean gloves
  • Sterile transparent dressing, tape, label, saline flush syringe, IV stand, infusion pump if needed, splint, sharps container, kidney tray

F. Procedure of starting an IV infusion

Preparation

  1. Check the order – type of fluid, volume, rate, additives; identify the patient with two identifiers
  2. Explain the procedure; ask about allergies; ensure privacy and comfort
  3. Hand hygiene; check the fluid – name, strength, expiry date, clarity, leaks
  4. Prepare the infusion – close the roller clamp, spike the bag aseptically, squeeze the drip chamber to fill it one-third to half, prime the tubing to remove all air, close the clamp, hang on the stand

Cannulation

  1. Select the vein by inspection and palpation; apply the tourniquet 10–15 cm above the site
  2. Ask the patient to open and close the fist; let the arm hang down or tap the vein gently to make it prominent
  3. Clean the site with antiseptic for about 30 seconds and let it dry; do not touch the site again
  4. Wear gloves; anchor the vein by stretching the skin below the site
  5. Insert the cannula bevel up at a 10–30° angle; watch for flashback of blood in the chamber
  6. Lower the angle, advance the cannula slightly, then slide the cannula off the needle into the vein
  7. Release the tourniquet; press over the vein beyond the cannula tip and withdraw the needle; discard it in the sharps container immediately
  8. Connect the infusion set (or flush with saline); open the clamp and check that fluid flows freely without swelling or pain
  9. Secure with a sterile transparent dressing; label with date, time, gauge and initials
  10. Regulate the flow rate as prescribed; make the patient comfortable
  11. Document – site, cannula size, fluid, rate, time, patient's response

G. Calculation of flow rate

  • Drops per minute = (Volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ (Time in minutes)
  • mL per hour = Total volume ÷ number of hours (for infusion pumps)
  • Example – 1,000 mL of normal saline over 8 hours with a 20-drop set: (1,000 × 20) ÷ 480 = about 42 drops/minute; pump rate = 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hour
  • With a micro-drip set (60 drops/mL), drops/minute = mL/hour

Factors affecting flow – height of the bottle, position of the arm, kinked tubing, cannula size, clot or infiltration, viscosity of fluid, venous spasm

H. Complications

Local

  • Infiltration – fluid leaks into the tissues: swelling, coolness, pallor, discomfort, slow flow → stop, remove the cannula, elevate the limb
  • Extravasation – leakage of an irritant (vesicant) drug (e.g. some anticancer drugs, potassium, calcium, dopamine) → tissue damage or necrosis; stop at once and follow protocol
