subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the administration of medicines by sublingual, buccal and topical (skin) routes, including transdermal patches.
answer_html:
Introduction These routes allow drugs to be absorbed through the mucous membrane of the mouth or through the skin. They are simple, painless and avoid injections, but need correct technique for the drug to act.

A. Sublingual route

  • The tablet is placed under the tongue, where it dissolves and is absorbed directly into the rich network of veins – bypassing the liver (no first-pass effect) and acting within minutes
  • Example – nitroglycerin (GTN) for angina; some antihypertensives and antiemetics
  • Procedure
    1. Check the order and rights; the patient should be sitting (GTN may cause dizziness and low BP)
    2. Place the tablet under the tongue; ask the patient to keep the mouth closed and let it dissolve
    3. Do not swallow, chew or drink until it has dissolved
    4. A tingling or burning feeling and a headache may occur with GTN; check BP and pulse; record relief of pain
  • GTN tablets are kept in their original dark bottle, tightly closed, away from heat and light

B. Buccal route

  • The tablet or liquid is placed between the cheek and the gum and allowed to dissolve
  • Examples – some antiemetics, buccal midazolam for seizures
  • Alternate cheeks to avoid irritation; the patient should not chew or swallow the tablet, or eat or drink until it dissolves

C. Topical application on the skin

  • Forms – ointments, creams, gels, lotions, pastes, powders
  • Procedure
    1. Check the order; explain; hand hygiene; wear gloves (protects the nurse and prevents infection)
    2. Clean the skin with soap and water and dry it (remove old medicine)
    3. Apply a thin, even layer with a gloved hand or spatula in the direction of hair growth; lotions are patted on; shake suspensions first
    4. Cover with a dressing only if ordered
    5. Observe for local irritation or allergy; record

D. Transdermal patches

  • Deliver a drug slowly and steadily through the skin into the blood over hours or days
  • Examples – nitroglycerin, fentanyl, nicotine, hormone patches, some analgesics
  • Procedure
    1. Remove the old patch first; fold its sticky sides together and discard safely (used patches may still contain drug)
    2. Choose a clean, dry, hairless area (upper arm, chest, back); rotate sites
    3. Apply the patch, press firmly for about 30 seconds; do not cut the patch
    4. Label with the date, time and initials
    5. Avoid heat (heating pads, hot baths) over the patch – it increases absorption
    6. Record the site; observe for side effects

Conclusion Sublingual and buccal tablets are dissolved under the tongue or against the cheek without swallowing, giving rapid absorption that bypasses the liver; topical medicines are applied thinly to clean skin with gloves, and transdermal patches are placed on rotated hairless sites after removing the old patch, labelled and kept away from heat.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the instillation of eye, ear and nose drops.
answer_html:
Introduction Instillation is the placing of liquid medicine drop by drop into a body cavity. Eye, ear and nose medicines are used for infection, inflammation, allergy, glaucoma, wax removal and congestion. Each needs a specific position and technique.

A. Eye drops and ointment

  1. Check the order (which eye – right, left or both), rights and the expiry/opening date
  2. Hand hygiene; wear gloves; explain
  3. Position – supine or sitting with the head tilted back
  4. Clean the eye with a sterile swab from the inner to the outer canthus
  5. Ask the patient to look up; gently pull the lower lid down to form the conjunctival sac
  6. Hold the dropper about 1–2 cm above the eye (never touching it) and instil the prescribed number of drops into the sac, not onto the cornea
  7. Ask the patient to close the eye gently (not squeeze) and press the inner canthus (over the tear duct) for 1–2 minutes – reduces systemic absorption
  8. Ointment – apply a thin ribbon along the lower lid from the inner to the outer canthus; ask the patient to close the eye and move the eyeball
  9. Wait about 5 minutes between different eye drops; give drops before ointment
  10. Use separate bottles for each patient; label with the opening date and discard as per instructions

B. Ear drops

  1. Warm the drops to body temperature in the hand (cold drops cause dizziness and nausea)
  2. Position the patient lying on the side with the affected ear upwards
  3. Straighten the ear canal:
    • Adults – pull the pinna upwards and backwards
    • Children under about 3 years – pull the pinna downwards and backwards
  4. Instil the drops along the side of the canal; do not touch the ear with the dropper
  5. Press the tragus gently; ask the patient to stay on the side for about 5 minutes
  6. A loose cotton plug may be placed if ordered

C. Nose drops and spray

  1. Ask the patient to blow the nose gently (unless contraindicated)
  2. Drops – lie supine with the head tilted back over a pillow (special head positions are used for the sinuses); instil without touching the nose; stay in position for about 5 minutes
  3. Nasal spray – sit with the head slightly forward; close one nostril; insert the nozzle into the other, aim away from the septum, and spray while breathing in gently
  4. Wipe the nozzle; one bottle per patient

D. After care and recording – observe for burning, blurred vision, dizziness or other reactions; record the drug, dose, site (eye/ear/nostril) and time

Conclusion Eye drops are instilled into the lower conjunctival sac with pressure on the inner canthus, ear drops are warmed and instilled with the canal straightened according to age, and nose drops or sprays are given with the head positioned correctly, using a separate bottle for each patient and never touching the dropper to the body.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the use of metered-dose and dry powder inhalers.
answer_html:
Introduction Inhalers deliver medicines directly to the airways, giving rapid action with small doses and few side effects. They are the mainstay of treatment for asthma and COPD, but many patients use them incorrectly, so teaching correct technique is a key nursing role.

1. Types

  • Metered-dose inhaler (MDI) – a pressurised canister that releases a fixed dose as a spray
  • MDI with spacer – a chamber attached to the MDI; easier for children, the elderly and breathless patients; more drug reaches the lungs
  • Dry powder inhaler (DPI) – the patient inhales a powder by a fast, deep breath (e.g. rotacaps, multi-dose discs)

2. Drugs commonly used

  • Bronchodilators – salbutamol, formoterol, ipratropium, tiotropium
  • Inhaled corticosteroids – budesonide, beclomethasone, fluticasone

3. Technique – metered-dose inhaler

  1. Remove the cap; shake the inhaler well
  2. Stand or sit upright; breathe out fully (away from the inhaler)
  3. Place the mouthpiece between the teeth and seal the lips around it
  4. Start breathing in slowly and at the same time press the canister once
  5. Continue to breathe in slowly and deeply
  6. Hold the breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly
  7. Wait 30–60 seconds before the next puff

4. With a spacer

  • Attach the MDI to the spacer, shake, press once into the spacer and breathe in and out through the spacer 4–5 times (or one deep breath and hold); a face mask spacer is used for small children

5. Technique – dry powder inhaler

  1. Load the dose as per the device (insert capsule and pierce it, or click the dose counter)
  2. Breathe out away from the device (moisture spoils the powder)
  3. Seal the lips and breathe in quickly and deeply
  4. Hold the breath for about 10 seconds; check that the capsule is empty

6. Important points

  • When both are prescribed, use the bronchodilator first, then the steroid after a few minutes
  • Rinse the mouth and gargle after steroid inhalers – prevents oral thrush and hoarseness
  • Clean the mouthpiece and spacer regularly; check the dose counter and expiry date
  • Carry the reliever inhaler at all times; know when to seek help (no relief after repeated doses)

7. Nurse's role – demonstrate, ask for a return demonstration, correct mistakes, check technique at every visit, and record

Conclusion Metered-dose inhalers are used by breathing out, then pressing the canister at the start of a slow deep breath and holding the breath, with a spacer for those who cannot coordinate; dry powder inhalers need a fast deep breath; mouth rinsing after steroids and repeated teaching of technique are essential.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the administration of intravenous medications.
answer_html:
Introduction Intravenous (IV) medications act immediately and reach full blood levels at once. This makes them valuable in emergencies and serious infections, but also dangerous – errors cannot be reversed, and wrong rate or dilution can cause speed shock, phlebitis or death.

1. Methods

  • IV bolus (IV push) – a small volume injected slowly into the cannula or injection port over the time stated (often 1–5 minutes)
  • Intermittent infusion – the drug diluted in a small bag (50–100 mL) and infused over 15–60 minutes (e.g. antibiotics), by gravity, a secondary (piggyback) set or a burette
  • Continuous infusion – the drug added to a large volume of IV fluid and infused over hours (e.g. potassium chloride, oxytocin), preferably by infusion pump
  • Syringe pump – for small, precise doses (insulin, inotropes, sedatives)

2. Before giving

  • Check the order, rights and allergies; know the drug, dilution, rate and compatibility
  • Check the IV site for patency, redness, swelling or pain; flush with normal saline
  • Prepare with aseptic technique; label syringes and infusion bags (drug, dose, time, signature)
  • Independent double-check for high-alert drugs

3. Procedure – IV bolus

  1. Identify the patient; explain
  2. Clean the injection port with alcohol and let it dry
  3. Flush with normal saline to check patency
  4. Inject the drug slowly at the recommended rate, watching the patient and the site
  5. Flush again with saline (clears the drug from the cannula, prevents mixing with the next drug)
  6. Observe for immediate reactions – flushing, breathlessness, rash, chest tightness, hypotension

4. Procedure – adding a drug to an IV bag

  • Inject the drug through the additive port of the bag (never into a running bag without stopping it), mix by inverting several times, attach a label and set the rate on the pump

5. Precautions

  • Never give potassium chloride as an IV push
  • Check compatibility before giving two drugs through one line; flush between drugs
  • Give drugs at the correct rate – too fast causes speed shock (flushing, headache, chest tightness, collapse)
  • Watch for extravasation of irritant drugs; stop at once if pain or swelling occurs
  • Keep emergency drugs (adrenaline, hydrocortisone, antihistamine) ready, especially for first doses of antibiotics

6. Documentation – drug, dose, dilution, route, rate, time, site condition and the patient's response

Conclusion IV medications are given as a slow bolus, intermittent infusion or continuous infusion, after checking the order, compatibility, dilution, rate and patency of the line, with flushing before and after, aseptic technique, close observation for reactions and accurate documentation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the storage of medicines in the ward, including controlled (narcotic) drugs.
answer_html:
Introduction Correct storage keeps medicines effective, safe and secure. Poor storage can make drugs ineffective or dangerous (e.g. insulin left in the sun) and can lead to errors, theft and misuse of narcotics.

1. General principles

  • Keep medicines in a locked cupboard or trolley; the keys are held by the nurse in charge
  • Arrange drugs systematically (alphabetically or by group) with clear labels; keep internal (oral) and external preparations separate
  • Store look-alike, sound-alike drugs and different strengths separately
  • Keep medicines in their original labelled containers; never transfer drugs from one container to another or relabel them
  • Protect from light (amber bottles), heat and moisture; follow the manufacturer's instructions
  • Disinfectants, antiseptics and poisons are stored separately from medicines
  • Keep patients' own medicines as per policy, labelled with their names

2. Refrigerated medicines (cold chain)

  • Vaccines, insulin, oxytocin, some antibiotics, eye drops and blood products are kept at 2–8 °C
  • Use a dedicated drug refrigerator (no food); record the temperature twice daily; do not freeze
  • Keep vaccines away from the freezer compartment and the door; follow national cold-chain guidelines

3. Checking stock and expiry

  • First-expiry, first-out – use the drug that expires first
  • Check expiry dates regularly (e.g. monthly); remove expired, discoloured, cloudy or damaged drugs and return them to the pharmacy
  • Label multi-dose vials and eye drops with the date of opening
  • Maintain emergency drug trays and crash carts, checked daily and after every use

4. Controlled (narcotic) drugs

  • Narcotics such as morphine, pethidine and fentanyl are controlled by the NDPS Act, 1985
  • Stored in a double-locked cupboard (a locked cupboard inside a locked cupboard); the key is kept by the nurse in charge
  • Every dose is recorded in the narcotic (controlled drug) register – date, time, patient's name, drug, dose, balance stock, and the signatures of the nurse who gives it and a witness
  • Count the stock at every change of shift by two nurses
  • Empty ampoules are returned to the pharmacy; any wastage is witnessed and recorded
  • Report discrepancies immediately

5. High-alert medicines

  • Concentrated potassium chloride and other concentrated electrolytes should not be kept in general ward stock where avoidable; label high-alert drugs with warning stickers

Conclusion Medicines in the ward are stored locked, labelled, systematically arranged and protected from light, heat and moisture; refrigerated drugs are kept at 2–8 °C with temperature records, expiry dates are checked regularly, and narcotics are kept double-locked with a register signed for every dose and checked at every shift.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Write the meaning of the following abbreviations used in prescriptions: OD, BD, TDS, QID, HS, SOS, STAT, AC, PC, NPO.
answer_html:
Abbreviation Meaning
OD once daily
BD / BID twice daily
TDS / TID three times daily
QID / QDS four times daily
HS at bedtime
SOS if necessary (usually once)
STAT immediately
AC before meals
PC after meals
NPO nothing by mouth

Also – PRN (as required), PO (by mouth), Q4H (every 4 hours).

Caution – write "units" and "daily" in full; unclear abbreviations cause errors.

Example – "Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg PO TDS PC × 3 days" means one 500 mg paracetamol tablet by mouth three times a day after meals for three days.

Route abbreviations – IM (intramuscular), IV (intravenous), SC (subcutaneous), ID (intradermal), SL (sublingual).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Differentiate between side effect, adverse reaction, toxic effect and allergic reaction.
answer_html:
• Side effect – a predictable, usually mild, secondary effect occurring at normal doses, often unavoidable (e.g. drowsiness with antihistamines, dry mouth with atropine)
  • Adverse drug reaction – a harmful and unintended response at doses normally used for treatment (e.g. hearing loss with streptomycin, bleeding with anticoagulants); must be reported
  • Toxic effect – harmful effect due to overdose or accumulation of the drug (e.g. digoxin toxicity – nausea, visual disturbance, arrhythmias; paracetamol overdose – liver damage)
  • Allergic reaction – an immune response to the drug in a sensitised person, not related to dose – rash, urticaria, itching, bronchospasm or anaphylaxis (e.g. penicillin)
  • Idiosyncrasy – an unusual, unexpected response due to genetic differences (e.g. haemolysis with primaquine in G6PD deficiency)

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define drug tolerance, cumulative effect, synergism and antagonism.
answer_html:
• Drug tolerance – a decreased response to a drug after repeated use, so that a larger dose is needed for the same effect (e.g. opioids, nitrates)
  • Cumulative effect – build-up of a drug in the body when it is taken in faster than it is eliminated, leading to toxicity (e.g. digoxin in kidney failure)
  • Synergism – the combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of their separate effects (e.g. trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole; dangerous combination – alcohol with sedatives)
  • Antagonism – one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another (e.g. naloxone reverses morphine; protamine reverses heparin)

Also – drug dependence is a physical or psychological need to continue a drug, with withdrawal symptoms on stopping.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the needle sizes, angles and volumes for intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular injections.
answer_html:
Injection Angle Needle gauge Needle length Usual volume
Intradermal 10–15° 26–27 G 3/8–1/2 inch 0.01–0.1 mL
Subcutaneous 45° (or 90°) 25–27 G 3/8–5/8 inch 0.5–1 mL (up to about 2 mL)
Intramuscular 90° 21–23 G 1–1.5 inch up to 3 mL (deltoid not more than 1 mL)
Intravenous (cannula) 10–30° 18–24 G – as prescribed

Note – a higher gauge number means a thinner needle; needle length is adjusted to the patient's size (shorter for thin adults and children).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What are high-alert medications? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition High-alert medications are drugs that carry a higher risk of causing serious harm to patients when they are used in error.

Examples

  • Insulin and oral hypoglycaemic agents
  • Anticoagulants – heparin, enoxaparin, warfarin
  • Concentrated electrolytes – potassium chloride, 3% sodium chloride, magnesium sulphate
  • Opioids (morphine, fentanyl) and IV sedatives (midazolam)
  • Anticancer (chemotherapy) drugs
  • Inotropes and vasopressors (dopamine, adrenaline, noradrenaline), IV oxytocin
  • Neuromuscular blocking agents

Precautions – independent double-check, standard concentrations, infusion pumps, separate storage with warning labels, limited access.

Example of harm – a tenfold insulin overdose or an IV push of concentrated potassium chloride can cause death, so these drugs are always checked by two nurses.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the administration of vaginal medications.
answer_html:
Forms – pessaries (vaginal suppositories), creams, gels, tablets, foams.

Uses – vaginal infections (e.g. clotrimazole for candidiasis), hormonal creams, and some drugs for cervical ripening (given by doctors or midwives).

Procedure

  1. Explain; ensure privacy; ask the patient to empty the bladder
  2. Position in dorsal recumbent with knees flexed and apart; drape
  3. Wear gloves; lubricate the pessary or use the applicator
  4. Insert along the posterior vaginal wall about 7.5–10 cm (the length of the index finger)
  5. Ask the patient to remain lying for 10–30 minutes; give at bedtime where possible so the drug is retained
  6. Provide a perineal pad; wash hands; record - Teach self-administration and hygiene; partner treatment and avoiding intercourse during treatment if advised

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: Explain the components of sensory experience and the factors affecting sensory function. Describe sensory alterations – sensory deficit, deprivation and overload – and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction We know the world through our senses. Normal sensory input keeps a person alert, oriented and able to think, learn and stay safe. Illness, ageing, hospitalisation and treatment can reduce or overload sensory input, causing confusion, anxiety, accidents and isolation. Nurses can prevent much of this by managing the patient's sensory environment.

PART A – COMPONENTS OF SENSORY EXPERIENCE

1. Reception – stimuli are received by sensory receptors:

  • Visual (eyes), auditory (ears), olfactory (smell), gustatory (taste), tactile (touch, pressure, temperature, pain)
  • Kinaesthetic – awareness of the position and movement of body parts
  • Stereognosis – recognising an object's size, shape and texture by touch
  • Visceral – sensations from internal organs (hunger, fullness)

2. Perception – the brain interprets the impulses and gives them meaning; it depends on attention, previous experience, consciousness and an intact nervous system

3. Reaction – the person responds to meaningful stimuli and ignores unimportant ones

4. Arousal mechanism – the reticular activating system (RAS) in the brainstem receives sensory input, keeps the brain awake and alert, and filters stimuli; both too little and too much input disturb it

PART B – FACTORS AFFECTING SENSORY FUNCTION

  1. Age – infants' senses are still developing; the elderly have reduced vision (presbyopia, cataract), hearing (presbycusis), taste, smell and touch
  2. Medications – ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, some diuretics), sedatives and opioids dull perception
  3. Environment – excessive noise and light (ICU) or a monotonous, dull environment
  4. Comfort level – pain, fatigue and lack of sleep reduce attention and perception
  5. Pre-existing illness – diabetes (neuropathy, retinopathy), stroke, hypertension, ear and eye disease
  6. Smoking – reduces taste and smell
  7. Noise exposure – occupational hearing loss
  8. Endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy – inability to speak
  9. Social isolation, culture, lifestyle and personality

PART C – SENSORY ALTERATIONS

1. Sensory deficit

  • Impaired reception, perception or both of one or more senses
  • Examples – visual (refractive errors, cataract, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy), hearing (wax, otitis media, presbycusis), balance (vertigo), taste and smell, touch (peripheral neuropathy), neurological deficits after stroke (loss of half of the visual field, neglect of one side)
  • Effects – the person may withdraw socially, become dependent, and is at risk of injury (falls, burns); other senses often compensate

2. Sensory deprivation

  • Inadequate quality or quantity of meaningful stimuli
  • Causes – isolation (infection control), immobility (traction, bed rest), confinement in a room without windows or company, eye patches after surgery, unconsciousness, the elderly in institutions, sensory deficits
  • Effects:
    • cognitive – reduced ability to learn, think and solve problems; disorientation
    • affective – boredom, restlessness, anxiety, depression, emotional swings, panic
    • perceptual – altered body image, hallucinations, distorted sense of time and space

3. Sensory poverty – an environment that is poor in variety and meaning (e.g. long-stay wards with little activity); its effects are similar to deprivation

4. Sensory overload

  • Too many stimuli reaching the brain at once, so that it cannot process them meaningfully
  • Causes – ICU (alarms, lights, frequent procedures, monitors), pain, lack of sleep, many visitors, noise, rapid admission and investigations
  • Effects – confusion, restlessness, irritability, racing thoughts, poor concentration, fatigue, anxiety; may contribute to ICU delirium

PART D – NURSING MANAGEMENT

1. Assessment

  • History – changes in vision, hearing, taste, smell or touch; use of glasses and hearing aids; effect on daily activities
  • Mental status – orientation, attention, mood, behaviour
  • Physical examination – visual acuity, hearing tests, sensation, position sense
  • Environment – amount and type of stimulation; safety hazards; social contact and support

2. Common nursing diagnoses

  • Risk for injury r/t visual or hearing impairment
  • Impaired verbal communication r/t tracheostomy or aphasia
  • Social isolation r/t hearing loss
  • Acute confusion r/t sensory overload and sleep deprivation

3. Health promotion

  • Screening – newborn hearing tests, school eye checks, regular eye and ear checks for the elderly and diabetics
  • Prevention – ear protection in noisy work, eye protection, rubella vaccination, careful use of ototoxic drugs, control of diabetes and hypertension
  • Ensure glasses and hearing aids are available, clean and used

4. Care of patients with sensory deficits

  • Maximise remaining senses; keep aids within reach and in working order
  • Safety – good lighting, clear paths, call bell within reach, side rails as needed, large-print labels, check water temperature for patients with reduced sensation
  • Use special communication techniques for visual, hearing and speech problems

5. Care of patients with sensory deprivation

  • Provide meaningful stimulation – conversation, touch, music, radio, TV, reading, games, visitors, personal photographs
  • Orientation – clock, calendar, window view, daily newspaper; call the patient by name
  • Mobility and change of environment (sitting in a chair, short walks)
  • Visit isolation patients often; allow phone or video calls

6. Care of patients with sensory overload

  • Reduce unnecessary stimuli – lower alarm volumes where safe, dim lights at night, close doors, reduce noise and talk at the bedside
  • Cluster nursing care to allow uninterrupted rest and sleep
  • Explain procedures and sounds; one person speaking at a time; limit visitors when needed
  • Control pain; maintain a day–night routine

7. Evaluation – the patient is oriented, safe from injury, communicates needs and takes part in self-care

PART E – Sensory changes in the elderly and their care

  • Presbyopia and cataract – reading glasses, good lighting without glare, large print, referral for cataract surgery
  • Presbycusis (high-frequency hearing loss) – hearing aids, face-to-face speech, low-pitched voice
  • Reduced taste and smell – flavour food with herbs, lemon and spices rather than extra salt; check that food is not spoiled; gas leak and smoke alarms at home
  • Reduced touch and temperature sensation – check bath water temperature, protect from burns and injuries, regular foot inspection
  • Home safety – night lights, grab bars, non-slip mats, contrasting colours on step edges, uncluttered floors

PART F – Sensory care in the intensive care unit (prevention of delirium)

  • Orientation – clocks, calendars, windows, calling the patient by name, telling him the day and time
  • Day–night routine – lights dimmed and noise reduced at night; clustered care to allow sleep; ear plugs and eye masks if helpful
  • Glasses and hearing aids in use; family visits and familiar objects
  • Explain alarms, sounds and procedures; minimise unnecessary sedation; early mobilisation
  • Screen for delirium regularly with a standard tool and report sudden confusion or agitation

PART G – Sensory stimulation in unconscious patients

  • Talk to the patient during care, call him by name, explain what is being done
  • Use gentle touch, familiar voices of family members, favourite music for short periods
  • Avoid continuous noise; give rest periods between stimulation

PART H – Teaching the family

  • Provide regular conversation, activity and orientation at home; keep the environment safe
  • Arrange regular eye and hearing check-ups, care of aids and early reporting of new sensory changes

Conclusion Sensory experience involves reception, perception and reaction, kept alert by the reticular activating system; age, drugs, environment, illness and other factors cause sensory deficit, deprivation, poverty or overload, and nurses assess sensory function, promote prevention and aids, ensure safety and adjust the environment to give meaningful but not excessive stimulation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: Explain the nursing care of an unconscious patient.
answer_html:
Introduction An unconscious patient is unaware of self and surroundings and cannot respond normally to stimuli. He is totally dependent on the nurse for every basic need, and is at high risk of airway obstruction, aspiration, pressure ulcers, contractures and infection.

1. Airway and breathing (first priority)

  • Lateral or semi-prone position with the head turned to the side, so the tongue does not fall back and secretions drain out
  • Oropharyngeal airway if needed; suction secretions; oxygen as prescribed
  • Monitor respiratory rate, pattern and SpO₂; chest physiotherapy and turning to prevent pneumonia; ventilator care if intubated

2. Neurological and vital signs

  • Glasgow Coma Scale, pupil size and reaction, limb movements, vital signs – hourly or as ordered; report any deterioration at once

3. Nutrition and fluids

  • IV fluids at first; then nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding with head end raised; intake–output chart, daily weight

4. Elimination

  • Catheter care (or condom catheter for men); prevent constipation with fluids, fibre in feeds and laxatives; record bowel movements

5. Hygiene and skin care

  • Daily bed bath, mouth care every 2–4 hours, hair and nail care, perineal care
  • Turn every 2 hours, use a pressure-relieving mattress, keep the skin clean and dry, and inspect pressure points

6. Eye care

  • The blink and corneal reflexes may be lost – clean the eyes with sterile saline, apply lubricating drops or ointment as prescribed, keep the lids closed with moist pads if they do not close – prevents corneal ulcers

7. Positioning and mobility

  • Maintain correct body alignment; passive range-of-motion exercises 2–3 times a day
  • Splints and a footboard to prevent foot drop and wrist drop; prevent contractures and deep vein thrombosis

8. Safety

  • Side rails up; padding for patients with seizures; no hot water bottles; restraints only when unavoidable and as per policy

9. Temperature control – tepid sponging and antipyretics for fever, warming for hypothermia, as ordered

10. Communication and sensory stimulation

  • Hearing may remain – talk to the patient, call him by name, explain every procedure, avoid careless talk at the bedside; gentle touch, familiar voices and music

11. Family support – explain the condition, involve the family in simple care, counsel and support them

12. Documentation – record observations, care given and changes in condition

Conclusion Care of the unconscious patient starts with a clear airway and close neurological observation, and includes nutrition, elimination, hygiene, mouth and eye care, two-hourly turning, passive exercises, safety, temperature control, communication and support of the family to prevent complications.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: Explain the levels of consciousness and the Glasgow Coma Scale.
answer_html:
Introduction Consciousness is a state of awareness of self and the environment, with the ability to respond to stimuli. A fall in the level of consciousness is often the earliest sign of brain deterioration (raised intracranial pressure, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia), so it must be assessed and recorded accurately.

1. Levels of consciousness

  • Alert (conscious) – fully awake, oriented to time, place and person, responds appropriately
  • Confused – disoriented, slow thinking, may be restless
  • Lethargic (drowsy) – sleepy but easily aroused, responds appropriately
  • Obtunded – aroused only with stimulation; slow, limited responses
  • Stupor – responds only to vigorous or painful stimuli
  • Coma – no response even to painful stimuli (reflex movements may be present)
  • Delirium – an acute, fluctuating state of confusion with agitation, disturbed attention and sometimes hallucinations
  • AVPU – a quick check: Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive

2. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

Response Score
Eye opening (E) 4 spontaneous; 3 to sound/speech; 2 to pressure/pain; 1 none
Verbal response (V) 5 oriented; 4 confused; 3 inappropriate words; 2 incomprehensible sounds; 1 none
Motor response (M) 6 obeys commands; 5 localises pain; 4 normal flexion (withdraws); 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate); 2 extension (decerebrate); 1 none
  • Total score – 3 to 15 (15 = fully conscious)
  • Severity – 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, 8 or less severe (coma) – the airway may need protection
  • Record as, for example, E3 V4 M6 = 13; if the patient is intubated, the verbal score is recorded as "T"

3. Method of assessment

  1. Speak to the patient in a normal voice, then louder
  2. If there is no response, apply a graded painful stimulus – central (trapezius squeeze, supraorbital pressure) for motor localisation, peripheral (nail-bed pressure) for eye opening and limb response
  3. Record the best response in each category
  4. Assess pupils (size, equality, reaction to light), limb power and vital signs along with the GCS (neurological observation chart)

4. Nursing significance

  • Trends matter more than single scores – a fall of 2 or more points, a new unequal or non-reacting pupil, or new weakness must be reported immediately
  • Rule out simple causes of a low score – hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sedatives
  • Modified paediatric scales are used for young children

Conclusion Consciousness ranges from alert to coma and is measured objectively by the Glasgow Coma Scale, which scores eye opening, verbal and motor responses from 3 to 15; regular, accurate recording with pupils and vital signs helps detect deterioration early.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: Explain the methods of communicating with patients who have aphasia, an artificial airway, visual impairment or hearing impairment.
answer_html:
Introduction Patients with speech, airway, visual or hearing problems often feel frustrated, isolated and anxious because they cannot communicate their needs. The nurse must adapt her methods so that every patient can understand and be understood.

1. Patients with aphasia (after stroke or head injury)

  • Face the patient, get attention, reduce background noise
  • Speak slowly and clearly in short, simple sentences; ask one question at a time, preferably with yes/no answers
  • Allow time to respond; do not hurry or finish sentences unless asked
  • Use gestures, pictures, communication boards and objects; writing may help in expressive aphasia
  • Praise efforts; treat the patient as an adult; do not shout (hearing is usually normal)
  • Refer to the speech therapist; involve the family

2. Patients with an artificial airway (endotracheal tube, tracheostomy)

  • Explain that the loss of voice is temporary (if so)
  • Provide a communication board, picture cards, pen and paper or a writing slate
  • Agree on simple yes/no signals – nodding, blinking, squeezing the hand
  • Ask closed questions; lip-reading for simple words
  • Speaking valves for tracheostomy patients, if ordered
  • Keep the call bell within reach; visit often; explain all procedures beforehand

3. Patients with visual impairment

  • Announce your presence and say your name when entering; speak before touching
  • Orient the patient to the room; keep furniture and belongings in the same place
  • Describe food on the plate using the clock method
  • When walking, let the patient hold your arm just above the elbow; walk half a step ahead
  • Provide good light without glare, large-print materials and contrasting colours; keep glasses clean and within reach
  • Tell the patient when you are leaving the room

4. Patients with hearing impairment

  • Get attention first (wave, or touch the arm lightly); face the patient in good light so he can lip-read
  • Speak clearly at a normal pace, slightly louder but do not shout; use a lower pitch
  • Reduce background noise; speak towards the better ear
  • Rephrase rather than repeat the same words; use written notes, gestures, pictures
  • Check that the hearing aid is in place, switched on and the battery works
  • Use a sign language interpreter when needed; visual alarms and signals

Conclusion Communication with sensory-impaired patients is improved by facing the patient, short simple messages and enough time for aphasia, boards and agreed signals for artificial airways, announcing presence and orientation for visual impairment, and lip-reading, writing and working hearing aids for hearing impairment.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: Name the types of aphasia.
answer_html:
Aphasia – loss or impairment of the ability to use or understand language due to brain damage (stroke, head injury, tumour).

  1. Expressive (Broca's, motor, non-fluent) aphasia – damage to Broca's area (frontal lobe); the patient understands but has difficulty speaking – slow, effortful, few words
  2. Receptive (Wernicke's, sensory, fluent) aphasia – damage to Wernicke's area (temporal lobe); speech is fluent but meaningless; the patient cannot understand spoken or written language
  3. Global aphasia – both expression and understanding are severely affected (large lesions)
  4. Conduction aphasia – difficulty repeating words
  5. Anomic aphasia – difficulty finding the names of objects

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: What is the reticular activating system (RAS)?
answer_html:
Definition The reticular activating system is a network of nerve cells in the brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla) with connections to the thalamus and cerebral cortex.

Functions

  • Maintains wakefulness, alertness and consciousness (arousal)
  • Filters incoming sensory stimuli, allowing attention to important ones (selective attention)
  • Regulates the sleep–wake cycle

Clinical importance

  • Damage to the RAS (head injury, stroke, raised intracranial pressure) causes coma
  • Sensory deprivation and overload disturb its function, causing drowsiness, confusion or agitation

Examples – an alarm wakes a sleeping person; a mother wakes to her baby's cry but sleeps through traffic noise – the RAS filters stimuli by their importance.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Sensory Needs and Care of Unconscious Patients
question: Explain eye care in an unconscious patient.
answer_html:
Need – unconscious patients may lose the blink and corneal reflexes, and the lids may not close fully, leading to dry eyes, corneal abrasions, ulcers and infection (exposure keratitis).

Care

  1. Clean the eyes with sterile normal saline swabs from the inner to the outer canthus, one swab per stroke, every 2–4 hours
  2. Instil artificial tears or lubricating ointment as prescribed
  3. If the lids do not close, keep them closed with moist saline gauze, hypoallergenic tape or a moisture chamber (clear protective cover)
  4. Remove contact lenses; avoid pressure on the eyes
  5. Observe for redness, discharge, swelling or corneal clouding and report

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: Explain the signs of approaching death and the nursing care of a dying patient and the family. Describe the care of the body after death (last offices).
tags: care of the body after death
answer_html:
Introduction Caring for a dying patient is one of the most important and sensitive duties of a nurse. When cure is no longer possible, the aim changes to comfort, dignity, relief of suffering and support of the family, so that the person can have a peaceful death. Care continues after death with respectful care of the body and support of the bereaved.

PART A – SIGNS OF APPROACHING (IMPENDING) DEATH

1. General

  • Decreasing appetite and fluid intake, difficulty in swallowing
  • Increasing weakness, sleepiness and decreasing level of consciousness
  • Confusion, restlessness, picking at bedclothes (terminal agitation)

2. Respiratory

  • Irregular breathing, Cheyne–Stokes respiration with periods of apnoea
  • Noisy breathing ("death rattle") due to secretions in the throat
  • Mouth breathing, dry mouth

3. Circulatory

  • Cold, pale, clammy extremities; mottling (blotchy bluish-purple skin) of knees, feet and hands
  • Rapid, weak, thready pulse, falling BP; cyanosis of lips and nails
  • Profuse sweating

4. Other

  • Decreased urine output, incontinence of urine and faeces
  • Loss of senses – vision blurs; hearing is believed to be the last sense to be lost
  • Relaxation of facial muscles, sagging jaw, eyes partly open and glazed

5. Signs of death – absence of pulse, heartbeat and respiration, fixed dilated pupils, no response to stimuli – death is declared by a doctor

PART B – NURSING CARE OF THE DYING PATIENT

1. Physical care

  • Pain relief – regular analgesics (including opioids) as prescribed; no patient should die in uncontrolled pain
  • Breathing – semi-Fowler's or lateral position; gentle oral suction; oxygen for comfort if it helps; drugs to reduce secretions as ordered; a fan or open window for breathlessness
  • Mouth care – frequent; keep the mouth and lips moist; this relieves thirst better than forcing fluids
  • Eye care – clean, moisten, keep closed if needed
  • Nutrition and fluids – small sips and soft foods the patient wants; do not force feeding
  • Elimination – incontinence care, catheter if needed for comfort, prevention of constipation
  • Skin care – gentle turning and pressure-area care, balanced against the patient's comfort
  • Hygiene – clean, dry clothes and linen; light covers (patients often feel hot)
  • Restlessness – check for pain, full bladder or constipation; calm, dimly lit, quiet surroundings; sedatives as ordered

2. Psychological care

  • Be present; listen actively; allow the patient to express fears, anger and wishes
  • Be honest while maintaining realistic hope (comfort, being with family, peace)
  • Respect the patient's choices about treatment and place of care; follow advance directives and do-not-resuscitate decisions made as per law and hospital policy
  • Help with unfinished business – meeting relatives, settling affairs, saying goodbye
  • Maintain dignity and privacy at all times

3. Spiritual care

  • Respect the patient's faith and rituals – prayers, holy water, recitation of scriptures, sacraments, presence of a priest, maulvi, pandit or granthi as wished
  • Allow religious objects at the bedside; do not impose one's own beliefs

4. Care of the family

  • Keep the family informed honestly and gently; involve them in simple care if they wish
  • Allow flexible visiting and privacy; provide a place to rest
  • Support anticipatory grief; inform them when death is near so they can be present
  • After death, allow them time with the body; give information about formalities; offer emotional support and refer for bereavement support if needed

PART C – CARE OF THE BODY AFTER DEATH (LAST OFFICES)

1. Purposes

  • To keep the body clean, dignified and in a natural position before rigor mortis sets in
  • To prevent discolouration and deformity
  • To ensure correct identification
  • To respect religious and cultural customs
  • To protect others from infection

2. Equipment

  • Gloves, apron or gown, basin of warm water, soap, towels, cotton, gauze, dressings, adhesive tape
  • Identification tags (two or three), clean gown, shroud or sheet, bandage for the jaw
  • Bags for clothing and belongings, list for valuables, biomedical waste bags

3. Procedure

  1. Ensure that death has been declared by the doctor and the time recorded; inform the nurse in charge
  2. Inform the relatives (usually with the doctor); allow them time with the body; ask about religious requirements (some families prefer to wash the body themselves)
  3. Find out whether it is a medico-legal case or an autopsy is required
    • In medico-legal cases, do not remove tubes, lines or drains (cut and cap them), do not wash the body, and preserve clothing and belongings as per police and hospital instructions
  4. Wear gloves and apron; ensure privacy
  5. Place the body flat on the back, limbs straight, arms by the sides or folded over the chest; one pillow under the head (prevents discolouration of the face)
  6. Close the eyes gently (moist cotton pads on the lids if needed)
  7. Close the mouth – insert dentures if possible; support the jaw with a rolled towel or chin bandage
  8. Remove tubes, cannulas and drains (if allowed), and cover wounds with clean dressings; pad orifices only if there is leakage
  9. Wash the body as needed, dry it, and dress in a clean gown; comb the hair
  10. Attach identification tags – name, age, sex, hospital number, ward, date and time of death – to the wrist or ankle and to the shroud
  11. Wrap the body in the shroud; a body bag is used for certain infectious cases as per guidelines
  12. List all valuables and belongings; hand them to the relatives with signatures and a witness; remove jewellery unless the family requests otherwise (record it)
  13. Transfer the body to the mortuary or hand it over to the relatives as per policy
  14. Clean and disinfect the unit (terminal cleaning)

4. Documentation

  • Time of death and the doctor who declared it, care given, belongings handed over, persons informed, time of transfer, and any medico-legal formalities

PART D – Managing common symptoms at the end of life

  • Pain – regular analgesics, including oral or injectable opioids, as prescribed; assess with a pain scale or facial expression in patients who cannot speak
  • Breathlessness – upright position, fan, calm presence, low-dose opioids or oxygen as ordered
  • Nausea and vomiting – antiemetics, small feeds, mouth care
  • Noisy secretions – change of position, gentle suction, drugs to dry secretions as ordered; explain to the family that it is usually not distressing to the patient
  • Agitation and delirium – look for pain, full bladder, constipation or fever; quiet surroundings, familiar people; sedatives as ordered
  • Constipation – laxatives, especially with opioids
  • Dry mouth – frequent mouth care, sips of water, ice chips, lip balm

PART E – Self-care of the nurse

  • Caring for dying patients is emotionally demanding; nurses may feel sadness and grief
  • Talking with colleagues, debriefing, peer support and rest help prevent burnout and allow continued compassionate care

Conclusion The dying patient shows signs such as decreasing consciousness, Cheyne–Stokes breathing, mottled cold extremities and a weak pulse; nursing care aims at comfort, dignity and spiritual and emotional support for the patient and family, and after death the body is cared for respectfully with correct positioning, identification, attention to medico-legal requirements and safe handover of belongings.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: Explain the grief responses and the stages of dying according to Kubler-Ross.
answer_html:
Introduction Grief is the emotional response to loss. Mourning is the outward expression of grief, shaped by culture and religion, and bereavement is the state of having lost someone close. Dying patients and their families both experience grief.

1. Grief responses

  • Physical – crying, sighing, tightness in the chest or throat, lack of energy, disturbed sleep and appetite
  • Emotional – sadness, anger, guilt, anxiety, loneliness, numbness, sometimes relief
  • Cognitive – disbelief, confusion, poor concentration, preoccupation with the deceased, sensing their presence
  • Behavioural – searching, social withdrawal, restlessness, avoiding or keeping reminders
  • Spiritual – questioning faith, searching for meaning

2. Stages of dying (Elisabeth Kubler-Ross, 1969)

  1. Denial and isolation – "No, not me. The report must be wrong." A temporary defence that cushions the shock
  2. Anger – "Why me?" Anger may be directed at God, family, doctors and nurses
  3. Bargaining – "Yes, me, but…" – trying to postpone death by promises to God or to change behaviour ("If I live until my daughter's wedding…")
  4. Depression – sadness about past losses and the losses to come; withdrawal and silence
  5. Acceptance – "I am ready." A calm stage of peace, often with less interest in surroundings - The stages do not always occur in order; a person may move back and forth or remain in one stage; families go through them too

3. Nursing care in each stage

  • Denial – do not force acceptance or argue; listen; give information as the patient asks for it
  • Anger – do not take it personally; accept the feelings; allow expression; stay calm and available
  • Bargaining – listen; help with unfinished business; respect the patient's hopes
  • Depression – be present, allow crying, use touch, avoid false cheerfulness; watch for severe depression
  • Acceptance – support, comfort and involve the family; help fulfil final wishes; maintain dignity

4. Rando's processes of mourning (the "six Rs") – recognise the loss, react to the separation, recollect and re-experience memories, relinquish old attachments, readjust to the new world, and reinvest emotional energy

Conclusion Grief produces physical, emotional, cognitive, behavioural and spiritual responses; Kubler-Ross described denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance as the stages of dying, and the nurse supports the patient and family at each stage with acceptance, presence and honest communication.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: Explain the types of loss and grief, and the nursing care of the bereaved family.
answer_html:
Introduction Loss is any situation in which something valued is changed or taken away. Every person experiences losses throughout life, and the reaction depends on the meaning of the loss, the person's coping and support. Nurses meet grieving families daily and can greatly help them.

1. Types of loss

  • Actual loss – recognised by others, e.g. death of a loved one, amputation, loss of a job
  • Perceived loss – felt by the person but not obvious to others, e.g. loss of confidence, youth or status
  • Maturational (developmental) loss – expected losses in normal development, e.g. a child leaving home, menopause, retirement
  • Situational loss – sudden, unexpected losses, e.g. accident, disaster, divorce, illness
  • Loss of a body part or function, possessions, familiar environment (hospitalisation, migration), relationships and aspects of self (independence, body image)

2. Types of grief

  • Normal (uncomplicated) grief – the usual reactions that gradually lessen over time
  • Anticipatory grief – grief before the actual loss, e.g. family of a terminally ill patient
  • Complicated (dysfunctional) grief – grief that is prolonged, delayed, exaggerated, masked or chronic, interfering with daily life
  • Disenfranchised grief – grief that is not openly acknowledged by society, e.g. after a miscarriage, death of an ex-partner or a pet
  • Ambiguous loss – e.g. a missing person, or a loved one with dementia who is physically present but psychologically absent

3. Nursing care of the bereaved family

  • Break bad news in a private place, with the doctor, using simple and compassionate words; allow silence and tears
  • Allow the family to see and spend time with the body; respect religious rites
  • Listen; accept all emotions – anger, guilt, disbelief; avoid clichés ("I know how you feel")
  • Give practical information – death certificate, release of the body, belongings, transport
  • Help them contact other relatives and spiritual leaders
  • Identify those at risk of complicated grief – sudden or violent death, death of a child, little social support, previous mental illness – and refer for counselling
  • Arrange follow-up and bereavement support where available
  • Nurses also need support and self-care after caring for dying patients

Conclusion Losses may be actual, perceived, maturational or situational, and grief may be normal, anticipatory, complicated, disenfranchised or ambiguous; nurses support bereaved families through compassionate communication, time with the deceased, practical help, respect for rituals and referral of those at risk of complicated grief.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: Explain the legal aspects related to death – declaration, certification, medico-legal cases, autopsy and organ donation.
answer_html:
Introduction Death has many legal consequences – for inheritance, insurance, police investigation and organ donation. Nurses must know the procedures so that they act correctly and protect the patient, the family and the hospital.

1. Declaration of death

  • Death is declared only by a registered medical practitioner after examining the patient
  • The exact time of death and the name of the doctor are recorded
  • The nurse records the events, informs the nurse in charge and helps inform the family

2. Death certificate

  • The doctor issues the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD) stating the cause of death
  • Death must be registered with the local registrar under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969
  • The family needs the certificate for funeral, legal and financial matters

3. Medico-legal cases (MLC)

  • Unnatural or suspicious deaths – accidents, burns, poisoning, assault, suicide, death in police custody, deaths of women within a few years of marriage under suspicious circumstances, deaths where the cause is unknown
  • The police must be informed; the body is not handed over until police formalities are complete
  • Nurse's role – do not remove tubes, drains or dressings; preserve clothes, belongings, vomitus, stomach wash and samples; label and hand over properly; maintain accurate, objective records

4. Autopsy (post-mortem examination)

  • Clinical (pathological) autopsy – to find the exact cause of death for medical reasons; needs consent of the relatives
  • Medico-legal autopsy – ordered by the police or magistrate in medico-legal cases; no consent of relatives is needed

5. Organ and tissue donation

  • Governed by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994 (amended)
  • Brain-dead persons may donate organs (heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, pancreas); eyes (corneas) and some tissues can be donated after circulatory death (corneas within about 6 hours)
  • Brain death is certified by a board of medical experts after tests done twice
  • Requires consent of the person (pledge) or next of kin; the nurse helps identify potential donors and informs the transplant coordinator, maintains the donor's body functions as ordered, and supports the family

6. Rights of the dying patient and advance directives

  • The right to dignity, information, pain relief, privacy, spiritual care, and to take part in decisions
  • Advance medical directives (living wills) and withdrawal of life support in terminal illness are legally recognised in India under Supreme Court guidelines, following a defined procedure

Conclusion Death is declared and certified by a doctor and registered by law; medico-legal deaths require police information and preservation of evidence, autopsies may be clinical (with consent) or medico-legal (by police order), and organ donation follows the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, with the nurse acting carefully, documenting accurately and supporting the family.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: What are the post-mortem changes?
answer_html:
1. Algor mortis – cooling of the body after death, roughly 0.5–1 °C per hour, until it reaches room temperature
  2. Rigor mortis – stiffening of the muscles due to loss of ATP; begins in about 2–4 hours in small muscles (eyelids, jaw, neck), involves the whole body by about 12 hours, and passes off in about 24–48 hours
  3. Livor mortis (post-mortem lividity) – bluish-purple discolouration of the dependent parts as blood settles by gravity; begins within an hour or two and becomes fixed after several hours
  4. Decomposition (putrefaction) – softening and breakdown of tissues by bacteria, beginning after about 24–48 hours (faster in hot weather)

Nursing implication – position the body, close the eyes and mouth and place a pillow under the head before rigor mortis sets in.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: Define brain death. State the criteria.
answer_html:
Definition Brain death is the irreversible loss of all functions of the brain, including the brainstem. A brain-dead person is legally dead, even though the heart may continue to beat on a ventilator.

Criteria

  1. Deep coma with a known, irreversible cause
  2. Exclusion of reversible causes – hypothermia, drugs, metabolic disturbances
  3. Absence of brainstem reflexes – pupillary light reflex, corneal reflex, doll's eye (oculocephalic) and caloric (oculovestibular) responses, gag and cough reflexes
  4. Apnoea test – no breathing effort when the ventilator is disconnected and blood CO₂ rises

In India – certified by a board of medical experts under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act; tests are done twice, at least 6 hours apart.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: Define palliative care. State its principles.
answer_html:
Definition Palliative care is an approach that improves the quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening illness, by preventing and relieving suffering through early identification and treatment of pain and other physical, psychological, social and spiritual problems.

Principles

  • Affirms life and treats dying as a normal process
  • Neither hastens nor postpones death
  • Provides relief from pain and distressing symptoms
  • Integrates psychological and spiritual care
  • Supports the family during the illness and in bereavement
  • Uses a team approach; can begin early, alongside curative treatment

Hospice care – palliative care in the last phase of life; India has a National Programme for Palliative Care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Care of Terminally Ill, Death and Dying
question: What is an autopsy? Name its types.
answer_html:
Definition An autopsy (post-mortem examination) is the examination of a dead body, including internal organs, to find the cause and manner of death.

Types

  1. Clinical (pathological / academic) autopsy – done for medical reasons, to confirm the diagnosis or for teaching and research; requires consent of the next of kin
  2. Medico-legal autopsy – ordered by the police or magistrate in unnatural, suspicious or unexplained deaths (accidents, poisoning, assault, custodial deaths); no consent required
  3. Psychological autopsy – a study of the person's life and circumstances to understand the reasons for an unexplained death

Nurse's role – preserve the body as it is in medico-legal cases (tubes and lines left in place), label and hand over specimens and belongings, and keep accurate records.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define self-concept. Explain its components, development and the factors (stressors) affecting it. Describe the nursing management of a patient with altered self-concept.
answer_html:
Introduction Every person carries a picture of himself – who he is, how he looks, what he can do and how much he is worth. This self-concept influences how a person behaves, copes with illness and relates to others. Illness, surgery, disability and hospitalisation can threaten self-concept, and nurses play an important role in helping patients maintain or rebuild a healthy view of themselves.

PART A – DEFINITION

  • Self-concept is a person's mental image and overall view of himself – his physical, emotional, intellectual, social and spiritual characteristics, abilities, limitations, values and beliefs
  • It is how a person thinks and feels about himself, and it develops from experiences and from the feedback of others

PART B – COMPONENTS

1. Identity (personal identity)

  • The inner sense of individuality – "who I am" – that stays consistent over time
  • Includes name, gender, family, cultural and religious identity, occupation, values and beliefs
  • Formed especially during adolescence

2. Body image

  • The person's perception of his own body – its size, shape, appearance and function – and the feelings about it
  • Influenced by culture, media, the reactions of others and changes due to illness or ageing

3. Role performance

  • The way a person carries out the roles expected of him – son, mother, husband, student, nurse, employee
  • Satisfaction comes from role mastery; illness often changes roles

4. Self-esteem

  • The overall feeling of self-worth – how much a person likes, values and respects himself
  • High self-esteem helps coping; low self-esteem is linked with depression, withdrawal and poor health behaviour

PART C – DEVELOPMENT OF SELF-CONCEPT

  • Infancy and early childhood – the child learns to separate self from others; trust develops from loving care; awareness of the body and of being a boy or girl
  • School age – sense of competence from achievements at school and play; comparison with peers
  • Adolescence – the key period for identity formation (Erikson's identity vs role confusion); intense concern with body image and peer acceptance
  • Adulthood – roles in work, marriage and parenthood shape self-concept; achievement and relationships matter
  • Old age – adjustment to changes in the body, roles (retirement) and losses; sense of integrity or despair
  • Throughout life, self-concept is built by interaction with significant others, success and failure, and the messages received from family, school and society

PART D – FACTORS (STRESSORS) AFFECTING SELF-CONCEPT

1. Identity stressors

  • Developmental changes (adolescence, ageing), illness affecting memory or thinking (dementia, head injury), loss of job or home, migration

2. Body image stressors

  • Loss of a body part – amputation, mastectomy, hysterectomy
  • Change in appearance – burns, scars, hair loss with chemotherapy, weight gain or loss, acne, skin disease
  • Change in function – paralysis after stroke, colostomy or urostomy, incontinence, impotence
  • Pregnancy, ageing, use of devices (wheelchair, catheter)

3. Role stressors

  • Role conflict – incompatible expectations (a working mother with a sick child)
  • Role ambiguity – unclear expectations (a new job)
  • Role strain – feeling unable to meet role demands (a full-time caregiver)
  • Role overload – too many roles or responsibilities
  • Loss of roles due to illness, hospitalisation, unemployment or retirement

4. Self-esteem stressors

  • Repeated failure, criticism, rejection, abuse or neglect
  • Chronic illness and dependence on others, unemployment, poverty, social stigma (e.g. leprosy, HIV, mental illness)

5. Other factors – family relationships and parenting, culture and gender expectations, socioeconomic status, education, personality and coping skills

PART E – SIGNS OF ALTERED SELF-CONCEPT

  • Avoiding eye contact, slouched posture, untidy appearance, soft or hesitant speech
  • Negative statements about self ("I am useless", "Nobody will marry me now")
  • Refusing to look at or touch a changed body part; hiding it
  • Social withdrawal, excessive dependence, or hostility and irritability
  • Inability to accept praise; over-apologising; difficulty making decisions

PART F – NURSING MANAGEMENT

1. Assessment

  • Ask open questions – "How do you feel about yourself since the surgery?", "What changes has this illness brought to your life?"
  • Observe behaviour, appearance and interaction; assess roles, support systems, coping and the meaning of the change to the patient
  • Identify strengths and resources

2. Nursing diagnoses

  • Disturbed body image r/t loss of a breast AEB refusal to look at the chest
  • Situational low self-esteem r/t loss of job and illness AEB negative self-statements
  • Ineffective role performance r/t prolonged hospitalisation
  • Disturbed personal identity r/t dementia

3. Goals – the patient will express feelings about the change, take part in self-care, identify personal strengths and resume suitable roles

4. Interventions

  • Therapeutic relationship – acceptance, warmth, privacy, active listening; encourage expression of feelings (crying, anger, fear) without judgement
  • Identify strengths and set small, realistic goals; give honest praise for achievements
  • Promote independence – encourage self-care and participation in decisions
  • Body image – prepare the patient before surgery; encourage gradual exposure (looking at, touching and caring for the stoma or stump); provide prostheses, wigs, clothing advice, grooming and make-up; arrange meetings with others who have adapted (support groups)
  • Role – help the patient and family plan role changes; discuss work and home adjustments; involve social services
  • Teach coping skills – problem solving, assertiveness, relaxation, positive self-talk
  • Involve family and significant others – they should show acceptance and avoid pity or rejection
  • Refer to a counsellor, psychologist or psychiatric services for severe or persistent problems (e.g. depression)
  • Respect dignity – avoid labelling, criticism and careless remarks

5. Evaluation – the patient speaks positively about self, looks after the changed body part, socialises and resumes roles

PART G – Self-concept in special groups

  • Children in hospital – may regress, feel ashamed of bed-wetting or being undressed; provide privacy, simple explanations, praise and familiar toys or people
  • Adolescents – very sensitive about body image (acne, weight, scars, hair loss); respect privacy, allow contact with friends, involve them in decisions
  • Elderly – loss of roles, independence and friends threatens self-esteem; encourage self-care, choices, reminiscence (talking about past achievements) and meaningful activities
  • Chronic illness and disability – stigma and dependence lower self-esteem; focus on abilities, rehabilitation and support groups

PART H – Promoting a healthy self-concept in everyday care

  • Address the patient by the preferred name; knock before entering; ensure privacy
  • Offer choices (time of bath, food, clothing) and involve the patient in planning care
  • Encourage grooming – combing hair, shaving, clean clothes

  • Avoid labels ("the diabetic in bed 5") and careless remarks; recognise efforts and progress

  • Introduce rehabilitation goals early so that the patient sees a future role for himself

Conclusion Self-concept is a person's view of himself, made up of identity, body image, role performance and self-esteem; it develops through life and is threatened by changes in the body, roles, identity and self-worth, and nurses help patients through a supportive relationship, expression of feelings, building on strengths, independence, body-image adjustment, family involvement and referral when needed.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain body image disturbance and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Body image is the mental picture a person has of his body and the feelings attached to it. Any sudden or major change in appearance or function can disturb body image and affect self-esteem, relationships and recovery.

1. Common situations causing body image disturbance

  • Amputation, mastectomy, hysterectomy, colostomy or urostomy
  • Burns, scars and facial disfigurement
  • Hair loss (chemotherapy), weight changes, skin diseases (vitiligo, psoriasis)
  • Paralysis after stroke or spinal cord injury; loss of continence
  • Pregnancy, ageing, acne in adolescents
  • Use of visible devices – tracheostomy, catheter, wheelchair

2. Usual pattern of adjustment

  • Shock and disbelief → withdrawal and grief for the loss → gradual acknowledgement → integration of the change into a new body image; the speed depends on the person, the meaning of the change and the support received

3. Signs of disturbed body image

  • Not looking at or touching the affected part; hiding it under clothes
  • Negative comments about the body; talking of the part as "it"
  • Refusing to take part in care (stoma care, dressings)
  • Social withdrawal, avoiding visitors, depression, anger
  • Excessive focus on the change or the past body

4. Nursing management

  • Pre-operative preparation – explain the expected changes honestly; show pictures or devices; introduce a person who has adjusted well
  • Accept the patient's feelings; allow time to grieve; listen without judgement
  • Encourage gradual exposure – first looking at the part, then touching it, then helping with its care, finally doing it independently
  • Give accurate information about recovery, prostheses, reconstruction, wigs and clothing
  • Help with grooming and appearance – clean clothes, hair care, make-up; it improves morale
  • Teach self-care skills so that the patient feels in control (stoma care, use of prosthesis)
  • Involve the family/partner – their acceptance is very important; prepare them before they see the change
  • Refer to support groups, counsellors or rehabilitation services
  • Watch for depression and refer early
  • Respect privacy and avoid showing shock or disgust

Conclusion Body image disturbance follows losses and changes in appearance or function; the nurse recognises signs such as avoidance and negative remarks and helps through preparation, acceptance of feelings, gradual exposure, information, grooming, self-care teaching, family involvement and referral.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain role performance and the role stressors, with nursing interventions.
answer_html:
Introduction A role is a set of expected behaviours linked with a person's position in society. Role performance is the way a person actually carries out these roles. Illness often prevents people from performing their usual roles, which affects self-esteem and family life.

1. Types of roles

  • Primary roles – determined by age and sex (child, adult, man, woman)
  • Secondary roles – related to family and society (husband, mother, teacher, farmer)
  • Tertiary roles – temporary, freely chosen roles (member of a club, volunteer, student)
  • Sick role – when ill, a person is excused from normal duties and is expected to want to get well and seek help (described by Parsons)

2. Role stressors

  • Role conflict – two or more roles with incompatible demands, e.g. a nurse who is also the mother of a sick child; or a person's values conflicting with role expectations
  • Role ambiguity – unclear expectations, e.g. a newly promoted staff nurse not sure of her duties
  • Role strain – frustration and stress when a person feels unable to fulfil a role, e.g. caregiver strain in families of patients with dementia or paralysis
  • Role overload – too many roles or responsibilities for the time and energy available
  • Role transition – changes in roles – developmental (becoming a parent, retirement), situational (death of spouse), and health–illness transitions (from active worker to dependent patient)

3. Effects of role problems

  • Anxiety, guilt, irritability, fatigue, low self-esteem, family conflict, neglect of health, depression

4. Nursing interventions

  • Assess the patient's roles, the changes caused by illness and their meaning for him and the family
  • Help clarify expectations – what the patient can and cannot do now; set realistic short-term roles (e.g. helping with planning at home while recovering)
  • Role rehearsal – practising new roles (a new mother bathing her baby with help)
  • Problem solving and time management – help prioritise tasks; share responsibilities among family members
  • Support caregivers – teaching, respite care, community and social services, support groups
  • Involve the family in planning; encourage open communication about changed roles
  • Encourage gradual return to usual roles as health improves (work, social activities)
  • Refer to social workers and vocational rehabilitation when needed

Conclusion Roles may be primary, secondary, tertiary or the sick role, and role conflict, ambiguity, strain, overload and transitions cause stress; nurses help by assessing roles, clarifying expectations, role rehearsal, problem solving, supporting caregivers and encouraging a gradual return to roles.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: State the factors influencing self-concept.
answer_html:
1. Developmental stage – infancy, adolescence (identity formation), old age
  2. Family and significant others – love, acceptance, criticism or neglect
  3. Culture and religion – values, gender roles, beauty standards
  4. Body image changes – surgery, amputation, burns, ageing, pregnancy
  5. Roles – role changes, conflict, loss of job or status
  6. Health and illness – chronic illness, disability, dependence
  7. Experiences of success and failure; achievements at school or work
  8. Socioeconomic status, education and social stigma
  9. Stress and coping ability, personality
  10. Relationships with peers and social support

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is personal identity?
answer_html:
Definition Personal identity is the conscious sense of being a separate, unique individual that remains consistent and continuous over time – "who I am".

Includes – name, gender, family, cultural, religious and ethnic belonging, occupation, values and beliefs.

Development – built through life from interaction with others; adolescence is the critical period (Erikson – identity vs role confusion).

Threats – rapid life changes, migration, loss of job, dementia, severe mental illness and serious brain injury; nurses support identity by calling patients by name, respecting their beliefs and choices, and encouraging familiar routines and personal belongings.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain sexual development across the life span. Describe the nursing assessment of sexual health and the role of the nurse in promoting sexual health, including prevention of sexually transmitted infections and unwanted pregnancy.
answer_html:
Introduction Sexuality is a natural and important part of human life at every age. It includes physical, emotional, social and spiritual aspects – gender identity and roles, relationships, intimacy and reproduction. Illness, treatment and hospitalisation can affect it. Nurses, as health educators and counsellors, address sexual health in a professional, respectful, confidential and non-judgemental way.

PART A – DEFINITIONS

  • Sexuality – a central aspect of being human throughout life, encompassing sex, gender identities and roles, sexual orientation, intimacy, pleasure and reproduction, expressed in thoughts, feelings, beliefs, behaviours and relationships
  • Sexual health – a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality; it requires a positive and respectful approach, and the possibility of safe experiences free of coercion, discrimination and violence

PART B – SEXUAL DEVELOPMENT ACROSS THE LIFE SPAN

1. Infancy and early childhood (0–5 years)

  • Gender identity begins to form by about 2–3 years
  • Natural curiosity about the body; touching the genitals is a normal exploration
  • Children learn modesty and privacy from parents
  • Body safety teaching begins – naming body parts correctly, "safe and unsafe touch", and telling a trusted adult

2. School age (6–12 years)

  • Learning of gender roles from family, school and media
  • Questions about where babies come from – answered simply and honestly
  • Preparation for puberty (especially menstruation in girls) before it begins
  • Continued body-safety education

3. Adolescence (puberty to about 19 years)

  • Puberty – development of secondary sexual characteristics; menarche in girls (around 12–13 years) and nocturnal emissions in boys
  • Sexual feelings and attractions; formation of sexual identity; strong influence of peers and media
  • Risks – early pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), sexual exploitation, misinformation
  • Needs – accurate information about body changes, menstrual hygiene, relationships, consent, contraception and STI prevention; adolescent-friendly health services (e.g. under the national adolescent health programme)

4. Young adulthood (20–40 years)

  • Intimate relationships, marriage, family planning, pregnancy and childbirth
  • Needs – contraception, preconception and antenatal care, infertility counselling, STI prevention

5. Middle adulthood (40–65 years)

  • Menopause in women – hot flushes, vaginal dryness, mood changes; gradual hormonal changes in men
  • Effect of chronic illness (diabetes, hypertension) and medicines on sexual function
  • Changing family roles

6. Older adulthood (above 65 years)

  • Interest in intimacy often continues; physical responses are slower
  • Vaginal dryness, erectile difficulties, effects of illness and drugs, loss of a partner
  • Need for privacy, dignity and respect; avoid assuming that the elderly have no sexual needs

PART C – NURSING ASSESSMENT OF SEXUAL HEALTH

  • Include sexual health as part of the routine health history, in privacy, after explaining why it is asked and with the patient's permission
  • Use open, simple, non-judgemental language; avoid assumptions about marital status or orientation
  • Ask about concerns related to illness, surgery or medicines (e.g. "Some people with diabetes notice changes in sexual function – have you had any concerns?")
  • Reproductive history – menstrual pattern, pregnancies, contraception used
  • STI risk – symptoms (discharge, ulcers, pain), past infections, protection used
  • Signs of abuse or violence – unexplained injuries, fear of the partner, inconsistent history
  • Physical examination and investigations as indicated (by trained staff, with a chaperone)
  • Maintain confidentiality of all information

Common nursing diagnoses – Sexual dysfunction r/t effects of medication; Ineffective sexuality pattern r/t fear of pain after surgery; Deficient knowledge regarding contraception; Risk for infection r/t unprotected intercourse

PART D – ROLE OF THE NURSE IN PROMOTING SEXUAL HEALTH

1. Health education and counselling
