  • Puberty education, menstrual hygiene, body changes and emotional development for adolescents
  • Healthy relationships, consent and respect; avoiding coercion
  • Use counselling frameworks such as PLISSIT (permission, limited information, specific suggestions, intensive therapy referral)

2. Prevention of sexually transmitted infections

  • Teach safer sex – abstinence, mutual faithfulness and correct, consistent condom use
  • Early diagnosis and complete treatment of STIs, including treatment of partners
  • Vaccination – hepatitis B and HPV (prevents cervical cancer)
  • Encourage HIV testing and counselling and syphilis screening in pregnancy
  • Remove stigma; maintain confidentiality

3. Prevention of unwanted pregnancy

  • Counselling on contraceptive choices – condoms, oral pills, weekly non-hormonal pill, injectable contraceptives, intrauterine devices (Copper-T), emergency contraception, and permanent methods (tubectomy, vasectomy) for those who have completed their families
  • Information on safe abortion services within the law and post-abortion contraception
  • Spacing of births for maternal and child health

4. Care during illness and hospitalisation

  • Discuss the effects of illness and treatment (heart disease, diabetes, cancer, stoma, hysterectomy, mastectomy) and when normal activity can be resumed, as advised by the doctor
  • Provide privacy in the ward; respect intimacy needs of long-stay patients and partners
  • Address body image concerns after surgery

5. Protection from abuse and exploitation

  • Teach children body safety; recognise and report child sexual abuse as required by law (POCSO Act, 2012)
  • Recognise and support survivors of sexual violence; refer to one-stop centres, counsellors and legal aid
  • Maintain safe, respectful workplaces (prevention of sexual harassment)

6. Referral – to gynaecologists, urologists, counsellors, sexual health clinics or psychiatrists for complex problems

7. Professional conduct

  • Confidentiality, respect for diversity and the patient's values, awareness of one's own attitudes, and maintenance of professional boundaries

PART E – Counselling points for common conditions (as advised by the doctor)

  • Heart disease (after myocardial infarction) – fear is common; normal activity is usually resumed gradually when the patient can manage moderate exertion (e.g. climbing two flights of stairs) without symptoms; report chest pain
  • Diabetes – may cause erectile difficulty in men and repeated vaginal infections in women; good sugar control and referral help
  • After hysterectomy or pelvic surgery – avoid intercourse for the period advised (often about 6 weeks)
  • Mastectomy and stoma – address body image; involve the partner; practical advice on clothing and appliance care
  • Spinal cord injury and stroke – adaptations, rehabilitation and specialist counselling
  • Medicines – report side effects affecting sexual function; do not stop medicines without advice, as alternatives may be possible

PART F – Barriers to discussing sexual health and how to overcome them

  • Barriers – embarrassment of nurse or patient, lack of knowledge, cultural taboos, lack of privacy, fear of offending, lack of time, assumptions about age or marital status
  • Overcoming them – training and self-awareness, using a framework (PLISSIT), choosing a private setting, offering a same-gender nurse when preferred, using simple and respectful words, and giving written information

PART G – Legal and ethical points

  • Confidentiality and consent for examinations; a chaperone for intimate examinations
  • POCSO Act, 2012 – mandatory reporting of sexual offences against children
  • Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (amended 2021) – abortion services only by authorised providers within the law
  • PCPNDT Act, 1994 – sex determination of the fetus is prohibited

Conclusion Sexual development continues from infancy to old age with changing needs at each stage; the nurse assesses sexual health privately and non-judgementally and promotes it through education, counselling (PLISSIT), STI prevention, contraception counselling, support during illness, protection from abuse and appropriate referral, while maintaining confidentiality and professional boundaries.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define sexual health. Explain the factors affecting sexuality.
answer_html:
Introduction Sexual health is a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality – not merely the absence of disease or dysfunction. It requires a positive and respectful approach to sexuality and relationships, and the possibility of safe experiences, free of coercion, discrimination and violence. Sexual health also includes the ability to make informed reproductive choices.

Factors affecting sexuality

1. Physiological factors

  • Age and developmental stage – puberty, pregnancy, postpartum period, menopause, ageing
  • Hormonal changes – thyroid disorders, diabetes, menopause
  • Chronic illness – diabetes (nerve and blood vessel damage), heart disease (fear of chest pain), arthritis (pain and stiffness), kidney failure, respiratory disease (breathlessness), cancer
  • Neurological conditions – stroke, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis
  • Surgery – hysterectomy, mastectomy, prostatectomy, colostomy – affecting function or body image
  • Pain, fatigue and disability
  • Medications – antihypertensives, antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioids, hormones, chemotherapy
  • Alcohol, tobacco and substance use

2. Psychological factors

  • Self-concept and body image – feeling unattractive after surgery or weight change
  • Stress, anxiety and depression
  • Fear – of pain, of pregnancy, of infection, of a heart attack
  • Past traumatic experiences including abuse
  • Knowledge and attitudes – myths, misinformation, guilt

3. Relationship factors

  • Quality of the relationship, communication, trust, conflict, separation or loss of a partner

4. Socio-cultural and religious factors

  • Cultural norms and taboos about discussing sexuality; gender roles and expectations
  • Religious beliefs about marriage, contraception and sexual behaviour
  • Family values, education and the influence of media
  • Socioeconomic status – housing, privacy, access to health services and contraception

5. Environmental factors

  • Lack of privacy in hospitals, shared housing or crowded homes
  • Long hospitalisation, separation from the partner

6. Legal and ethical factors

  • Laws on age of consent, marriage, abortion and protection from violence

Nurse's role

  • Assess these factors sensitively; provide accurate information; review medicines; address body image; refer to specialists; ensure privacy; maintain confidentiality

Clues that a patient may have sexual health worries – indirect questions ("Will I be normal after this operation?"), jokes, anxiety before discharge, or stopping a medicine without explanation; the nurse responds by giving permission to talk and offering information.

Conclusion Sexual health is physical, emotional, mental and social well-being related to sexuality, and it is influenced by physiological factors (age, illness, surgery, drugs), psychological factors (self-image, stress, fear, past trauma), relationships, culture and religion, environment and law.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain how a nurse should deal with inappropriate sexual behaviour of a patient.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses sometimes face inappropriate sexual behaviour from patients – remarks, jokes, requests, touching or exposure. It may be caused by illness (confusion, dementia, brain injury, mental illness, drugs causing disinhibition) or may be intentional. The nurse must protect her own safety and dignity while continuing to give professional care.

1. Examples

  • Suggestive comments, jokes or questions about the nurse's private life
  • Requests for unnecessary intimate care; deliberate touching of the nurse
  • Exposing oneself; sexual gestures or advances; showing obscene material

2. Immediate response

  • Stay calm and maintain a professional manner; do not laugh, ignore, encourage or react with anger
  • Set limits clearly and firmly – describe the behaviour and state that it is not acceptable: "Please stop. This behaviour is not acceptable. I am here to care for you."
  • Redirect the patient to the task or another topic
  • If the patient persists or you feel unsafe, stop the care and leave the room; return with a colleague

3. Protective measures

  • Give intimate care with a chaperone or a second staff member where needed
  • Keep the door or curtain partly open when appropriate; maintain professional boundaries in conversation and touch
  • Do not share personal information

4. Assess the cause

  • Look for delirium, dementia, head injury, mania, side effects of drugs, loneliness or misunderstanding of care (e.g. confusion during bathing)
  • In confused patients, behaviour is not deliberate – use simple explanations, distraction, consistent caregivers and treat the cause

5. Report and document

  • Inform the nurse in charge and the doctor; record the behaviour objectively (exact words and actions, time, response)
  • Plan a consistent team approach (care plan) so that all staff respond in the same way
  • Serious incidents such as assault are reported as per hospital policy and law (the Internal Complaints Committee or police as appropriate)

6. Support for staff

  • Staff may feel upset or embarrassed; offer debriefing and support; change assignments if needed
  • Training in recognising and managing such behaviour

7. Respect for the patient

  • Even while setting limits, treat the patient with dignity; avoid gossip and labelling

Conclusion When a patient behaves inappropriately, the nurse stays calm and professional, sets clear limits, redirects or leaves if necessary, uses a chaperone, assesses medical causes such as confusion or disinhibition, reports and documents objectively and follows a consistent team plan, while maintaining the patient's dignity.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is the PLISSIT model?
answer_html:
PLISSIT is a model for counselling about sexual concerns, developed by Jack Annon (1976). It has four levels:

  1. P – Permission – the nurse gives permission to talk about sexual concerns and reassures that they are normal
  2. LI – Limited Information – gives factual information about how the illness, surgery or medicine may affect sexuality
  3. SS – Specific Suggestions – gives practical advice for the particular problem (e.g. timing, rest, managing pain or fatigue, lubricants)
  4. IT – Intensive Therapy – refers to specialists (counsellor, sex therapist, psychiatrist) for complex problems

Most nurses can provide the first three levels.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: List the methods of contraception.
answer_html:
1. Temporary (spacing) methods

  • Barrier – male and female condoms, diaphragm
  • Hormonal – combined oral contraceptive pills, progestin-only pills, injectable contraceptive (every 3 months), implants
  • Non-hormonal weekly pill – centchroman (ormeloxifene)
  • Intrauterine devices – Copper-T (including postpartum IUCD), hormonal intrauterine system
  • Natural methods – calendar (standard days) method, cervical mucus method, lactational amenorrhoea method
  • Emergency contraception – emergency contraceptive pill (as early as possible, within 72 hours) or Copper-T within 5 days

2. Permanent methods

  • Female sterilisation (tubectomy) – laparoscopic or minilaparotomy
  • Male sterilisation (vasectomy) – including no-scalpel vasectomy

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: What is sexual harassment at the workplace? State the main provisions of the law in India.
answer_html:
Definition Sexual harassment is any unwelcome sexually determined behaviour – physical contact and advances, a demand or request for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, showing pornography, or any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature.

Law – the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act):

  • Every workplace with 10 or more employees must form an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC), headed by a senior woman employee and including an external member from an NGO or similar body
  • A Local Committee at district level handles complaints from smaller workplaces
  • A complaint is made in writing, usually within 3 months of the incident
  • Employers must prevent harassment, display information and conduct awareness programmes
  • Hospitals – including nurses and patients' complaints – fall under this law

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the sources and indicators of stress and the nursing assessment of a patient under stress. Describe coping strategies, stress management techniques and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Stress is part of everyday life, and illness and hospitalisation are major stressors. A moderate amount of stress can motivate a person (eustress), but excessive or prolonged stress (distress) harms physical and mental health, slows recovery and reduces cooperation with treatment. Nurses help patients recognise, reduce and cope with stress.

PART A – DEFINITIONS

  • Stress – the non-specific response of the body to any demand placed on it (Hans Selye); a state of tension when demands exceed a person's resources
  • Stressor – any event, situation or stimulus that causes stress
  • Adaptation – the process by which a person adjusts to stressors to maintain balance (homeostasis)
  • Coping – the thoughts and actions a person uses to manage stressful demands

PART B – SOURCES AND TYPES OF STRESSORS (brief)

  • Internal (fever, pain, hunger, fear, emotions) and external (noise, heat, family conflict, financial problems)
  • Developmental (adolescence, marriage, parenthood, retirement) and situational (accident, illness, death of a relative, job loss)
  • Physical, chemical, microbiological, physiological, psychological and socio-cultural stressors
  • Hospital stressors for patients – unfamiliar environment, loss of privacy and independence, pain and procedures, fear of diagnosis, separation from family, cost of treatment, uncertainty about the future

PART C – INDICATORS (MANIFESTATIONS) OF STRESS

1. Physiological

  • Increased pulse, BP and respiration, dilated pupils, sweating, dry mouth, cold hands
  • Muscle tension, headache, backache, fatigue
  • Loss of appetite, nausea, indigestion, diarrhoea or constipation; frequent urination
  • Sleep disturbance; raised blood sugar; lowered immunity (frequent infections); menstrual changes
  • Long-term stress contributes to hypertension, peptic ulcer, heart disease and other illnesses

2. Emotional (psychological)

  • Anxiety, fear, irritability, anger, mood swings, depression, guilt, feeling overwhelmed or helpless

3. Cognitive

  • Poor concentration, forgetfulness, indecision, confusion, negative thinking, reduced problem-solving ability

4. Behavioural

  • Restlessness, crying, withdrawal, nail biting, changes in eating and sleeping
  • Increased smoking, alcohol or drug use, accidents, absenteeism, aggressive outbursts

5. Spiritual – questioning the meaning of life or suffering, hopelessness

PART D – NURSING ASSESSMENT OF A PATIENT UNDER STRESS

  • Identify the stressors – "What is worrying you most at present?"
  • The patient's perception of the stressor and its meaning
  • Coping resources – family and social support, finances, health, beliefs, knowledge
  • Coping methods being used and whether they are working
  • Signs of stress (as above); sleep, appetite, vital signs
  • Tools – perceived stress scales, life-event scales (e.g. Holmes–Rahe social readjustment rating scale)

Common nursing diagnoses – Anxiety r/t unknown diagnosis; Ineffective coping r/t multiple stressors; Fear r/t impending surgery; Disturbed sleep pattern r/t hospital environment; Readiness for enhanced coping

PART E – COPING STRATEGIES

1. Problem-focused coping – acting on the cause of stress: gathering information, planning, problem solving, seeking help, changing the situation

2. Emotion-focused coping – managing the feelings: talking about feelings, relaxation, distraction, prayer, positive reappraisal, humour

3. Adaptive and maladaptive coping

  • Adaptive – exercise, talking with others, problem solving, hobbies, spiritual practices, healthy routines
  • Maladaptive – prolonged denial, substance misuse, overeating or not eating, social withdrawal, aggression, excessive sleep
  • Defence mechanisms (unconscious) – denial, projection, rationalisation, regression – may protect temporarily but should not replace active coping

PART F – STRESS MANAGEMENT TECHNIQUES

  1. Relaxation techniques – slow deep (diaphragmatic) breathing, progressive muscle relaxation (tensing and relaxing muscle groups in turn), guided imagery, meditation, yoga and pranayama
  2. Physical exercise – walking, yoga; adequate sleep, balanced diet, limiting tea, coffee and alcohol; no smoking
  3. Time management – prioritising tasks, realistic goals, breaks, learning to say no
  4. Social support – family, friends, support groups; sharing feelings
  5. Cognitive techniques – positive self-talk, reframing negative thoughts, problem-solving skills
  6. Recreation and diversion – music, reading, hobbies, games, humour, play for children
  7. Spiritual practices – prayer, worship, spiritual reading
  8. Information and health education – knowing what to expect (e.g. pre-operative teaching) reduces fear
  9. Counselling and crisis intervention; referral to mental health professionals when needed
  10. Complementary methods – massage, music therapy, aromatherapy, biofeedback

PART G – ROLE OF THE NURSE

  • Orient the patient to the ward and staff; explain procedures and the plan of care
  • Provide privacy, comfort and pain relief; promote sleep (reduce noise and light at night)
  • Listen actively; allow expression of feelings; give honest, simple information
  • Involve the family; allow familiar objects and flexible visiting where possible
  • Respect cultural and religious needs; arrange spiritual support
  • Teach relaxation and coping skills; encourage self-care and participation in decisions
  • Create a therapeutic environment and provide recreation
  • Recognise severe stress reactions (panic, depression, hopelessness) and refer early
  • Care for her own stress – rest, teamwork, support and healthy habits

PART H – Steps of progressive muscle relaxation (to teach patients)

  1. Choose a quiet room; sit or lie comfortably; loosen tight clothing; close the eyes and breathe slowly
  2. Tense the muscles of the feet for about 5–10 seconds, then relax them for 20–30 seconds and notice the difference
  3. Move upwards in turn – calves, thighs, buttocks, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, neck and face – tensing and relaxing each group
  4. Finish with a few slow, deep breaths; practise 10–20 minutes daily

PART I – Stress in special groups

  • Children – separation from parents causes separation anxiety (protest, despair, detachment); allow parents to stay, use play, keep routines, explain procedures simply
  • Adolescents – worry about appearance, privacy and peers; allow contact with friends and involve them in decisions
  • Elderly – multiple losses, sensory problems and unfamiliar surroundings may cause confusion under stress; orient often and involve the family
  • Critically ill patients – noise, lights, tubes and inability to speak cause intense stress; explain, reassure, provide means of communication and rest

PART J – Example: a patient before surgery

  • Stressors – fear of anaesthesia, pain, the outcome, the cost and absence from work
  • Signs – raised BP and pulse, poor sleep, repeated questions, irritability
  • Interventions – pre-operative teaching, meeting the anaesthetist, explaining what will happen, teaching deep breathing and relaxation, allowing family presence and prayer, giving prescribed premedication
  • Evaluation – the patient says he feels calmer, sleeps well and his vital signs are within his normal range

PART K – Health education for stress prevention

  • Teach patients and families to recognise early warning signs of stress (poor sleep, irritability, headaches)
  • Encourage regular exercise, adequate sleep, balanced meals, hobbies and time with family and friends
  • Discourage the use of alcohol, tobacco or sleeping pills to cope

  • Inform about counselling services, helplines and support groups available in the community

  • Practise slow breathing for a few minutes during stressful moments, such as before an injection or an examination

Conclusion Stress is the body's non-specific response to demands; it arises from many internal, external, developmental and situational stressors and shows itself through physiological, emotional, cognitive, behavioural and spiritual indicators; the nurse assesses stressors and coping, supports problem-focused and emotion-focused coping, teaches stress management techniques and provides a therapeutic, supportive environment.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the general adaptation syndrome (GAS).

diagram.caption: Stages of general adaptation syndrome
labels: graph of resistance to stress over time
alarm reaction with initial drop then rise
stage of resistance at a high level
stage of exhaustion with fall below normal

answer_html:
Introduction The general adaptation syndrome (GAS) was described by Hans Selye (1956). It is the generalised, non-specific physiological response of the whole body to stress, produced mainly through the sympathetic nervous system and the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis. It occurs in three stages.

1. Stage of alarm reaction

  • The body recognises the stressor and prepares for "fight or flight"
  • Hypothalamus → sympathetic stimulation → adrenaline and noradrenaline from the adrenal medulla
  • Pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol (raises blood sugar, reduces inflammation) and aldosterone (retains sodium and water)
  • Signs – increased heart rate, BP and respiration, dilated pupils, raised blood sugar, sweating, increased muscle tension, alertness; blood is diverted to the heart, brain and muscles
  • Has a brief shock phase (resistance falls) followed by a counter-shock phase
  • Lasts from minutes to hours; if the stressor is overwhelming, death may occur

2. Stage of resistance

  • The body tries to adapt and restore balance
  • Hormone levels, vital signs and blood sugar move back towards normal
  • Resistance to the particular stressor is high, but resistance to other stressors is lowered
  • If adaptation succeeds, the person recovers; if the stressor continues, energy is gradually used up – prolonged stress may lead to "diseases of adaptation" such as hypertension, peptic ulcer and lowered immunity

3. Stage of exhaustion

  • The body's adaptive energy is used up; it can no longer resist
  • Signs of the alarm stage reappear; the person becomes fatigued and ill
  • If the stressor is not removed, death may result; with rest and support, recovery is possible

Nursing implications

  • Recognise signs of each stage – e.g. tachycardia, raised blood sugar and anxiety after injury or surgery
  • Reduce stressors – relieve pain, give information, ensure rest and sleep
  • Support coping and adaptation; provide good nutrition, fluids and oxygen
  • Prevent exhaustion – plan rest periods, limit unnecessary procedures, involve the family
  • Monitor for complications of prolonged stress (infection, ulcers, high BP)

Conclusion The general adaptation syndrome is the whole-body response to stress described by Selye, with an alarm reaction (fight or flight), a stage of resistance (adaptation) and, if stress continues, a stage of exhaustion; nursing care aims to reduce stressors and support adaptation before exhaustion sets in.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the local adaptation syndrome (LAS).
answer_html:
Introduction The local adaptation syndrome (LAS) is the localised response of a tissue, organ or body part to stress such as injury or infection. If the local response cannot control the stressor, the general adaptation syndrome is activated.

1. Characteristics of LAS

  • Localised – does not involve the whole body
  • Adaptive – needs a stressor to stimulate it
  • Short-term – does not last indefinitely
  • Restorative – helps to restore balance (homeostasis) in the affected area

2. Examples of LAS

a. Reflex pain response

  • A local response of the nervous system to pain – an immediate, automatic movement away from the stimulus, e.g. pulling the hand away from a hot object
  • Protects the tissue from further damage

b. Inflammatory response

  • A protective response of tissue to injury or infection, which localises and destroys the harmful agent and prepares for repair
  • Stage 1 – Vascular and cellular response
    • Brief vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation and increased capillary permeability
    • Cardinal signs – redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function
    • White blood cells (neutrophils, then macrophages) move to the area and phagocytose microorganisms and debris
  • Stage 2 – Exudate formation
    • Fluid, cells and dead tissue collect – serous (clear), serosanguineous (pink), sanguineous (bloody) or purulent (pus)
  • Stage 3 – Reparative (healing) phase
    • Regeneration of damaged cells, or replacement by granulation tissue and a fibrous scar

c. Other local responses – blood clotting at a wound, formation of a callus on the skin due to repeated friction, constriction of the pupil in bright light

3. Nursing implications

  • Rest and elevation of the inflamed part; application of cold or heat as appropriate and as ordered
  • Wound care – keep clean, observe exudate, change dressings aseptically
  • Pain relief; adequate nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc) for healing
  • Observe for spread of infection – fever, rising pulse, spreading redness – which shows that the general response is being activated

4. Relationship with GAS – if local responses fail (for example, a wound infection spreads), the whole body responds with fever, raised white cell count, rapid pulse and malaise – the general adaptation syndrome is activated.

Conclusion The local adaptation syndrome is a localised, adaptive, short-term and restorative response, such as the reflex pain response and the inflammatory response with its vascular-cellular, exudate and repair stages; nursing care supports these responses through rest, wound care, pain relief, nutrition and observation for spread.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the therapeutic environment and the role of recreation in patient care.
answer_html:
Introduction A therapeutic environment is the physical and psychosocial setting that promotes healing, safety, comfort and well-being. Florence Nightingale emphasised that the nurse's work is to put the patient in the best condition for nature to heal. Recreation forms part of this environment and helps patients cope with stress and boredom.

A. Physical environment

  • Cleanliness of the ward, linen and equipment; good ventilation
  • Comfortable temperature and humidity
  • Lighting – natural daylight during the day, dim lights at night; avoid glare
  • Noise control – soft voices, quiet trolleys, phones on low volume, alarms answered promptly, quiet hours at night
  • Safety – call bell within reach, side rails, non-slip floors, clear passages, good lighting at night
  • Privacy – screens and curtains, proper draping, closed doors during procedures
  • Pleasant surroundings – soothing colours, plants, pictures, clean toilets, access to gardens or windows
  • Comfortable furniture, space for personal belongings, orientation aids (clock, calendar)

B. Psychosocial environment

  • A caring, respectful attitude of all staff; calling patients by name
  • Clear communication and information about care and routines
  • Family involvement and suitable visiting arrangements
  • Predictable routines that still allow choices
  • Respect for culture, religion and personal values; spiritual support
  • Trust, confidentiality and dignity

C. Recreation

1. Meaning – activities done for enjoyment, relaxation and diversion from illness

2. Benefits

  • Reduces stress, anxiety and boredom; improves mood and sleep
  • Encourages socialisation and a sense of normal life
  • Maintains mental alertness, motor skills and self-esteem; aids rehabilitation

3. Types of recreational (diversional) activities

  • Reading, newspapers, music, radio and television
  • Indoor games – carrom, chess, cards, puzzles, ludo
  • Arts and crafts – drawing, knitting, embroidery, clay work; gardening
  • Group activities – celebrations of festivals, singing of bhajans or prayers, discussions
  • Play for children – toys, play rooms, story telling, drawing; therapeutic play to prepare children for procedures
  • Short walks and outings for long-stay patients; occupational therapy

4. Nurse's role

  • Select activities suited to the patient's age, condition, interests, ability and culture
  • Ensure safety and infection control (clean toys and games, especially in children's wards)
  • Avoid over-exertion; plan activities between treatments and rest
  • Encourage participation and involve families and volunteers
  • Arrange a recreation room or day room where possible

Conclusion A therapeutic environment combines a clean, safe, quiet, well-lit and private physical setting with a caring, respectful psychosocial climate, and recreation – reading, music, games, crafts, group activities and play – reduces stress and boredom and promotes healing, socialisation and rehabilitation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Name the types (dimensions) of adaptation with examples.
answer_html:
1. Physiological adaptation – the body adjusts to maintain homeostasis, e.g. faster breathing during exercise, shivering in cold, increased red cells at high altitude
  2. Psychological adaptation – emotional and mental adjustment through coping and defence mechanisms, e.g. learning to live with diabetes
  3. Developmental adaptation – adjusting to the tasks of each stage of life, e.g. puberty, parenthood, retirement
  4. Sociocultural adaptation – adjusting to the norms and expectations of society or a new culture, e.g. a migrant learning the local language
  5. Technological adaptation – adjusting to new technology, e.g. using an insulin pen or a home oxygen concentrator
  6. Spiritual adaptation – finding meaning and peace in difficult experiences

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define crisis. Name its types.
answer_html:
Definition A crisis is a state of disequilibrium that occurs when a person faces a stressful event and his usual coping methods fail; it usually resolves (positively or negatively) within about 4–6 weeks.

Types

  1. Maturational (developmental) crisis – occurs during expected life transitions, e.g. adolescence, marriage, parenthood, retirement
  2. Situational crisis – caused by an unexpected event, e.g. serious illness, accident, job loss, divorce, death of a loved one
  3. Adventitious (social) crisis – caused by unplanned events affecting many people, e.g. floods, earthquakes, epidemics, war, violence

Crisis intervention – short-term help to restore the person's coping and safety: assessment, support, problem solving and use of resources.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Concepts of Cultural Diversity and Spirituality
question: Explain cultural diversity and cultural competence. Describe culturally responsive (transcultural) nursing care, including cultural assessment and the use of interpreters.
answer_html:
Introduction India is one of the most culturally diverse countries in the world, with many religions, languages, castes, tribes, food habits and health beliefs. Patients bring these differences into the hospital. Care that ignores culture leads to misunderstanding, mistrust and poor outcomes, while culturally responsive care improves trust, cooperation and recovery.

PART A – BASIC TERMS

  • Culture – the learned, shared and transmitted values, beliefs, norms and practices of a group that guide thinking and behaviour
  • Subculture – a group within a larger culture with its own distinct features, e.g. a tribal community, a religious sect, or an occupational group such as nurses
  • Cultural diversity – the variety of cultural differences among people – religion, ethnicity, language, region, caste, socioeconomic status, gender, age and lifestyle
  • Race – a classification of people by inherited physical features (often a social category rather than a biological one); ethnicity – a shared ancestry, language, traditions and sense of belonging
  • Transcultural nursing – a field of nursing that studies cultures and provides culturally congruent care (developed by Madeleine Leininger)

PART B – CULTURAL COMPETENCE

  • Cultural competence is the ongoing process in which the nurse strives to work effectively within the cultural context of each patient, family and community
  • Campinha-Bacote's model – five components (memory aid ASKED):
    1. Cultural Awareness – examining one's own beliefs, biases and assumptions
    2. Cultural Skill – ability to collect cultural data and perform a culturally sensitive assessment
    3. Cultural Knowledge – learning about other cultures' beliefs, health practices and disease patterns
    4. Cultural Encounters – direct interactions with people of different cultures
    5. Cultural Desire – genuine motivation to want to become culturally competent
  • Cultural humility – a lifelong attitude of self-reflection, respect and learning from patients

PART C – LEININGER'S MODES OF CULTURE CARE ACTION

  1. Culture care preservation/maintenance – support helpful or harmless practices, e.g. family members staying with the patient, prayer, a safe traditional postnatal diet
  2. Culture care accommodation/negotiation – adapt hospital routines to cultural needs, e.g. vegetarian or halal food, prayer times, a female nurse for women, fasting adjustments with medicines
  3. Culture care repatterning/restructuring – gently help change harmful practices with explanation and respect, e.g. discarding colostrum, giving pre-lacteal feeds, applying cow dung on the umbilical cord, delaying care for "evil eye" beliefs

PART D – CULTURAL ASSESSMENT The Giger and Davidhizar transcultural assessment model describes six cultural phenomena:

  1. Communication – language, dialect, literacy, eye contact, touch, use of silence, gestures
  2. Space – comfort with personal space, touch and physical closeness; modesty
  3. Social organisation – family structure, who makes decisions, gender roles, religion, community ties
  4. Time – orientation to past, present or future; attitude to appointments and schedules
  5. Environmental control – health beliefs (biomedical, magico-religious such as evil eye or karma, holistic such as hot and cold foods or Ayurveda), use of traditional healers and home remedies
  6. Biological variations – genetic disease risks (e.g. sickle cell disease in some tribal groups, thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency), skin assessment in dark skin (check mucosa, nail beds, palms), dietary patterns, drug responses

Practical questions

  • Preferred language and name; religion and its practices; dietary restrictions and fasting (e.g. Ramadan, Navratri)
  • Who should receive information and make decisions; preference for a same-gender caregiver
  • Beliefs about the cause of illness and expected treatment; home remedies being used
  • Customs related to birth, menstruation, illness and death

PART E – CULTURALLY RESPONSIVE NURSING CARE

1. Attitudes

  • Self-awareness; avoid ethnocentrism (judging others by one's own culture), stereotyping and cultural imposition
  • Treat every patient with equal respect, without discrimination by religion, caste, gender, language or economic status

2. Communication

  • Use respectful greetings and titles; be sensitive to eye contact, touch and gestures
  • The LEARN model – Listen to the patient's view, Explain your view, Acknowledge differences and similarities, Recommend treatment, Negotiate a plan acceptable to both

3. Use of interpreters

  • Use a trained medical interpreter where possible; avoid using children or relatives for sensitive matters
  • Speak to the patient, not to the interpreter; use short sentences and simple words
  • Check understanding by the teach-back method; maintain confidentiality; use a same-gender interpreter when appropriate
  • Provide written material in the local language with pictures

4. Daily care

  • Diet – respect vegetarian, halal, Jain and other diets; plan medicines around fasting with the doctor
  • Modesty and privacy – same-gender caregivers when possible; cover the body during care
  • Religious practices – allow prayer, holy books and religious objects; do not remove sacred threads or amulets without permission (secure them if they must be moved for a procedure)
  • Family involvement – many Indian families make decisions together; involve them while respecting the patient's own wishes
  • End-of-life and death rituals – allow last rites and family customs where safe

5. Health education – use culturally familiar examples, local foods and the patient's language; build on safe traditional practices

PART F – BENEFITS

  • Greater trust and satisfaction, better communication and adherence, fewer misunderstandings, improved outcomes and reduced health inequalities

PART G – Examples of cultural practices and the nursing response

  • Newborn care – giving honey or water before breastfeeding (pre-lacteal feeds) and discarding colostrum → repattern with explanation of the value of colostrum and early breastfeeding; oil massage → preserve (with safe oil and warmth); kajal in the eyes → gently discourage because of infection and lead risk
  • Postnatal confinement (rest for about 40 days) → preserve the rest, but ensure good nutrition, hygiene and early mobility
  • Hot and cold food beliefs – e.g. avoiding certain fruits or curd during illness → accommodate by suggesting acceptable alternatives with similar nutrients
  • Evil-eye beliefs – black threads or amulets → preserve if harmless; do not delay medical care
  • Religious needs – fasting, prayer times, Sikh articles of faith (uncut hair, kara), sacred threads, holy water → accommodate and secure items during procedures
  • Death customs – wish to die at home, last rites, holy water, prompt burial or cremation → accommodate as far as hospital rules allow

PART H – Barriers to culturally competent care

  • Language differences and lack of interpreters
  • Lack of knowledge about other cultures; stereotypes and prejudice
  • Time pressure and rigid hospital routines
  • Power imbalance between staff and patients, discrimination based on caste, religion or poverty
  • Overcome through training, self-reflection, interpreters, flexible policies and a respectful hospital culture

PART I – Evaluation of culturally competent care

  • The patient and family feel respected and understood, communicate freely, follow the agreed plan and take part in decisions
  • Cultural needs (diet, prayer, modesty, rituals) are documented in the care plan and met as far as possible

Conclusion Cultural diversity is the variety of cultures among patients, and cultural competence – awareness, skill, knowledge, encounters and desire – enables nurses to give culturally congruent care; using Leininger's preservation, accommodation and repatterning, the six-phenomena cultural assessment, respectful communication and trained interpreters, nurses provide care that respects each patient's culture while protecting health.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Concepts of Cultural Diversity and Spirituality
question: Explain the concept of spirituality and the spiritual needs of patients. Add a note on the factors influencing spirituality.
answer_html:
Introduction Spirituality is a person's search for meaning and purpose in life and a sense of connection with self, others, nature and a higher power. It may or may not be expressed through religion. Serious illness often raises spiritual questions, and spiritual care is part of holistic nursing.

1. Related concepts

  • Faith – belief and trust in something that cannot be proved, such as God or a higher power, or in a set of values
  • Hope – expectation of a positive future; a source of strength in illness
  • Religion – an organised system of beliefs, worship, rituals and community (e.g. Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism)
  • Spiritual well-being – a sense of harmony, peace and purpose, in relation to a higher power (vertical) and to self, others and nature (horizontal)
  • Transcendence, connectedness, love and forgiveness

2. Spiritual needs of patients

  • Meaning and purpose – "Why is this happening to me?"
  • Love and belonging – feeling cared for and not abandoned
  • Forgiveness – giving and receiving forgiveness; freedom from guilt
  • Hope and courage to face illness
  • Connection with God or a higher power through prayer, worship and rituals
  • Peace, dignity and acceptance, especially near death

3. Factors influencing spirituality

  • Developmental stage – children have simple, concrete beliefs; adolescents question; older adults reflect on life and death
  • Family and culture – beliefs learnt in childhood, cultural traditions
  • Religion and the religious community
  • Life experiences – illness, loss, crises and recovery may strengthen or shake faith
  • Personal beliefs and values, education
  • Health status – acute, chronic or terminal illness
  • Hospital environment – routines may limit prayer, fasting or rituals

4. Nursing role

  • Assess spiritual needs using simple questions or tools such as FICA (Faith, Importance, Community, Address in care)
  • Respect beliefs without imposing one's own; provide privacy and time for prayer
  • Allow religious articles, scriptures and music; respect dietary and fasting practices
  • Arrange visits by a spiritual leader of the patient's faith when requested
  • Offer presence and active listening; include spiritual care in the care plan

Conclusion Spirituality is the search for meaning, purpose and connection, closely linked with faith, hope and religion; patients need meaning, love, forgiveness, hope and peace, and their spirituality is shaped by age, family, culture, religion, experiences and health, so nurses assess and respect these needs as part of holistic care.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Concepts of Cultural Diversity and Spirituality
question: Explain spiritual distress and its nursing management. Add a note on near-death experience.
answer_html:
Introduction Spiritual distress is a disturbance in a person's sense of meaning, purpose, faith or connectedness, often caused by serious illness, suffering or loss. It can increase pain, anxiety and hopelessness, and it needs sensitive nursing care.

1. Causes

  • Serious, chronic or terminal illness; severe pain and suffering
  • Loss of a loved one, body part, role or independence
  • Conflict between beliefs and treatment – e.g. blood transfusion, organ donation, termination of pregnancy, end-of-life decisions
  • Separation from the religious community; hospital routines that prevent prayer or rituals
  • Feelings of guilt or punishment

2. Signs

  • Questioning the meaning of life and suffering; "Why has God done this to me?"
  • Anger at God or feeling abandoned or punished
  • Hopelessness, guilt, fear of death
  • Inability or refusal to pray or take part in usual religious practices – or a sudden increased need for them
  • Crying, withdrawal, sleep disturbance; requests for spiritual help

3. Nursing management

  • Assess spiritual concerns gently and privately; recognise signs early
  • Be present and listen actively; allow expression of anger, doubt and fear without judgement or argument
  • Support hope – realistic hope for comfort, relief, reconciliation and peace
  • Facilitate religious practices – prayer, meditation, reading scriptures, devotional music, holy water, prayer beads, fasting, prayer times
  • Arrange spiritual support – priest, maulvi, pandit, granthi, monk or chaplain, as the patient wishes
  • Help with forgiveness and reconciliation with family members
  • Encourage life review (reminiscence) to find meaning and achievements
  • Involve the family and faith community; respect informed decisions based on faith
  • Refer to counsellors when distress is severe; never impose personal beliefs

4. Near-death experience (NDE)

  • A profound experience reported by some people who were close to death or were resuscitated (e.g. after cardiac arrest)
  • Common features – a feeling of peace, a sense of leaving the body, moving through a tunnel towards a bright light, meeting deceased relatives, and a review of life
  • After-effects – reduced fear of death, changed values and priorities; some people may feel confused or disturbed
  • Nursing care – allow the patient to talk freely about the experience, listen without judgement, do not dismiss or over-interpret it, reassure that many people report similar experiences, and offer spiritual support or referral

Conclusion Spiritual distress is a disturbance in meaning, faith or connectedness seen as questioning, anger, guilt and hopelessness; nurses respond with presence, listening, support of hope, facilitation of religious practices and spiritual leaders, and acceptance of experiences such as near-death experiences.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Concepts of Cultural Diversity and Spirituality
question: Differentiate between acculturation and assimilation.
answer_html:
Point Acculturation Assimilation
Meaning Adopting some traits (language, dress, food) of another (dominant) culture through prolonged contact Complete absorption into the dominant culture
Original culture Retained to a large extent Gradually lost
Speed Can occur within one generation Usually takes several generations
Example A migrant family in a city learns the local language and food but keeps its own festivals Descendants of migrants who no longer follow the original language or customs

Related term – enculturation: learning one's own culture from birth through socialisation.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
unit_title: Concepts of Cultural Diversity and Spirituality
question: Define ethnocentrism, stereotyping and cultural imposition.
answer_html:
• Ethnocentrism – the belief that one's own culture is superior and judging other cultures by its standards
  • Stereotyping – assuming that all members of a group are the same, without considering individual differences (e.g. "all elderly people are hard of hearing")
  • Cultural imposition – forcing one's own cultural beliefs and practices on others (e.g. insisting on a diet that is against the patient's religion)
  • Cultural blindness – ignoring cultural differences altogether

Effects – mistrust, poor communication and non-adherence to treatment. Nurses avoid them by practising cultural humility, asking rather than assuming, and treating each patient as an individual.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define nursing theory. Explain its purposes, components and types. Describe Orem's self-care deficit theory and its application in nursing practice.

diagram.caption: Orem's three nursing systems
labels: partly compensatory (nurse and patient share care)
supportive-educative (patient does care with nurse's teaching and guidance)

answer_html:
Introduction Nursing theories give nursing its own body of knowledge. They explain what nursing is, why nurses act as they do and what results they aim for. Theories guide assessment, planning and evaluation, separate nursing from other professions and form the basis of nursing education and research.

PART A – DEFINITION

  • A nursing theory is an organised set of concepts, definitions, relationships and assumptions that presents a systematic view of nursing phenomena in order to describe, explain, predict or prescribe nursing care

PART B – PURPOSES

  1. Provide a framework for nursing practice – guide assessment, interventions and evaluation
  2. Distinguish nursing from other health professions and define its scope
  3. Provide a basis for nursing research and evidence-based practice
  4. Guide curriculum planning and nursing education
  5. Improve communication among nurses with a common language
  6. Promote professional autonomy and accountability
  7. Help in nursing administration – care delivery models, standards and documentation

PART C – COMPONENTS (BUILDING BLOCKS)

  • Concepts – ideas or mental images of a phenomenon (e.g. self-care, adaptation, environment)
  • Definitions – theoretical (meaning) and operational (how it is measured)
  • Propositions – statements describing relationships between concepts
  • Assumptions – statements accepted as true without proof
  • Model – a conceptual framework, often shown as a diagram

PART D – TYPES OF NURSING THEORIES

1. According to scope (level of abstraction)

  • Grand theories – broad and abstract, covering the whole of nursing (Orem, Roy, Rogers, Leininger)
  • Middle-range theories – focus on specific phenomena and are easier to test (Peplau's interpersonal relations, Pender's health promotion, Mishel's uncertainty in illness)
  • Practice (situation-specific) theories – narrow, for particular clinical situations (e.g. a pain-management approach)

2. According to goal

  • Descriptive – describe and explain phenomena
  • Prescriptive – prescribe nursing actions and predict outcomes

3. According to focus (schools of thought)

  • Needs theories – Henderson, Orem, Abdellah
  • Interaction theories – Peplau, King, Orlando
  • Outcome theories – Roy, Johnson, Levine
  • Caring and humanistic theories – Watson, Leininger

PART E – OREM'S SELF-CARE DEFICIT THEORY Developed by Dorothea E. Orem (first described in 1959 and expanded later), it consists of three related theories.

1. Theory of self-care

  • Self-care – activities that individuals start and perform on their own behalf to maintain life, health and well-being
  • Self-care agency – the person's ability to perform self-care
  • Therapeutic self-care demand – the total care actions needed at a particular time
  • Self-care requisites:
    • Universal – needs common to all: sufficient air, water and food; care related to elimination; balance between activity and rest; balance between solitude and social interaction; prevention of hazards; promotion of normal human functioning
    • Developmental – needs related to stages of life (pregnancy, infancy, adolescence, ageing) and events affecting development (loss, illness)
    • Health-deviation – needs arising from illness, injury, disability and treatment – seeking medical care, following treatment, coping with its effects and changed self-image

2. Theory of self-care deficit

  • Nursing is needed when the demands for self-care are greater than the person's ability to meet them – this gap is the self-care deficit
  • Five methods of helping – acting or doing for, guiding, supporting (physically or emotionally), providing a developmental environment, and teaching

3. Theory of nursing systems

  • Wholly compensatory system – the nurse performs all self-care for the patient who cannot do it (e.g. an unconscious patient, a patient under anaesthesia)
  • Partly compensatory system – nurse and patient share self-care activities (e.g. a post-operative patient who can wash his face but needs help to walk)
  • Supportive-educative system – the patient performs self-care with the nurse's teaching, guidance and support (e.g. a newly diagnosed diabetic learning insulin injection, an antenatal mother)

4. Orem's view of the metaparadigm

  • Person – a unified whole with the potential for self-care
  • Environment – conditions that affect the person's ability to perform self-care
  • Health – structural and functional soundness and wholeness
  • Nursing – a helping service that overcomes self-care deficits

PART F – APPLICATION OF OREM'S THEORY IN NURSING PRACTICE

1. In the nursing process

  • Assessment – identify the universal, developmental and health-deviation self-care requisites, the patient's self-care ability and the deficits
  • Diagnosis – state the self-care deficits (e.g. Bathing self-care deficit r/t left-sided weakness)
  • Planning – choose the nursing system and the helping methods
  • Implementation – carry out compensatory or supportive-educative actions
  • Evaluation – judge the increase in the patient's self-care ability

2. Example – a patient with stroke

  • In the acute stage (unconscious) – wholly compensatory care: airway, feeding, hygiene, positioning
  • During recovery – partly compensatory: the patient feeds himself with an adapted spoon while the nurse helps with bathing and walking
  • Before discharge – supportive-educative: teaching the patient and family exercises, safe transfers, diet and medicines

3. In other areas

  • Rehabilitation and chronic illness (diabetes, COPD, stoma care) – promoting independence
  • Community health – health education for self-care
  • Nursing education – curriculum based on self-care; research on self-care ability
  • Administration – planning staff according to the level of patient dependency

4. Strengths and limitations

  • Strengths – simple and practical, applicable in all settings, emphasises independence and patient participation
  • Limitations – in cultures where the family usually provides care (as in India), the idea of self-care must be adapted to include family members

PART G – Other important theories (brief overview)

  • Florence Nightingale – environmental theory: fresh air, light, cleanliness, quiet and nutrition help nature to heal
  • Virginia Henderson – the nurse assists the person in 14 basic activities (breathing, eating, elimination, movement, sleep, dressing, temperature, hygiene, safety, communication, worship, work, play, learning) until independence is regained
  • Hildegard Peplau – interpersonal relations theory, with orientation, identification, exploitation and resolution phases of the nurse–patient relationship
  • Madeleine Leininger – culture care theory (transcultural nursing)
  • Jean Watson – theory of human caring
  • Callista Roy – adaptation model

PART H – Application of theories in other fields of nursing

  • Education – theories organise the curriculum and help students understand the purpose of nursing actions
  • Research – theories generate research questions and are tested by research, building evidence for practice
  • Administration – theories guide the philosophy of nursing services, care delivery models, assessment formats and standards

PART I – Criteria for evaluating a theory

  • Clarity – concepts and relationships are clearly defined
  • Simplicity – few concepts, easy to understand
  • Generality – applicable to many situations
  • Testability – can be tested by research

  • Usefulness – helps improve nursing practice and patient outcomes

  • Consistency – the concepts and propositions do not contradict each other, and the theory fits with nursing's values of holistic, patient-centred care

Conclusion A nursing theory is an organised set of concepts, definitions, propositions and assumptions that describes, explains or prescribes nursing; theories may be grand, middle-range or practice theories, and Orem's self-care deficit theory – with self-care requisites, self-care deficits and wholly compensatory, partly compensatory and supportive-educative systems – guides nurses to meet patients' needs while promoting their independence.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain Roy's adaptation model.
answer_html:
Introduction Sister Callista Roy developed the adaptation model (1970s). It views the person as an adaptive system constantly interacting with a changing environment, and the goal of nursing is to promote adaptation.

1. The person as an adaptive system

  • Input – stimuli from the internal and external environment
  • Control processes – coping mechanisms
  • Effectors – the four adaptive modes
  • Output – responses that are either adaptive (promote integrity) or ineffective
  • Feedback – responses act again as input

2. Stimuli

  • Focal stimulus – the stimulus immediately confronting the person (e.g. pain from a surgical wound)
  • Contextual stimuli – other stimuli present that contribute to the effect (e.g. noisy ward, lack of sleep, fear)
  • Residual stimuli – factors whose effects are unclear (e.g. past experiences, beliefs, attitudes)

3. Coping mechanisms

  • Regulator subsystem – physiological (neural, chemical and endocrine responses)
  • Cognator subsystem – cognitive–emotional (perception, learning, judgement, emotion)

4. Four adaptive modes

  1. Physiological–physical mode – oxygenation, nutrition, elimination, activity and rest, protection, senses, fluids and electrolytes, neurological and endocrine function
  2. Self-concept–group identity mode – physical self (body image, sensation) and personal self (self-consistency, self-ideal, moral–ethical–spiritual self)
  3. Role function mode – performance of primary, secondary and tertiary roles
  4. Interdependence mode – relationships – giving and receiving love, respect and value; significant others and support systems

5. Roy's metaparadigm

  • Person – an adaptive system; Environment – all conditions and stimuli affecting the person; Health – a state and process of being and becoming integrated and whole; Nursing – promotion of adaptation in the four modes

6. Application – nursing process

  • Assessment of behaviour (first level) in the four modes, then assessment of stimuli (second level – focal, contextual, residual)
  • Diagnosis, goal setting, intervention by managing stimuli (altering, increasing, decreasing, removing or maintaining them) and evaluation
  • Example – a woman after mastectomy: physiological (wound pain – analgesia), self-concept (body image – counselling, prosthesis), role (mother and worker – planning help at home), interdependence (husband's support – involve him in teaching)

Conclusion Roy's adaptation model sees the person as an adaptive system responding to focal, contextual and residual stimuli through regulator and cognator coping mechanisms in four adaptive modes – physiological, self-concept, role function and interdependence – and nursing promotes adaptation by managing stimuli.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the metaparadigm of nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction A metaparadigm is the most global and abstract set of concepts that defines the subject matter of a discipline. In nursing, it consists of four concepts (described by Jacqueline Fawcett) that appear in every nursing theory, though each theorist defines them differently.

1. Person (human being)

  • The recipient of nursing care – an individual, family, group or community
  • Seen as a holistic being with physical, psychological, social and spiritual dimensions, with unique needs, values and abilities

2. Environment

  • All the internal and external conditions, circumstances and influences surrounding and affecting the person – physical, social, cultural, economic and political surroundings, including the health care setting

3. Health

  • The person's state of well-being, seen on a continuum from high-level wellness to illness and death
  • Includes physical, mental, social and spiritual well-being (WHO's definition) and the person's own perception of health

4. Nursing

  • The actions, characteristics and attributes of nurses providing care – the science and art of helping people achieve, maintain or restore health, or die peacefully

5. How some theorists view these concepts

  • Nightingale – the environment is central; nursing manipulates the environment so that nature can heal
  • Henderson – nursing assists the person in 14 basic activities until he becomes independent
  • Orem – the person is a self-care agent; nursing meets self-care deficits
  • Roy – the person is an adaptive system; nursing promotes adaptation

6. Importance

  • Unifies the nursing discipline and gives it a distinct focus
  • Provides the base for developing theories, research and curricula
  • Helps nurses see the patient holistically in relation to the environment and health

7. Example – applying the metaparadigm to a patient

  • Person – a 65-year-old widow with diabetes, her beliefs, fears and family
  • Environment – a rural home far from the clinic, a supportive son, limited income
  • Health – her blood sugar control, foot condition and her own view of her health
  • Nursing – teaching insulin injection, diet and foot care, involving the son, linking her to the nearest health centre

Conclusion The nursing metaparadigm comprises person, environment, health and nursing; these four concepts define the focus of the discipline and are interpreted differently by each nursing theory, guiding practice, education and research.

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Explain the concepts of Florence Nightingale's environmental theory.
answer_html:
Nightingale's environmental theory (from Notes on Nursing, 1859) states that nursing is to put the patient in the best possible condition for nature to act upon him, mainly by controlling the environment.

Main concepts (canons)

  1. Ventilation and warmth – fresh, pure air without chilling the patient (the most important)
  2. Light – especially sunlight
  3. Cleanliness of rooms, walls, bed and bedding, and personal cleanliness
  4. Health of houses – pure air, pure water, efficient drainage, cleanliness and light
  5. Avoidance of unnecessary noise
  6. Nutrition and timely taking of food
  7. Variety – change of surroundings, flowers, colours
  8. Observation of the sick and petty management (continuity of care)
  9. Avoiding false reassurance ("chattering hopes and advices")

Metaparadigm – person (recipient of care), environment (central), health (being well and using one's powers), nursing (managing the environment).

subject: Nursing Foundation II (including Health Assessment module)
question: Define the terms concept, proposition, assumption and model in nursing theory.
answer_html:
• Concept – an idea or mental image of a phenomenon, expressed in a word or phrase, e.g. self-care, adaptation, environment, pain
  • Proposition – a statement describing the relationship between two or more concepts, e.g. "When self-care demand exceeds self-care ability, a self-care deficit occurs"
  • Assumption – a statement accepted as true without proof, on which a theory is built, e.g. "Every person has the potential for self-care"
  • Model (conceptual model) – a framework or diagram that shows how concepts are linked, giving a broad view of nursing (e.g. Roy's adaptation model)
  • Theory – an organised set of concepts, definitions and propositions that describes, explains, predicts or prescribes a phenomenon
